News.title: Body of missing grandmother, 68, found inside suitcase dumped in fire station parking lot just hours after she vanished
News.content:
CASE KILLER Body of missing grandmother, 68, found inside suitcase dumped in fire station parking lot just hours after she vanished







Next

THE BODY of a missing grandmother has been found stuffed inside a suitcase that was dumped in a fire station parking lot.

Lorretta M Moody, 68, from Wichita, Kansas, had been reported missing just after 1:30am on September 16, and her body found just hours later around 6pm.



The suitcase was dumped by two people in the parking lot of Wichita Fire Station 22, investigators said.

While a cause of death has not been revealed, it has been ruled a homicide, The Wichita Eagle reported.



When Lorretta was reported missing, she had last been seen in the 2400 block of South Mosley, less than a mile from where her body was found.

Her family described her as 4 feet, 11 inches and weighing 70 pounds or less.

They explained in a Facebook post that she could barely walk on her own and should be on oxygen at all times.

When she was reported missing, Lorretta was reportedly not using a walking aid or getting any additional oxygen or taking her medications.

Investigators have revealed that the two people who took her body in the suitcase and left it at the fire house are not currently considered as suspects.

“We’re not calling them persons of interest; they’re not suspects,” spokesperson Andrew Ford told the news outlet.



“They’re just people we are talking to.”

Their identities have not been released and it remains unclear how they ended up with the body and how it ended up in a suitcase.

The investigation is ongoing as authorities say there is no apparent threat to the public.

Meanwhile, Lorretta’s family have issued heartbreaking tributes on social media.

“Trying to make sense of the senseless. I’ll miss our conversations every single day,” her granddaughter Angelyna Moody-Fletcher wrote.



“I’ll miss how you’d call me at random times and we’d talk on the phone for hours.

“I only hope you truly know how cherished and loved you were by us all Nama.

“I will never stop talking about you. I will never stop fighting for you. I don’t care what it takes.”

Meanwhile, Lorretta’s sister has vowed to get justice.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

“Can’t put into words how much I miss my sister over a very cruel death,” she wrote on Facebook.



“My heart is broken. Rest high, my beautiful angel. We will get justice for you.”

News.title: We live in ‘abandoned’ village next to ‘Ground Zero’ Piddington – but we’re fighting own battle over huge ‘mega-sheds’
News.content:
LOOMING LARGE We live in ‘abandoned’ village next to ‘Ground Zero’ Piddington – but we’re fighting own battle over huge ‘mega-sheds’







Next

LOCALS are up in arms over plans to build a series of mega-warehouses on their doorstep – just a few miles from the “abandoned” village of Piddington.

Residents of Stoke Lyne, Oxfordshire, are fiercely pushing back against a proposal which would see 13 huge warehouses built on a jaw-dropping six million sq ft patch of land.



Developers Tritax Big Box had argued the project on Baynards Green would offer thousands of jobs and business opportunities.

The firm was initially granted planning permission in July 2025 – but this was overturned by Lib Dem councillors in January after seething locals warned of increased traffic and the destruction of greenfield sites.



The refusal triggered an appeal, due to be held next week, but it has since emerged the councillors will no longer be there to defend their position.

Residents of Stoke Lyne will be left to fight their own corner, as the council steps back from debate following “legal and professional advice”.



Located just 10 miles from Piddington – where locals are objecting to a huge migrant centre proposal – Stoke Lyne shares a similar tale of governmental neglect.

It comes after Piddington villagers launched a symbolic referendum last week to declare independence from the UK, with 285 out of 312 voting to take back control of their area and stall plans for the migrant hub.

Stoke Lyne residents see themselves in Piddington’s plight, backed up against a wall by the developer giant and “abandoned” by the council.

Deputy leader Chris Brant said the council had considered the chances of “successfully defending” the refusal, but ultimately decided to back down.



He said earlier this year that the decision had “not been taken lightly”.

“Regrettably, the evidence available to the council is not considered strong enough to provide a realistic prospect of success at appeal,” he said.

Now, community campaign Stoke Lyne Action Team appear to be the village’s only hope against the gargantuan warehouse project.

It has raised an astonishing £50,000 in legal funds through crowdsourcing.



Telling the Mail in a statement, they said: “Cherwell District Council refused every one of them [the warehouses].

“It will not be there to defend them.

“That leaves a community of a few hundred people to face two huge national developers and their planning teams with no local authority standing alongside them.”

Residents fear the complex will take up large swathes of green space that are not even acknowledged in the council’s blueprint yet.

Each warehouse will be an eye-watering 75 ft tall – about the height of “eight coaches stacked on top of each other”.



Baroness Prentis of Banbury, the former MP for the constituency, said: “These warehouses are not in the Local Plan, and to my mind that is where this matter should begin and end.

“Cherwell District Council reached the right conclusion when it refused these applications. It should now stick to its guns and support the people who are relying on it to stand behind that decision.”

Local Craig Mitchell said: “I work in the construction industry and have built industrial distribution centres of a similar size before.”

“The impact of these will be worse than everyone realises.

“They make promises of mitigation during the planning process; it never happens in reality.”



Hugo Brown, a former Cherwell District councillor, added: “It’s acres and acres of open countryside to be built up.

“The planning case for these sheds is unacceptable.”

The council blew through its entire £100,000 budget for planning appeals in the first four months of the last financial year, forcing former PM Keir Starmer to override its autonomy in June.

The appeal could last up to 18 days and is being held by the Planning Inspectorate.

An open letter addressed to the council has been signed by over 400 Stoke Lyne residents, urging them to stand up for the community.



Despite also lacking support from key statutory bodies like Highways England and the Environment Agency, locals remain optimistic.

And their request is not without precedent: a far smaller proposal in the same area was rejected on appeal back in 2019.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

The current project is some 80 times larger.

The Sun has contacted Cherwell District Council for comment.

News.title: No evidence of crime or third-party involvement before three sisters died in sea at Brighton beach as cops give update
News.content:
SEA TRAGEDY No evidence of crime or third-party involvement before three sisters died in sea at Brighton beach as cops give update







Next

AN INVESTIGATION into the deaths of three Brighton sisters has revealed no evidence of criminality or third-party involvement.

Jane Adetoro, 36, Christina Walters, 32, and Rebecca Walters, 31, all drowned off Brighton Beach on May 13.



The post-mortem has found the three sisters all died by drowning, according to cops.

The police investigation found the three women were dropped off near the beach by a taxi on May 12.



Sussex Police have not found any evidence to suggest they visited a nightclub or bar in the area.

It revealed there was “no evidence the women came to harm by any individuals”.



An inquest opened back in May is expected to continue through to October, hoping to establish the facts around the case.

This will include where, when, and how the sisters died.



Ch Supt Adam Hays said: “From the outset of this complex and challenging investigation, we have been acutely aware of the speculation surrounding this incident, the public’s unanswered questions and their desire for answers.

“Our priority throughout has been uncovering the truth for the loved ones of Jane, Rebecca and Christina, because at this incident’s core there has always been a grieving family coming to terms with an unthinkable tragedy and loss.

“However, our inquiries have now concluded, pending any new information coming to light.”

This comes after the girls’ cousin announced their mother had died in a similar tragic way 16 years ago.

Speaking to the Sunday Times, Natalie said her cousins, aged 20, 16, and 15 at the time, never got over the death of their mother Janice Adetoro, who drowned near their family home in Birmingham in 2010.



She said: “To lose their mum at the ages that they were, it was the crucial stages of growing up and becoming young women.

“The years where a mother’s presence and guidance and reassurance and love should be, they didn’t receive that.

“And for them to come to Birmingham, to take that moment that they did within the lake and also to see their mother, I think that there is definitely a connection there.”

This was not long after the girls’ dad, Joseph, spoke out about their deaths, saying “no words can truly describe the pain of losing three daughters” in a heartbreaking tribute reported by the BBC.

“You were more than my daughters: you were my joy, my strength and the beautiful light that filled my life with love,” he wrote in the order of service.



“There are moments when it feels unbearable, but I hold tightly to the memories we shared, the love we knew and the bond that nothing can ever take away.

“Jane, I will never forget your strength. Tina, your kindness touched so many lives. Becky, your warmth and joyful spirit brought happiness wherever you went.”

The women’s cousin said at the funeral that their “lives will never be forgotten” and their “memory will live on forever”.

A GoFundMe page set up by their uncle at the time has raised more than £45,000 towards funeral costs.

The page reads: “No parent should ever have to bury their child, let alone all three.



“While trying to process this unimaginable tragedy, my brother is now also faced with the heartbreaking task of arranging three funerals.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

“As a family, we simply want to give the girls the loving and dignified farewell they deserve.

“Any contribution, no matter how small, will help ease the burden on the family during this incredibly difficult time.”

News.title: Second man arrested over ‘murder’ of mum-of-three after human remains ‘unearthed by wildfire’ at UK beauty spot
News.content:
MURDER PROBE Second man arrested over ‘murder’ of mum-of-three after human remains ‘unearthed by wildfire’ at UK beauty spot







Next

A SECOND man has been arrested on suspicion of murder after a mother’s remains were discovered following a wildfire in London.

Joanne Sheen, 44, was travelling from Fareham to her home city of Southampton, Hampshire, when she vanished on December 2019.



The last known sighting was on December 5, when she travelled from Fareham to Southampton by train with a friend.

She was reported missing by her family in February 2020.



Police have now re-arrested a 56-year-old man from Southampton on suspicion of murder.

This follows the arrest of another 56-year-old man from Southampton on suspicion of conspiracy to commit murder.

The second man has since been released on bail with conditions, pending further enquiries.

It comes after a wildfire exposed a woman’s bones in West London on August 12, with cops racing to identify them.



A fresh probe was launched after the finding, with Hampshire Police confirming earlier this week the bones belong to Jo.

Five people were arrested on suspicion of conspiracy to murder her in 2020, but were released with no further action.

Detective Chief Inspector Toby Elcock, from the Major Crime Team, said: “This is a significant development in what has been a long and complex investigation and provides us with several new lines of enquiry, which we are exploring with our dedicated team.

“While this tragic discovery is not the outcome Joanne’s family, or any of us, had hoped for, we hope the identification of her remains can at least begin to provide some answers after many years of uncertainty.

“Throughout this investigation, Joanne’s family have shown tremendous strength and dignity in the face of unimaginable circumstances, and our thoughts remain with them at this incredibly difficult time.



“As our investigation progresses, we remain committed to establishing exactly what happened to Joanne and ensuring that those responsible are held accountable.”

Police have asked for anyone with information to get in touch with the reference 44200068330, or call Crimestoppers anonymously.

News.title: Twisted rise of shady Brit ‘cocaine-fluencers’ sampling ‘nose beers’ around the world in brazen viral drug vids
News.content:
POWDER KEG Twisted rise of shady Brit ‘cocaine-fluencers’ sampling ‘nose beers’ around the world in brazen viral drug vids







Next

WANDERING through South America, a young Brit has made a name for himself rating one of the continent’s most notorious exports.

The 21-year-old travels from country to country rating cocaine, known in some circles as “packet”. Much to the horror of many critics who fear they could be normalising drug taking.

4 Credit: Tiktok



In one video he asks: “How good is the packet in Brazil?”

Others see him discuss the price and quality of the Class A drug as he makes his way through South and Central America.



And he is far from alone.

Across TikTok and Instagram, British creators are racking up thousands, and sometimes millions, of views with videos joking about “packet”, “nose beers”, lines, “seshes” and afters.

No data found



Another Brit regularly posts ‘sesh’ content to his 16,000 followers. One clip joking about getting “on the packet” on a Wednesday has been viewed 1.1million times.

Meme accounts also rack up tens of thousands of views with posts including: “Morning, because if it was a good morning I would already be sniffing.”

Addiction expert Ian Hamilton warned the content risks making cocaine appear normal and even glamorous to huge audiences.

“It’s glamorising an illegal drug,” says Ian, an Honorary Fellow and Associate Professor in Addiction at the University of York’s Department of Health Sciences.



“It’s dangerous, pushing the reach of harmful substances far beyond the usual word on the street or your mate’s advice, as it was decades ago.

“The social media companies have to do more to tackle this.”

He fears children could be among those watching.



“We know how young some children are when they are accessing these types of information,” he said.

“It is potentially reaching an audience much younger than in the past.

“Early teens are far more suggestible and far more likely to be influenced.”

The 21-year-old Brit is perhaps the most brazen example of the trend.

And lately his videos have taken an even stranger turn.



In a recent podcast interview, he revealed how his bizarre online career began.

“I came out here to start social media and, in all honesty, nothing went well with just normal travel content,” he said.

“So I was a big fan of the packet back home and I decided to test it out on social media.”

It worked.

He said the cocaine videos went “almost viral overnight” after he started posting them earlier this year.



And repeated bans have done little to stop him.

He claims to have lost two Telegram channels with 17,000 and 8,500 members, Instagram accounts with 85,000 and 10,000 followers and TikTok pages followed by 60,000 and 25,000 people.

His first video to take off was filmed in a favela in São Paulo and discussed the price of cocaine in Brazil.

The trips have not been without danger.

He described meeting a dealer in Paraguay before accidentally pulling out the wrong banknote.



“That had someone pull a gun out on me,” he said.

“I’ve never run faster in my life.”

More recently, he said he spent two nights sleeping rough in Mexico after losing his passport and being thrown out of hotels while drunk.

“I was in a very bad way,” he said. “I’ve never felt so vulnerable in my life.”

Yet his notoriety is now helping to pay for the travelling.



“Due to the social media presence, if you’re able to monetise social media, you can just do some promos,” he said.

“As for now, it’s mainly a social media brand deal.”

His Instagram stories and videos have also featured promotions for online poker and gambling sites.

One tells followers: “Use code PACKET to claim a 150% bonus.”

Research suggests young people are already being exposed to drug content on a huge scale.



A UCL study of more than 1,100 British secondary school pupils aged 13 to 18 found six in ten had encountered drug-related content on social media.

Funny posts and memes were the most common type they reported seeing.

Almost a third had encountered adverts for illegal drugs.

Of those youngsters, 83 per cent said the adverts had simply appeared in their feeds rather than being something they searched for.

Ian says cocaine itself has also become far more normalised.



“When I first got involved in this, a lot of people were very wary of cocaine,” he said.

“There has been a definite shift. Cocaine has become very normalised.

“It is accessible, cheap and potent.

“It is still seen as affluent and has an element of risk attached to it which can be seen as quite exciting.”

Britain already has a huge appetite for the drug.



The National Crime Agency estimates around 117 tonnes of cocaine are consumed in the UK every year, with Britain believed to have the second-highest consumption rate in the world.

Deaths involving cocaine have risen ten-fold in a decade and hit another record high last year.

Cocaine was involved in 23 per cent of drug poisoning deaths recorded, up from 20 per cent the year before.

You would not know it from many of the videos.

University of Queensland researchers analysed cocaine-related videos on TikTok and found 66.8 per cent promoted substance use.



Among videos depicting cocaine use, 89.6 per cent portrayed it positively.

Just 4.7 per cent portrayed it negatively.

And it is not just videos of people taking it.

A University of Huddersfield study analysed 90 TikTok posts featuring cocaine producers, distributors and users.

Some showed cocaine being taken to upbeat music with a party going on around it.



Others featured producers and dealers apparently enjoying what they were doing and appearing proud of their part in the trade.

The biggest posts attracted huge audiences, with engagement reaching around 269,000.

Researchers warned social media videos could “humanise” people involved in the cocaine trade, presenting them as ordinary people rather than the criminals usually associated with it.

Similar accounts have pulled in huge audiences before.

A string of British creators have made their names with cocaine and “sesh” content.



Many of the TikTok handles used by those creators at the time are now either unavailable or no longer active under the names previously published.

But the content has not disappeared with them.

And some of what is slipping through goes much further than jokes.

Experts warn that the content is pushing a drug that is more dangerous than ever.

The cocaine being sold in Britain is now far purer than it once was.



“It is a lot purer than it used to be,” Ian said.

“You don’t need a lot because it is potent, cheap and strong.”

Cocaine can cause serious cardiovascular problems and, at its most extreme, a fatal overdose.

Ian warned people do not necessarily need years of heavy consumption before they begin running into problems.

“You don’t need many exposures to become dependent,” he said.



“And that means you are facing the same risks.”

He also questioned whether the huge audiences being built around cocaine could eventually attract the attention of the organised criminals supplying it.

There is no evidence any of the creators featured here are being paid or supplied by criminal gangs, and Ian stressed he could not prove organised crime was involved.

But he said: “I find it hard to believe they aren’t interested in it.

“It would make sense given the reach that they would have.



“Are they supplying them or paying them? We don’t know.”

Ian believes social media firms should be doing far more to stop it.

“The platforms really need to be doing more,” he said.

“It is an illegal drug. It is well within the scope of these providers to make a good dent in it.

“They can do it, but they are choosing not to.”



RECOMMENDED STORIES

A Meta spokesperson: “We have removed the content brought to our attention for violating our policies.”

TikTok were approached for comment.

News.title: Will Britain be attacked by DRONES? Warning UK must brace for strike from sky by terrorists or rogue states
News.content:
Next

THE risk of a devastating drone attack in the UK is “growing every day”, experts have warned.

Drones are a common sight in UK skies for police work, filming, surveys and even deliveries – but there are fears they could be used in a future terror wave on our shores.



Experts warned drones could be used to drop bombs, harmful powders, as kamikaze “suicide” weapons, or even chillingly to “herd” crowds towards danger.

It comes as it was revealed hundreds of drones of unknown origin have menaced British military sites, according to a Freedom of Information request.



Last month’s suspected Russian drone attack on Leipzig Airport further highlighted the threat, as security experts told The Sun Britain is “behind the curve” in stopping a similar attack here.

One former British intelligence officer told The Sun it’s “only a matter of time” before terrorists or rogue states like Russia or Iran use drones in a UK attack now they’re cheaper, more readily available and capable of carrying bigger payloads like explosives, powder or poison.

Another expert said “weaponised drones” can be built by anyone who can turn an off-the-shelf quadcopter into an airborne improvised bomb.

The warnings come despite one defence chief recognising last year that drones “are a real weapon and resource of the future” and “something we all have to take account of”.



Pilots in the UK need official ID to fly drones if they’re over a certain weight, and according to drone laws introduced this year, the Civil Aviation Authority bans flying them above 120m, near airports and crowds or out of your own eyesight.

But security analysts say more needs to be done to protect the UK from drones because “any attacker who wants to use one for terror doesn’t care what the law is”.

The UK’s national terror threat level was raised to “severe” earlier this year after the anti-semitic Golders Green attack.

Military intelligence expert Philip Ingram MBE said: “The threat of attack is high and growing on a daily basis – it has been ever since drones became the centre of attention in Ukraine.”



Outlining some of the chilling methods terrorists could use for a drone attack in Britain, he added: “There could be the dropping off of flamable petrol bombs from a drone into a crowded space – a concert or sports ground – a white powder which people don’t know what it is, which would cause panic, to dropping explosives or even a suicide drone to a crowded place or politcal space.

“Suicide drones with explosives could even be flown in with FPV goggles, in the same way Ukraine or Russia are currently using – that’s very easy.”

Ingram also didn’t rule out terrorists copying Ukraine’s “spider web drone attack”, where drones with explosives are smuggled into a country, unwittingly transported to a target and detonated.

And most alarmingly, he said it’s even possible that drones could be used to push crowds “like sheep” towards an improvised explosive or gun-wielding terrorist.



In previous written evidence submitted to the House of Commons Defence Committee, Dr James Rodgers said nuclear power plants, HS2 or Eurostar trainlines, schools, military bases, banking districts and prisons are all possible attack targets for drones.

The UK has experienced drone chaos before – most famously when a suspected sighting at Gatwick shut down one of the UK’s busiest airports for two days in Christmas 2018.

Despite a lengthy, £1m police investigation, no culprit was ever prosecuted – and experts say the ease of avoiding detection makes drones even more appealing to terrorists.



Professor David Dunn, who provided evidence and wrote recommendations in 2019 for the Government in tackling drone threats, said Britain doesn’t have clear rules and protocols on how to engage with a hostile incident involving the aircraft.

He said: “There’s a new raft of imaginative ways in which drone tech is being developed. Batteries are more efficient, so give greater range, greater durability and there is better tech to avoid them getting jammed.



“There are quadcopters and drones with jet-powered engines, even balloons launching drones to give a greater range – they’re floated into the atmosphere and then the engines start.

Britain's anti-drone countermeaures Despite fears from experts about Britain's preparedness, ministers and authorities say the UK has various anti-drone countermeasures. The RAF say they have a “layered” defence which includes technology for taking over drone communications, a counter-drone system for detection and tracking, and a lightweight missile system. Royal Air Force typhoon aircraft are also equipped with low-cost anti-drone missiles – although these are currently only for operations in the Middle East. The Sun revealed last month how Britain’s biggest airports are also deploying cutting-edge technology to stop hostile drones. Operators at some airport hubs will be able to jam or even launch a mid-air cyber attack to seize control of rogue aircraft. The Army, meanwhile, say they’ve deployed “Halo Shields” – a counter-drone detection system for defending their bases. Defence chiefs also this week revealed their latest anti-drone countermeasure. The “Terrahawk Raptor” is a remote weapon station designed to sit on top of vehicle so it can blast drones out the sky.

The UK has also not spent enough on defending against drones and doesn’t have the right resources to bring down a quadcopter, drone or similar aircraft if they were central to an attack, he said.

Prof Dunn added: “The SDR talked about the need to address drones and their threats – what the government isn’t good at is the funding of resources.

“The air defence of the UK is configured for different sorts of threats – we have aircraft with very expensive missiles to respond to bombers in our airspace -but when you’ve got small, cheap drones, that resource is inappropriate.



“It’s not cost-effective to take out something costing £4,000 with something which costs hundreds of thousands. We are not in a position to respond in an adequate way.”

Criminal use of drones is not a new problem for police and authorities.

Police forces are desperate to crack down on drone smuggling incidents in UK prisons – which surged to more than 1,700 incidents of drugs and weapons being sent behind bars between April 2024 and March 2025.

Keir Starmer’s government outlined a raft of defence measures to tackle drone threats in Labour’s Strategic Defence Review (SDR) last year.

A new security drive this year saw the UK take lessons from Ukraine’s battle-tested tactics in fighting prison incidents.



The Ministry of Defence said in the SDR that in Ukraine, drones ‘kill more people than traditional artillery’.

The Sun revealed last year how Britain’s “weak defences” mean our stockpile of drones “would run out within hours of war starting”.

The Government said supporting Ukraine’s drone warfare is key to keeping up with the technology.

Minister pledged £350m in supporting drone technologies in 2025/26, having committed nearly £400m in 2024/25.

Prof Dunn said drones are changing the face of warfare across the world.



The Government has said it wants to recruit gamers in the Armed Forces as the UK’s new “cyber military recruits” who can help pilot drones.

Prof Dunn added: “Techniques from drone racing 10 years ago are now also part of how they’re operated.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

“Warfare is becoming gamified. Soldiers in Ukraine are given points by how many people they can kill, as a way of incentivising it.

“Warfare has changed from being infantry soldiers fishing across trenches, now there’s a demilitarised zone where it’s just a kill zone for unoccupied vehicles like drones and ground vehicles, where all the supplies and ammunition are supplied by drones.”

News.title: Kim Jong-un fires two ballistic missiles into sea in latest show of strength – after US, Japan and South Korea drills
News.content:
Next

NORTH Korea has fired short-range ballistic missiles towards the East Sea in a military prowess flex aimed at the US.

Shifting the needle from mad to dangerous, Supreme Leader Kim Jong-un ordered the two launches – about three hours apart – despite apparent efforts by the US to revive diplomacy between the two nuclear nations.



The first missile flew about 279 miles, while the second 372 miles, analysis from Japan and South Korea show.

“We are closely monitoring North Korea‘s various activities and maintain the capability and readiness to overwhelmingly respond to provocations, under the staunch South Korea-US combined defence posture,” South Korea’s Joint Chiefs of Staff said.



Japan said the projectile is believed to have fallen outside of its exclusive economic zone, Kyodo News reported.

Defence Minister Shinjiro Koizumi “strongly condemned” the launch, which violates relevant UN Security Council resolutions.



This comes after Donald Trump scaled back a joint military exercise with South Korea last month

Shrugging off the gesture of good will, Kim’s sister and senior official, Kim Yo Jong, warned that it does not change “provocative, aggressive nature.”

And just in case the US was unsure of North Korea’s stance, 10 short-range ballistic missiles were launched toward the sea later on.

On Friday, Kim’s sister again slammed another recent US-led maritime drill in the region as a “frantic military move” meant to prolong the hegemony in the Asia-Pacific area.



The “Pacific Vanguard” exercise brought together the US, South Korea, Japan, Australia, New Zealand and Canada.

She claimed that “regular US-led war rehearsals” are the main source of worsening tensions in the Korean Peninsula and the region.

“Our will to defend our sovereignty will be expressed in clearer action and there will be never ever change in the course of intensifying the nuclear war deterrence,” she said.



It comes just days after the US President revealed plans to meet with the North Korean dictator.

Boasting about their relationship, he said: “You know what, the fact that I get along with him, that’s a good thing not a bad thing.

“He has 57 very powerful nuclear weapons. Should have never allowed it to happen.”

But Trump shared no further details on the plan.

If it happens, it would be their first meeting since Trump’s first term in the White House.



Kim has had his eye on expanding his nuclear arsenal ever since then, and has only deepened his ties with both China and Russia.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

Experts say he likely thinks he now has greater leverage in possible fresh diplomacy with Trump.

Earlier this year, Kim said he could return to talks if the US drops its “hostile policy” against his country and respects what he calls the North’s status as a nuclear state.

News.title: M25 grinds to a halt after THREE crashes as drivers stranded in 90-minute delays & six miles of traffic
News.content:

TRAVEL CHAOS M25 grinds to a halt after THREE crashes as drivers stranded in 90-minute delays & six miles of traffic







Next

A MAJOR motorway has ground to a halt following three separate crashes.

The M25 is currently shut in the clockwise direction between J10 and J11.



Contractors are currently clearing up an oil spill after a multi-vehicle collision.

Drivers have reported 70 minute delays, with queues stretching back to Cobham services.



Further closures have been announced in the anti-clockwise direction between J13 and J12.

Lanes 3, 4 and 5 have been shut whilst emergency services work at the scene.

Motorists should expect 30 minute delays between J15 and J12.

Another closure has been announced between J6 and J5 in the anti-clockwise direction, with cops closing lanes 1, 2 and 3.

Drivers are reportedly facing 90 minute delays and six-mile tailbacks.

News.title: Harry and Meghan's media treatment echoes what happened to Diana, Earl Spencer tells BBC
News.content:
Earl Spencer's interview with the BBC was his first since the Palace issued a strongly worded response to his claims about King Charles.

That statement said the King was "mindful that the pain of fraternal grief can cloud reason, affect judgement and colour memory in ways others do not recognise, even many years after such a loss".

Earl Spencer, in comments first reported on Friday, reacted to it by saying: "Well, is he furious? Is he furious or is he embarrassed?"

He added: "I've only ever had two calls on the line with Prince Charles at any stage of my life.

"I was hyper alert to what he was saying and those are precisely the words that he said and I promise that to you now. Genuinely, that is what he said. I don't hear him saying he didn't say that."

Pressed on whether he had evidence to back up the claim, he said he told family and friends at the time what had been said "because it was so monstrous".

In his response to the Palace disputing his account, Earl Spencer, who shares his first name with the King, said: "They've sort of smudged that one, haven't they? They've said that recollections may vary."

When asked which Charles the public was meant to believe, he said: "I'm telling the truth."

Speaking to the Mail on Sunday, Earl Spencer accused the King of psychological manipulation over the palace's statement.

"It is not every day you wake up to find you've been gaslit by the King," he said. "It was astonishingly provocative and below the belt because it was essentially trying to say I'd lied without the King being able to deny what I'd said".

Journalist Richard Kay, who had been close friends with Diana, also wrote in the newspaper on Sunday that in the week between her death and funeral, Earl Spencer had told him of a "furious row" with Charles.

"It was 'about the boys', but he was reluctant to go further," said Kay, adding that Earl Spencer said the then prince had been "utterly pathetic".

However, speaking to BBC Radio 4's Broadcasting House on Sunday, Dame Julia Cleverdon, a trusted aide and friend of the King, said the claims about his response to Diana's death did not reflect "the language or the behaviours of a man I've known for 40 years".

Earl Spencer's book, Swan Song: Diana, My Sister, is due to be published next week and is expected to be highly critical of the Royal Family.

In further extracts published on Thursday, he claimed how the King "sounded giddily elated" when he called him after Diana's death, alleging Charles sounded like a "lottery winner".

Dame Julia said: "To say that the Prince of Wales was elated and somehow took any pleasure... he was as if a 10-tonne truck had fallen on him.

Her own husband had died a fortnight before Diana and she said Charles "could not have been more supportive, loving, concerned about the children and interested".

News.title: Key takeaways from BBC interview as Earl Spencer defends claims about King
News.content:
Earl Spencer has told the BBC writing his book about sister Princess Diana, which has made headlines for its criticism of King Charles, was his "duty...as an eyewitness to history".

In an interview with the BBC's Laura Kuenssberg ahead of the memoir's release on Tuesday, Earl Spencer said he wanted "to put things down once and for all that were true".

Among claims made in Swan Song about the King, who was then the Prince of Wales, was that he said "we'll forget her soon enough" during an argument over whether Princes William and Harry should walk in Diana's funeral procession.

In a strongly worded response, Buckingham Palace said the King was "mindful that the pain of fraternal grief can cloud reason, affect judgement and colour memory in ways others do not recognise, even many years after such a loss".

Here are the key moments from Earl Spencer's interview, which include his first account of how he was told about Diana's death and criticism of press coverage of the Duke and Duchess of Sussex.

News.title: Watch: Emotional Earl Spencer says he misses sister Diana every day
News.content:
Earl Spencer, brother of Diana, Princess of Wales, said he misses his sister every day during an interview with the BBC.

"That's the thing with sibling loss, you never get over it," he told Laura Kuenssberg.

His book, Swan Song: Diana, My Sister, is due to be published on Tuesday and is expected to be highly critical of the Royal Family.

He said one of the reasons the book is called Swan Song is because it is his "sign off" as Diana's brother and "final take on the situation".

"This is my swan song too. I'm not here to bang on about Diana, this is my final word, celebration of her," he added.

The full interview, Princess Diana: My Sister's Story, is available on BBC iPlayer and will be broadcast on BBC One at 18:30 BST on Sunday.

News.title: German Chancellor Merz vows to stay on despite 'disaster' in state election
News.content:
Embattled German Chancellor Friedrich Merz has vowed to stay on despite exit polls in two local elections suggesting damaging defeats for his centre-right Christian Democratic Union (CDU) party.

In the north-eastern state of Mecklenburg-Vorpommern, the party was projected to only just scrape into parliament, while the AfD was on track to win the most votes. Merz called the result "a disaster".

In Berlin, the ruling CDU was also expected to be beaten by Die Linke (The Left).

Merz is under mounting pressure, with poor approval ratings and rumours he could even be replaced mid-term in a so-called chancellor swap.

Votes took place on Sunday, a fortnight after the CDU saw its vote halved as the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) won a major victory in the state of Saxony-Anhalt.

Polls for both states closed at 18:00 local time (17:00 BST), with a final result expected in the coming hours.

According to public broadcaster ZDF, the AfD was projected to take 38% of the vote share in Mecklenburg-Vorpommern. However, it is unlikely to govern in the state as other parties refuse to work with it.

For Berlin, the broadcaster put the CDU on 20% of the vote share when polls closed, behind Die Linke on nearly 26%.

Prior to Sunday's elections, there had been intense speculation in Germany that Merz could be replaced unless his party's political fortunes improved.

Earlier this week, the leaders of eight German states backed Merz, who has only held the post for 16 months.

This is a breaking news story and will be updated.

News.title: Ed Davey calls for immediate 10p cut to fuel duty
News.content:
Sir Ed Davey is calling on the government to immediately cut fuel duty by 10p a litre until Christmas as part of a package of policies aimed at cutting the cost of living.

The Liberal Democrat leader is also urging the government to scrap a permanent increase in fuel duty which is set to take effect in January.

Fuel duty was frozen under the Conservatives in March 2022 and Sir Keir Starmer's government continued the freeze, deciding in May to push back a planned 3p increase in September until the end of this year.

The Lib Dems claim cutting 10p from fuel duty now would mean fuel would drop by 12p per litre at the pump.

Sir Ed claimed drivers should be supported and a temporary three-month fuel duty cut would pay for itself by stimulating the economy.

"Petrol and diesel prices are higher than they've been for a long time because of Trump's mad war with Iran, and people need help now," he said.

The policy would cost about Â£2bn, he said, adding: "It's a three-month package, a temporary package, but if you look at the extra money the government will get through the energy profits levy, from gas taxes, from VAT and fuel duty, it's self-funding."

In a speech to his party's conference on Tuesday, Sir Ed will make further calls to cut the bus fare cap from Â£3 to Â£1, and reduce rail fares by 10%.

He will also call for VAT to be dropped from public charging points for electric vehicles and a review of network costs the Lib Dems have labelled unfair.

Chancellor John Healey is under pressure to raise taxes or cut spending at his Budget next month, amid soaring government borrowing costs.

Asked about Sir Ed's call for a fuel duty cut, Labour Party chair Bridget Phillipson told Laura Kuenssberg: "I'm sure John Healey will be open to any and all suggestions ahead of the budget but actually this is an area where the Labour government has taken action on fuel duty already.

"Whilst I recognise what the Lib Dems have to say on this topic, this is the element of politics about it - they've got their conference, they're making their pitch, good luck to them."

Sir Ed also ruled out scrapping the state pension triple lock after party grandee and former business secretary Sir Vince Cable said at a fringe event it was unsustainable and should be "phased out".

Speaking at Q&A on the conference stage, Sir Ed said the policy had been introduced by the Lib Dems during the Conservative coalition to address inequalities and there was still work to do to tackle pensioner poverty.

"It has not finished the job," he told party members, who were split in a show of hands about whether the triple lock should be scrapped if the Lib Dems win power.

The triple lock guarantees that the state pension goes up each year in line with either inflation, wage increases or 2.5% - whichever is the highest - but critics say it is unaffordable and unfair to younger people.

News.title: Kelsey Parker welcomes baby after 'devastating' stillbirth last year
News.content:
Kelsey Parker, the widow of The Wanted singer Tom Parker, has welcomed a baby after last year announcing a "devastating" stillbirth.

The podcaster and author, 35, had two children with British boy band star Tom Parker before he died in 2022, aged 33, after being diagnosed with terminal brain cancer.

She is now in a relationship with Will Lindsay and last June revealed the "earth-shattering news" that they had lost their baby Phoenix.

On Sunday, a post on her Instagram account showed a photo of a newborn baby's arm next to a pink sign with the word River. "Welcome to the world, River. Our little bit of hope," the caption said.

Celebrities including The Saturdays singer Rochelle Humes, TV presenter Susanna Reid and reality TV star Holly Hagan-Blyth have congratulated Kelsey Parker on social media.

"Congratulations angel," Rochelle Humes wrote.

"Oh my goodness â this is so wonderful â welcome River," Susanna Reid said.

Hagan-Blyth commented "I am SO happy for you xxxx".

Kelsey Parker's Instagram bio says "turning life's hardest moments into hope".

Last year she posted a poem online after the loss of her stillborn baby.

It was called Born Sleeping, Forever Loved, and began "the world grew quiet as you arrived, So loved, so longed for, yet not alive. Our precious boy, our angel light, Born with wings, took silent flight".

News.title: Top Gear star Richard Hammond thanks emergency crews 20 years on from crash
News.content:
Former Top Gear presenter Richard Hammond has thanked emergency services for their help on the 20th anniversary of the crash in which he was nearly killed.

Hammond was seriously injured in September 2006 when the 320mph (515km/h) jet-powered Vampire dragster he was driving veered off the track at Elvington airfield, near York, during filming for the BBC show.

In an Instagram post, Hammond said he wanted to thank the members of the staff who rescued him and supported him following the accident "from the bottom of my heart".

In the post, he spoke of the events of that day and said he would be "forever grateful" to all those who helped him in the aftermath of the crash.

He wrote: "Twenty years ago today, I came to an abrupt stop upside down in a Yorkshire field, convinced I was about to die."

He said he recalled having pulled the lever to release the car's parachute before trying to steer it away from disaster, "but disaster was, it seemed, my fate".

"Having done everything I could to avert it, I gave myself over to that fate," he said.

News.title: Watch: Earl Spencer says he felt Charles had 'giddy tone' during call after Diana's death
News.content:
Earl Spencer has said he felt there was a "lightness" in the tone of the then-Prince Charles during a phone call following the death of his sister, Diana, Princess of Wales.

In an interview with the BBC's Laura Kuenssberg, he said he took a call at his home in Cape Town from Charles, who told him how he had broken the news to Princes William and Harry at Balmoral Castle.

"I felt there was a sort of giddy tone," Earl Spencer told the BBC. "I'd had a lot of calls that day from people who cared, who were stunned... and I just felt there was a lightness in his tone about Diana's death that really jarred with me."

Buckingham Palace released a rare statement on Wednesday in response to claims made by Earl Spencer in his book Swan Song: Diana, My Sister, which is due to be published on Tuesday.

It said the King was "mindful that the pain of fraternal grief can cloud reason, affect judgement and colour memory in ways others do not recognise, even many years after such a loss".

The full interview, Princess Diana: My Sister's Story, is available on BBC iPlayer and will be broadcast on BBC One at 18:30 BST on Sunday.

News.title: Homes evacuated over fears fire at seaside hotel weakened building's structure
News.content:
Speaking to the BBC, John Dighton, who was evacuated from Pavilion Court, said that he was told to leave his flat at about 19:00 on Saturday.

The 50-year-old said: "We don't know how long we will be out for but we have grabbed stuff for a couple of days.

"The worst thing is the not knowing. We are at a hotel over the road from the flats."

Ross Honeycomb, 39, was staying at the hotel with his family and told the BBC on Saturday how they were woken by fire alarms at about 01:00.

He said: "I thought I was dreaming, it was horrifying.

"We looked out and there was smoke billowing from the underground car park. Later we started hearing explosions."

Kevin Crawford, 91, and his wife Kathleen, 82, said they had booked in for a two-week stay at the hotel.

The couple, from London, told the BBC that they were in their room on the sixth floor when they heard a fire alarm.

"We saw the fire but we thought the fire brigade had it under control," said Kevin.

"We managed to sleep through it. At the time, we didn't realise how bad the fire was."

The council's chief executive, Susan Priest, said on Saturday: "The extent of support of organisations, including Three Hills, Morrisons and the Salvation Army, has been amazing and helped to ensure that visitors and residents were looked after, supported and had food and hot drinks.

"This was an extremely difficult day, firstly for the hotel guests and this evening for our residents who have had to move out of their homes."

News.title: Billionaire Man United owner loses moral high ground after tax exile, Labour chair says
News.content:
The Labour Party chair has said Sir Jim Ratcliffe loses "the moral high ground" by making statements about the UK while living in tax exile.

Speaking to Sunday with Laura Kuenssberg, Bridget Phillipson said she would take the billionaire businessman's comments that the UK was "on the slide" with a "pinch of salt".

Sir Jim, the founder of petrochemical giant Ineos and Manchester United's co-owner, told the BBC he has lost confidence in the UK due to a combination of high taxes and high immigration.

He has been a tax resident in Monaco since 2020 and said "things would have to get better" in the UK for him to return.

When questioned over the remarks, Phillipson said Sir Jim loses "the moral high ground" by "making these kinds of pronouncements while choosing to make decisions, that he is within his rights to make, to become a tax exile".

Pushed on whether it bothers her that people who create jobs and pay a lot of tax were leaving the UK, the minister said she was "optimistic about our country's prospects".

Other high profile billionaires have left the UK, including including steel tycoon Lakshmi Mittal and most recently the UK's third biggest taxpayer, hedge-fund boss Chris Rokos.

But, Philipson argued the country was in a good position ahead of the Budget next month, and Andy Burnham has shown a "sense of hope and optimism whilst recognising that many families are still struggling and there is more to do."

"Of course, there are challenges, including big international headwinds, but I fundamentally believe that we are in a strong position going into this budget because of the decisions taken over the last two years, and I believe our country's best days lie ahead of us," she said.

Philipson declined to speculate over whether there would be tax rises in the Budget on 28 October, and said the government remained committed to being disciplined about its spending rules.

News.title: The deadly new drugs making Scotland's fight against addiction even harder
News.content:
Efforts to bring down Scotland's sky-high rate of drug deaths are being frustrated by the arrival of hundreds of powerful new synthetic substances that experts warn are making the deadly drugs crisis even more dangerous.

In the past three years, there has been an explosion in the supply of new synthetic cannabinoids and opioids, transforming the illicit drugs trade and increasing the risk of fatal overdoses.

Annual figures to be released on Wednesday are expected to show a rise in the number of drug-related deaths in Scotland, which already has an unenviable record as the drugs death capital of Europe.

"The illicit drug supply in Scotland is getting more and more dangerous," said Dr Lorna Nisbet of Dundee University's Leverhulme Research Centre for Forensic Science.

News.title: Man rearrested after missing mum's remains found
News.content:
A 56-year-old man has been rearrested on suspicion of conspiracy to commit murder and further arrested on suspicion of murder after human remains were identified as a missing mother-of-three.

Joanne Sheen, then aged 44, was last seen when she travelled from Fareham to Southampton with a friend on 5 December 2019.

Metropolitan Police officers were called to Padstow Walk in Feltham, London, on 12 August after bones were found in shrubland damaged by a fire a week earlier.

The man, from Southampton, first arrested in 2020, has been released on conditional bail. Another man, also 56 and from Southampton, was released on bail after being arrested on suspicion of conspiracy to commit murder.

News.title: Strictly returns with new hosting trio as celebrities find out dance pairings
News.content:
Writing in the Independent, external, Rachel McGrath and Lauren Morris ask if three hosts is "truly a crowd" but decide the trio are "certainly off to a good start".

"Emma Willis is undoubtedly doing the heavy lifting, but that makes sense as she is the presenter with the most experience," they note.

"At times, when the three of them were all together, it did feel a little crowded - but there is more than enough presenting to go around..."

The pairings "as usual, seem very well matched", they add, singling out Antonia and Xu.

"Did it take three to tango?" asked Michael Hogan in the Guardian, external's live blog.

"It will take some getting used to, of course, but I thought it worked pretty well. Emma Willis seemed completely at home and smoothly steered the ship. Johannes Radebe was a legend and his understanding of the contest from a pro's perspective will prove invaluable. Josh Widdicombe was enthusiastic and entertaining, although the loud laughing into his mic might need to be turned down...

"An even sterner test will come next weekend, of course, as we go live for the first time. No pressure, you three. But a promising start."

In her analysis of the show for the Guardian, external, Emine Saner says "the presenters look terrified and some of the celebs are hard to identify, but Strictly remains a rare refuge of joy".

"The vibe" the new presenters are "going for is can't-quite-believe-we-got-the-gig humility combined with superfan credentials, which is absolutely the right note", she says.

But she suggests "the pro dancers must now be better-known than some of their celebrity partners" to "which the response can only be 'no, me neither'".

Writing in the Telegraph, external, Anita Singh clearly sees Willis and Radebe as the company, and Widdicombe the crowd.

"Why has the BBC hired jokeless Josh?" she asks.

"Can someone come and collect little Josh from the Strictly studio, please? The poor thing got left behind after the Year 7 school trip and accidentally found himself on Saturday night TV."

By contrast, her initial concerns about Radebe's ability to make the jump from dancing to presenting now look misplaced as he is "so at home in the studio, and so genuine in his interactions with the celebrities and professionals".

And Willis is "great, a pro who could do this job in her sleep", Singh writes.

But both male presenters clearly must do better if they are to impress Sasha Morris of the Express, external who declares that "Strictly's new Tess and Claudia are total car crash".

"Just seconds after seeing the three new hosts... bumble onto the set together, my hope died, and quickly," she writes.

"Poor Josh... looked like a deer in headlights and was completely out of his depth from start to finish...

"Backstage with the stars, both male hosts were too often wide-eyed, nodding and smiling as if they were being held hostage, while charismatic Emma showed them up, moving seamlessly from one position to the next."

"Having three presenters seemed unnecessary, too, as if the bosses didn't feel they could trust Josh or Johannes to hold a role on their own," she adds.

However, for Morris too "the real test will be next week".

News.title: JLR suppliers call for shift to aerospace
News.content:
Major Jaguar Land Rover suppliers have urged the government to help automotive manufacturers move into aerospace and defence, warning that large-scale car production in the UK faces long-term decline.

In an open letter to the prime minister, chancellor and West Midlands Mayor Richard Parker, industry leaders argued Britain's automotive supply chain was "not in decline" but "in the wrong market".

The intervention comes nearly a fortnight after JLR announced plans to cut 4,000 jobs.

The Treasury said it recognised the uncertainty facing workers and was supporting the automotive sector through grants, lower energy costs and investment in electric vehicle production.

JLR has its global headquarters in Coventry and plants in Solihull, Wolverhampton and Halewood.

Signatories to the letter said the redundancies were "the first visible crack" in a UK automotive supply chain supporting about 183,000 manufacturing jobs.

News.title: Maddy Cusack 'more than a number on a shirt' as anniversary falls during inquest delay
News.content:
Sitting on a bench dedicated to her memory, Maddy Cusack's sister and cousin fondly remember her as their sunshine and someone with a real sense of fun.

Olivia Cusack says her big sister was the person "I looked up to my whole life", while for Emily Reilly, her cousin Maddy's the one who "used to get us in trouble with my dad".

But as they come to remember the former Sheffield United footballer on the third anniversary of her death, they're still waiting for answers.

An inquest examining what happened to Maddy Cusack, who was 27 when she was found unconscious at her home in Derbyshire, started in June and should've finished in July.

But it has been paused for months while her former club Sheffield United looks for documents linked to her medical records.

It means her family will have to wait until at least December to hear more evidence, a wait Olivia describes as "extremely overwhelming".

"It is very emotional and you can find yourself frustrated at times," she tells BBC Newsbeat.

"They're very difficult days."

News.title: Tens of thousands of fridge freezers left at docks as household collections suspended
News.content:
People have reported storing broken fridges and freezers in their gardens for months because some council collections have been suspended.

It follows the closure of specialist treatment facilities and a wider shortage of capacity to process cooling appliances, the Local Government Authority (LGA) said.

Recycling company Unimetals, which had dozens of sites in the UK, filed for liquidation in 2025 leaving tens of thousands of fridge freezers at Newport Docks.

The Department for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs (Defra) said it was working to manage the capacity shortages.

Almost a quarter of Welsh councils say they have suspended household collections of fridge-freezers due to a shortage of space at disposal sites.

Cardiff is one of these and Lee Young, who lives in the city, has been trying to get rid of his broken fridge-freezer for two months.

"I tried to take it to the recycling centre in July but was told it wasn't accepted. Someone said the council would collect it, but they won't either."

It has been sitting in his back garden ever since and he does not know when council collections will resume.

News.title: The Independent’s Climate 100 list is a much needed celebration of hope in a troubled world
News.content:

Whether it's investigating the financials of Elon Musk's pro-Trump PAC or producing our latest documentary, 'The A Word', which shines a light on the American women fighting for reproductive rights, we know how important it is to parse out the facts from the messaging. It is sometimes said that people don’t become radicalised by reading books or listening to speeches, but by their own direct experience. If so, then the increasingly tangible evidence of the way climate change is threatening the very way of life of so much of humanity has convinced more and more people that the need to act is both real and urgent.

Tackling the climate crisis is critical to the future of humanity, and freakish weather from pole to pole, and from oceans to deserts and disappearing islands, is as powerful an argument for action as any.

Nonetheless, the existential struggle for the future of life on Earth needs its scientists, its advocates, its activists, influencers, businesspeople, politicians and artists to plot the evidence, make plans of action, raise awareness, win arguments and make the laws, and sign the international conventions that are the only hope of mankind’s survival.

These are the outstanding personalities from across the globe being celebrated in the third of The Independent’s Climate 100 lists.

It would be invidious to attempt to rank achievers from so many different fields, and hardly in the spirit of what is a collective endeavour. So the Climate 100 is divided into leaders among discrete groups – and it is but a minuscule fraction of the millions who do whatever they can to protect the environment.

It is a reminder that the cause is far from lost, even as vested fossil fuel interests and mercenary, powerful politicians try to convince their followers that the change they see happening before their eyes is a “hoax”, a scam or simply something nothing can be done about. These are the pernicious lies that are being exposed by the Independent Climate 100. For that they deserve thanks and praise.

Some of the names are already familiar – Greta Thunberg, a world-recognised name and still only 23. The “real” Erin Brockovich, a pioneer of protest, the Prince of Wales, soon to launch his sixth Earthshot Prize event in Mumbai, and Mayor Mamdani of New York also come into this category.

Others are far less famous, but also influential and just as dedicated and effective. Raoni Metuktire, for example, the chief of Brazil’s Kayapo tribe, who has spent a lifetime protecting the Amazon and its precious rainforests, so rich in biodiversity – one of the planet’s “lungs”. We are also delighted to honour Ralph Regenvanu, Vanuatu’s minister for climate change. The ecosystems of this small Pacific nation of scattered islands are at risk of long-term collapse, through no fault of their own. Minister Regenvanu has been instrumental in Vanuatu’s campaign for an advisory opinion from the International Court of Justice on countries’ legal – and not simply moral – obligations to tackle climate change.

Another example of leadership is that of Omoyemi Akerele, founder of Lagos Fashion Week, who has ensured that every designer at her shows must demonstrate responsible practices, from sourcing and dyeing materials to production and transport. Alongside the runway, Akerele has developed skills programmes that strengthen local supply chains, revive traditional craftsmanship and turn waste materials into valuable resources.

What these 100 brilliant, imaginary pacesetters are doing should serve as an inspiration to all; and shame those who, for sometimes dishonourable motives, use the energy and cost of living crises to belittle and attack essential international Net Zero targets. It is possible to restrain global greenhouse emissions and stop the rise in global temperatures that are causing so much harm.

Indeed, great progress has been made over the past few decades in convincing people of the phenomenon. Much of this is down to visionary individuals who were tirelessly campaigning long before any sort of consensus had been formed – of which Sir David Attenborough, an international treasure, was always the exemplar.

Today, wars, AI and economic challenges threaten once again to embolden climate change deniers and, understandably, distract the public from what remains an enormous challenge. Yet, so many of these issues are linked – the huge energy demands for data centres to power AI; and the role of fossil fuels in wars that drive up the cost of energy and cause inflation. Plentiful clean, green energy from sustainable sources could in fact liberate humanity from these constraints on its growth.

The Climate 100 is a celebration of those fighting to make the world a better, more prosperous and peaceful place. It’s about hope. That’s well worth commemorating.

News.title: Iran-backed Houthi rebels warn against joining Saudi Arabia in Yemen's growing civil war
News.content:

Whether it's investigating the financials of Elon Musk's pro-Trump PAC or producing our latest documentary, 'The A Word', which shines a light on the American women fighting for reproductive rights, we know how important it is to parse out the facts from the messaging. At such a critical moment in US history, we need reporters on the ground. Your donation allows us to keep sending journalists to speak to both sides of the story. And unlike many other quality news outlets, we choose not to lock Americans out of our reporting and analysis with paywalls. We believe quality journalism should be available to everyone, paid for by those who can afford it. Your support makes all the difference. Read more

A senior official with the Iran-backed Houthi rebels is warning countries against joining Saudi Arabia in Yemen’s revived civil war, telling The Associated Press on Sunday that his group has assured the Trump administration that it won’t attack U.S. vessels in the Red Sea.

Mohamed al-Bukhaiti, a member of the Houthis’ political bureau, said Washington reached out to the rebels after their rapid advance down Yemen’s western coast to the Bab el-Mandeb Strait earlier this month.

“We confirmed that we are not targeting the United States, or any other nation, in the strait, with the sole exception of the Saudi enemy,” he told the AP in a Zoom interview from the rebel-held Yemeni capital, Sanaa. “That remains the case.”

U.S. President Donald Trump last weekend said his administration has “had discussions” with the Houthis, but did not say when. “The Houthis called us, and they don’t want to fight with us,” he said. “They would much prefer not having us involved, and they’re letting most ships go through.”

The AP later reported that Oman hosted a meeting between U.S. and Houthi representatives last weekend, citing a Houthi official and another individual familiar with the talks. They spoke on condition of anonymity because they were not authorized to brief the media.

However, al-Bukhaiti only confirmed indirect contacts with U.S. officials through longtime mediator Oman, which brokered a 2025 ceasefire between the Houthis and the Trump administration. That ended a weekslong U.S. bombing campaign against the rebels in return for them ceasing attacks on U.S. vessels in the Red Sea.

“The goal of our military operations is not to close the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, but rather to ensure freedom of navigation through it for everyone, including Yemen,” he said.

The Houthis claim they can fight a war on multiple fronts

Al-Bukhaiti said the rebels have the capacity to fight a war on multiple fronts “should any nation become implicated in the aggression against Yemen alongside Saudi Arabia.”

“Today, Yemen is capable of waging battle — not merely an internal conflict, but an international one as well,” he said.

He said the Houthi attacks against neighboring Saudi Arabia will persist until Riyadh ends its decade-long blockade on rebel-held areas in Yemen and allows vessels to reach Houthi-controlled ports on the Red Sea. Then they will be ready to negotiate, he said.

Al-Bukhaiti blamed Saudi Arabia for the latest escalation of violence in Yemen, which he said erupted after an airstrike blamed on the Saudi-led coalition fighting the rebels hit the Sanaa international airport. The strike prevented an Iranian flight carrying a Houthi delegation to land. The flight was a Houthi attempt to challenge the coalition's air and naval blockade.

The Houthis responded with missile and drone strikes on Saudi Arabia, including one that targeted Riyadh on Saturday before being intercepted. Saudi officials said debris from a Houthi drone also killed one civilian and injured others.

The Houthis also declared a blockade on Saudi shipping in the Bab el-Mandeb Strait and the Red Sea, attacking Saudi-linked vessels and oil facilities inside the kingdom, the world's top oil exporter.

The Saudis and their allies have long struggled to contain the Houthis, and may be tempted to seek a diplomatic solution to halt attacks. That might ultimately require U.S. concessions to Iran, the only country with leverage over the Houthis. But Washington's negotiations with Tehran over their own war fell apart weeks ago.

The U.S., which bombed the Houthis under the Biden and Trump administrations, has shown no interest in getting involved militarily this time around.

The rebels believe power has shifted in their favor

The rebels' advance inside Yemen seized the crucial port city of Mokha and key Red Sea islands that allow them to better monitor shipping traffic through the Bab el-Mandeb, through which some 12% of world trade normally passes.

The Saudi-backed Yemeni government forces, long divided into factions, withdrew but have vowed to regroup.

The escalation ended a 2022 ceasefire that largely ended fighting in Yemen's civil war, which started when the Houthis swept in from their mountainous heartland and seized much of northern and central Yemen, including Sanaa, 12 years ago.

The Saudi-led coalition entered the war the following year on behalf of the internationally recognized government. The civil war killed at least 150,000 people, according to U.N. estimates, and pushed the country to the brink of famine.

Now, with Houthis in control of Yemen's western coast overlooking the Red Sea shipping corridor, “the balance of power has shifted in favor of the Sanaa government,” al-Bukhaiti said, referring to the rebels' de facto authorities there.

“Ultimately, (Saudi Arabia) lost its most critical card: the west coast,” he said.

News.title: Fulham v Man United LIVE: Lisandro Martinez own goal ignites life into dire Premier League contest
News.content:
Why Michael Carrick’s Man United ISN’T Working

Fulham host Manchester United in the Premier League with Michael Carrick under pressure for the first time since taking charge.

A dismal week for United went from bad to worse as they crashed out of the Carabao Cup at home to Brighton, just days their controversial Manchester derby defeat at Old Trafford.

With a three-week international break around the corner, Carrick could do with a win at Craven Cottage to lift the mood, but another defeat could also increase the scrutiny around his position.

Fulham earned their first point of the season under Alvaro Arbeloa at Anfield last weekend and then knocked West Ham out of the Carabao Cup in midweek. But the Cottagers come into this afternoon’s fixture bottom of the table and with Arbeloa also desperate for a win to change the narrative ahead of the international window.

Authorities are investigating after a Florida man said he accidentally shot his 4-year-old daughter and wife at their Deltona home over the weekend.

The man told police that he was trying to clear his handgun before going to a shooting range when it accidentally discharged just before 10 a.m. on Saturday, the Volusia Sheriff’s Office said in a statement.

When authorities arrived, the father was carrying his daughter, who had “obvious injuries to her chest and arm,” the sheriff’s office said.

The mother was found inside the home with a “towel on her gunshot wound to her leg,” authorities added.

Both the mom and daughter were conscious and alert, authorities said.

open image in gallery A Florida dad accidentally shot his 4-year-old daughter and wife while clearing his gun over the weekend, authorities said ( Getty/iStock )

First responders provided care, applying tourniquets to both the victims, as well as a chest seal on the little girl.

The girl was airlifted to Orlando Health Arnold Palmer while the mother was taken to HCA Florida Lake Monroe Hospital.

The father told authorities that he was getting ready to go to the shooting range when his gun fired, with one shot hitting both his wife and their daughter.

“The facts and evidence gathered during the investigation support an accidental gunshot,” the sheriff’s office said.

The little girl and mother’s conditions were not immediately known Sunday. The Independent has contacted the Volusia Sheriff’s Office for more information.

No criminal charges had been filed as of Sunday.

Former President Barack Obama blasted President Donald Trump's “unimaginable” decision to ban three news outlets from the White House — and mused about the likely reaction if he'd tried the same thing.

“My imagination could not foresee some of the stuff that's going on right now,” Obama said during an appearance at Colgate University. “I'm trying to think what would have happened if I had said, ‘You know what, Fox News? You're out of here.’”

The Friday comments drew laughter and applause, with Obama saying, “It's unimaginable.”

“But the point I'm making here is: If you have a certain cohort — let's call it 30 to 35 percent of the country right now — which thinks that's OK, well, what that means is we have not developed the kind of understanding of what democracy requires. And we've got to shore that back up,” he said.

In response to an inquiry from The Independent, the White House declined to comment beyond Trump’s remarks on the subject.

open image in gallery Former President Barack Obama, seen here in Chicago on June 18, 2026, wonders what would have happened if he’d banned news outlets from the White House like President Donald Trump has ( Getty )

Trump announced Friday that he was banning journalists from CNN, MS Now and Politico from the White House, calling them “fake news.”

“They purposely write negative news. And they do that because they want to try and diminish the Republicans and a Republican administration,” he said.

The president followed up Sunday by posting an AI-generated image on social media of three stuffed trash bags labeled CNN, MSNBC (the former name of MS Now) and Politico outside the White House.

Reporters from all three outlets were denied access to the White House and saw their press passes seized when they tried to enter Saturday morning. Their employers vowed to challenge the president's move, which he has suggested may be extended to other news organizations, including The New York Times and The Washington Post.

Shortly after his return to the White House last year, Trump sparked an ongoing legal battle when he banned The Associated Press from the Oval Office and Air Force One after it refused to adopt his name change for the Gulf of Mexico, which the president ordered renamed to the Gulf of America.

open image in gallery Trash bags labeled CNN, MSNBC and Politico sit outside the White House in an AI-generated image posted by Trump on social media on Sunday, September 20, 2026 ( Truth Social/@realDonaldTrump )

During Trump's first term, the White House revoked the “hard pass” issued to then-CNN reporter Jim Acosta following a contentious exchange with Trump during a news conference.

A federal judge later ordered the return of Acosta's hard pass — which allows expedited access to the White House campus — leading to new, stricter eligibility rules.

On Sunday, House Majority Leader Steve Scalise defended Trump, telling ABC's This Week that “I don't think we've had a president that's been more open to the press...but he wants a free and fair press.”

Scalise also claimed that former President Joe Biden “removed the press credentials from over 400 different agencies,” prompting pushback from host Jonathan Karl.

“So, first of all, that's actually not true about Biden. They — the 400 individual reporters who had credentials — did not reapply. There was only one that was actually denied a credential, and all of those who didn't reapply were allowed to come in. They were not banned from the White House,” he said.

open image in gallery Trump talks to reporters in the Oval Office after announcing his White House ban on CNN, MS NOW and Politico ( AFP/Getty )

In addition to Obama's comments about Trump's media ban, the former president also attacked Trump's opposition to government regulation of the artificial intelligence industry.

Obama said that AI “models are getting powerful enough that if they get in the hands of bad humans, they can do bad things” but that Trump — who's claimed he provides all the necessary guardrails — believes regulation is “for losers.”

“So, we’ve got a gap of at least a couple of years where things are moving really fast and we have an administration that is not capable of or willing to — I would argue both — putting together a serious regulatory framework," Obama said, according to The Post-Standard of Syracuse, New York.

On Saturday, Trump said on social media that he planned to create an "AI Force" and appoint an AI czar to oversee the development of the cutting-edge technology, which some industry insiders have warned could kill all humans within 10 years.
