Sports.title: Pierre Sage appears to have saved his job at Crystal Palace for now after his well-drilled side played out a disciplined stalemate against Leeds, writes BOBBY MANZI
Sports.content:
Pierre Sage will be breathing a sigh of relief heading into the international break.

The pressure was on as Crystal Palace travelled to Leeds United with whispers suggesting Sage could become the first manager sacked if the performance was unpropitious. Sage admitted feeling the pressure.

They may not have won but their second positive league result of the season was a step in the right direction after conceding 11 goals in the first four Premier League games.

Palace defended as a cohesive, disciplined unit as they kept a Premier League clean sheet for the first time in the Sage era.

This was their second clean sheet of the week after beating Lech Poznan 4-0 in their maiden Europa League tie on Thursday. But the manner of those defensive performances could not have been more different.

Palace were fragile defensively in Europe and offered chances a better attacking team would have taken advantage of.

On Sunday, though, Palace were rejuvenated. Their main problem has been committing too many players.

Both Tyrick Mitchell and Anan Khalaili have been joining attacks, leaving the back three isolated and enabling efficient, punishing transitions.

Pierre Sage appears to have bought himself time as Crystal Palace manager

This was more measured. Palace picked their moments to initiate intelligently and offered Leeds very few chances. That is what the Palace hierarchy wanted to see and Sage adapted adeptly.

There were very few occasions where Leeds looked a threat as Palace nullified their frontline. A fantastic stop by Walter Benitez denied Dominic Calvert-Lewin from six yards but aside from that, there were no real nervy moments.

Palace were even handed a blow in the game. Takehiro Tomiyasu, who started at central centre-back and was one of Palace's strongest performers in the first half, was forced off at half time.

But that lack of consistency did not bother Palace as Jefferson Lerma replaced him and Chris Richards shifted into the middle while their control did not suffer.

That, in itself, is progress. Palace's back three has changed in every Premier League game this season and, as a result, little consistency has been developed in the backline.

But here, they consistently won their duels. Jaydee Canvot, who was dropped in the previous two games, improved drastically and made a vital interception in the dying minutes to prevent Calvert-Lewin bombing through on goal.

Palace had planned to consider Sage's future at the beginning of the three-week long international break but the manner of the performance leaves very little justification for his dismissal.

Even if Palace had lost at Leeds, it would have been questionable to sack him. The offensive ideas are exciting, the defence had just struggled to click.

He has been trying to integrate a change to the style of play, pressing higher and playing on the front foot more often than not and that has exposed the weaknesses of the defence. Effective transformation cannot be achieved overnight, though.

He came into a new job with two of his centre-backs signed in the final week of the window while the club did not purchase a replacement for Maxence Lacroix, relying on Axel Disasi on loan from Chelsea instead.

His other options were Chris Richards, who struggled to settle without Lacroix's presence guiding him through games, and Canvot, a teenager who will make mistakes.

Sage has had plenty of problems thrown his way and he has calmly dealt with them. He deserves time to implement his ideas. At Lens, he showed he can get a team competing above their perceived level, finishing second to PSG and winning the French Cup.

He is a talented, young and progressive manager. That was the right style appointment in the summer and remains exactly what Palace should want. Sacking him would have been premature, as he proved at Leeds.

Sports.title: Andoni Iraola takes more positives than negatives into the international break as Alexander Isak finally shows his sharpness in hard-fought 1-0 victory... but there is still plenty to fix, writes LEWIS STEELE
Sports.content:
Andoni Iraola takes more positives than negatives into the international break as Alexander Isak finally shows his sharpness in hard-fought 1-0 victory... but there is still plenty to fix, writes LEWIS STEELE

Andoni Iraola toasted to a happy homecoming – and then prepared to jet off on his holidays knowing his work-in-progress Liverpool side are heading in the right direction, slowly but surely.

It would be wrong to say the Reds’ victory at Iraola’s old stomping ground Bournemouth was thoroughly deserved or even convincing but as the new boss takes stock over the international break, he will have more positives than negatives to evaluate.

Match-winner Alexander Isak is finally showing the sharpness and attacking efficiency the Anfield top brass thought they were paying £125million for a year or so ago, while other new signings are settling and previous sub-par performers look back to their best.

It was Isak’s second-half strike that helped Liverpool on their way to their second league victory of the new era and ensured the three-week break from Premier League can be enjoyed knowing they are still unbeaten.

This was not the perfect afternoon by any stretch and the result probably glosses over the fact that, like last Saturday’s goalless draw with Fulham, Iraola’s side did demonstrate several frailties and areas to improve.

But given the limited pre-season owing to the World Cup and late returns to camp, the new boss is needing to learn on the job and righting the wrongs of last season is akin to fixing a plane while it is airborne.

Match-winner Alexander Isak is finally showing the sharpness and attacking efficiency the Anfield top brass thought they were paying £125million for a year or so ago

It was Isak’s second-half strike that helped Liverpool on their way to their second league victory of the new era and ensured the three-week break from Premier League can be enjoyed

The win, therefore, makes the three-week break between this fixture and a home clash against league leaders Manchester City all the more relaxing for Iraola and Co.

This was a banana skin for Liverpool, who at times were sluggish and the front four – especially Florian Wirtz and new signing Bradley Barcola – flattered to deceive. But they came through unscathed and Bournemouth, perhaps in a European hangover, never severely threatened.

This game was not a pinch-me moment in the same way that midweek trip to San Sebastian – and win in Europe over Real Sociedad – was for the Cherries fans but it still was a day to remember as Iraola, the man who took them to the continental stage, returned.

Telling a Bournemouth supporter that their manager would one day be poached by Liverpool might have prompted the same disbelief as informing them they would be playing in European competition, and Iraola deserves acclaim for their journey as much as anyone.

The Basque boss created a monster down here on the south coast, one that had lost just two matches in 2026 – to Arsenal and Manchester City – before this match. And it was those energetic, resilient traits that plagued his new team in the first half.

Just like in Iraola’s three years here, Bournemouth strangled their opposition and allowed them barely a second of peace on the ball. They were dangerous going the other way and Liverpool looked vulnerable in the opening stages.

Iraola created a monster down here on the south coast, one that had lost just two matches in 2026 – to Arsenal and Manchester City – before this match

Iraola’s return to his old stomping ground was an apt opportunity to make a true evaluation of his new team and how much they had improved so far this season

Evanilson had the best chance when a zapping one-touch team move culminated in Marcus Tavernier squaring for his Brazilian striker, who unleashed an audacious flick only to be denied by a smart, reflex stop by compatriot Alisson.

Iraola’s return to his old digs was an apt opportunity to make a true evaluation of his new team and how much they had improved so far this season. In the early stages, however, they put in the sort of performance we became accustomed to last year.

MATCH FACTS BOURNEMOUTH (4-2-3-1): Petrovic 6; Smith 6 (Cook 75, 6), Hill 7, Silva 6, Truffert 6; Adams 6 (Gannon-Doak, 88), Scott 6; Rayan 6 (Toth 89), Christie 6 (Jebbison 75, 6), Tavernier 7 (Brooks 75, 6); Evanilson 6. Subs not used: Di Gregorio, Soler, Diakite, Sanchez. Booked: None. Scorers: None. Manager: Marco Rose 6. LIVERPOOL (4-1-4-1): Alisson 7; Araujo 6, JACQUET 8, Van Dijk 7, Kerkez 6; Mac Allister 6; Barcola 5 (Munoz 71, 6), Szoboszlai 5 (Gravenberch 81), Wirtz 4 (Nyoni 71, 6), Gakpo 7; Isak 7 (Koumas 81). Subs not used: Mamardashvili, Frimpong, Gomez, Ngumoha, Tsimikas Booked: Szoboszlai, Isak. Scorers: Isak 57. Manager: Andoni Iraola 6. Referee: Michael Oliver 5. Attendance: N/A.

Like Arne Slot’s second season, Liverpool were lacking in ideas going forward and appeared to be lethargic, lacking the verve and intensity Iraola craves. If not for some canny defending by the imperious new boy Jeremy Jacquet, they might have fallen behind.

Indeed, Bournemouth’s energy and impetus belied the fact they had played in the Basque country less than 72 hours earlier. All the excitement Liverpool showed in the Carabao Cup on Tuesday – with ten chances and a few academy kids starring – was gone.

Saying that, Alisson was never severely threatened other than Evanilson’s early chance. Ryan Christie had two chances at the start of the second half but fluffed his lines on both counts, unable to wrap his boot round one to find the correct angle, then pulling another wide.

Marco Rose might have felt the happier manager for the majority of the first hour but his team never capitalised on the lethargic mood of his predecessor’s team. Soon, Rose’s Cherries were punished as Isak opened the scoring after 57 minutes.

The goal came after fine work from Cody Gakpo on the left flank, the Dutchman eventually finding Isak who needed no second invitation to pull the trigger and put his side ahead, firing hard and low past Djordje Petrovic.

It was the sort of goal all forwards need. A quiet day at the office had preceded it but when the chance fell to Isak, he did not hesitate in taking it. The Swede could have had a couple more in the ten minutes that followed but was thwarted by strong defending.

Gakpo deserves praise, too, and has been Liverpool’s most-improved player year on year. The Dutchman has seven goal involvements in his first six games this season and is currently the first forward Iraola will sketch on to his team-sheets.

In the end, Liverpool held on for a well-fought victory and their fans could enjoy their day on the sunny south coast. The three-week break will feel all the sweeter for Iraola, too, who marked his return to Bournemouth with three points.

Sports.title: Micah Richards reveals he would not have been able to cover England's World Cup game live on the BBC after the death of his dad without Mark Chapman
Sports.content:
Micah Richards reveals he would not have been able to cover England's World Cup game live on the BBC after the death of his dad without Mark Chapman

Micah Richards has opened up on how his BBC colleague Mark Chapman helped him cope with the unexpected death of his father, Lincoln, on the day of England's semi-final against Argentina.

Richards, 38, was preparing to go on air with the broadcaster in Atlanta when he received a phone call from his brother informing him that Lincoln had died at the age of 66.

The former Manchester City defender went ahead with his punditry duties alongside Joe Hart and Wayne Rooney, aided by presenter Chapman.

He told The Sunday Times: 'On the day it happened my brother rang me, before the semi-final, and I’m going into it thinking how am I going to perform here? How am I going to act? I was on the phone to Chappers (Mark Chapman) for an hour. And he was saying, "Your dad would have wanted you to do it. This is what you’ve worked for since you’ve come into punditry."

'I didn’t want to tell Joe and Wayne, because I’ve known Joe since I was 17 and didn’t want to affect them, and Chappers said, "If in the first ten minutes you’re having a wobble let me know and we can just continue with the rest of the guys."

'If it wasn’t for him, I wouldn’t have got through it. One hundred per cent. And it was weird because when I’m on camera I’m sort of loud and obnoxious at times, but if you watch the footage I keep tapping my foot. I was just trying to hold it together.'

The former Manchester City defender revealed that he heard the news moments before going on air for the BBC's coverage of England's World Cup semi-final defeat by Argentina

News of Richards' heartbreak only emerged after the broadcast, which was watched by 24 million people, when he shared an emotional post on social media.

He wrote: 'Not long before going on air today, I received the awful news that my father Lincoln had passed away.

'His death was unexpected, and he has left us all too soon. He was my greatest fan. He barely missed a game my entire life.

'He would take me wherever I needed to go when I was a kid and he was the proudest parent possible during my professional career.

'It was so rare for him to not be by my side.

'I know how much watching England World Cup games means to everyone at home, and how the experience bonds families together across the generations, like nothing else.

'I know, particularly as a proud old-school Yorkshireman, Dad would’ve wanted the show to go on this evening. And so it did.

'Thinking of my siblings and all my wider family today as we remember my father Lincoln, my hero and inspiration.'

Micah Richards' father Lincoln, right, has died, the pundit said in an emotional social media post

Richards, whose middle name is Lincoln, has regularly praised the influence of his father – who came to the UK from St Kitts in the 1960s - on his career.

'I grew up in Chapeltown, a rough area of Leeds,' Richards said in 2007. 'There was all sorts of stuff – drugs and fighting. There is a point when you are 15 or 16 when you might want to get involved in it. There was definitely a temptation but I stayed grounded.

'I have been able to deal with all the stuff that has come my way. That's down to Dad. He's brought me up well. My Dad is a strong character. He is very principled. He's a Rastafarian. He has set standards for me.

'It's been great to have that sort of person behind me but at the same time I learned how to be my own man. Dad's always been here for me. He has missed only one game I have ever played in and that was my debut at Arsenal when I wasn't even been supposed to be in the squad.'

In 2023, Richards described his father as 'my rock and my hero' but said their relationship had changed after his dad and mother, Heather, separated.

In his interview with the Sunday Times, Richards described how his retirement from playing football had left his father, who he described as having found 'a purpose' following his career and attending his games, taking 'a turn for the worse'.

Sports.title: The balance of power in Glasgow has shifted, ignore the league table... Rangers look like the real deal under Derek McInnes: Celtic 0-1 Rangers
Sports.content:
The balance of power in Glasgow has shifted, ignore the league table... Rangers look like the real deal under Derek McInnes: Celtic 0-1 Rangers

A week after his first victory as a manager in an Old Firm game was greeted with noise to make the eardrums bleed, Derek McInnes was able to savour the sound of silence as he repeated the trick on enemy soil.

Any thought that Rangers’ emphatic triumph at Ibrox was some kind of anomaly can now be dismissed.

Ignore what the league table may say at this early juncture in the season. The balance of power in Glasgow has shifted and it’s done so in what feels like the blink of an eye.

All over the place in the early weeks of the campaign as they stumbled from one horror show to the next, Rangers now look like the real deal under their new manager.

They won the battle here and played football with a fluency and an intelligence which Celtic could only aspire to. How long ago that dismal loss to Jablonec now feels.

On the back of six straight victories, the Ibrox men go into the international break feeling that it’s an interruption they could well live without.

Ryan Naderi scores what proved to be the only goal of the game to silence Celtic Park

Not only have they turned the corner, they’re motoring. If they maintain this rate of travel, Celtic’s slender two-point lead in the title race will be overtaken in short order.

Not only did McInnes have the right game plan to back up the victory in the League Cup, he had all the best players on the field. They had more energy, desire and craft than anyone in the opposing side.

From the instant Ryan Naderi turned home a loose ball with 12 minutes of the first half remaining, the Ibrox men already looked good for the victory.

They dealt with Celtic’s threats – such as they were – with effortless ease. They played with courage and composure. The only thing missing from their display was the second goal which would have removed all doubt long before the final whistle.

All Old Firm games feel hugely significant. This was especially so for McInnes and also for the increasingly forlorn figure of Martin O’Neill.

For the first time as Celtic manager, the Northern Irishman had presided over three straight defeats.

With the capitulation in LASK the catalyst for the debacle at Ibrox and the meek surrender to Ferencvaros, this was a game O’Neill had to win – or at the very least, see some signs of promise from his charges.

It was another pitiful effort from all concerned. In terms of the hierarchy’s unfathomable approach to running a football club, the chickens came home to roost a long time ago.

German forward Naderi slides to his knees in celebration after a week of injury uncertainty

This, though, felt like the day when any hope that O’Neill’s sorcery could keep the whole thing afloat ended.

The veteran should have walked away in the summer on the back of an unlikely Double ahead of a major reset.

He should never have been asked to go again by the club’s powerbroker and he should never have accepted. It all now feels destined to end in tears.

After two dismal performances, O’Neill really had no choice but to change tack. For the first time this season, he switched to a back three. Luke McCowan was the surprise inclusion in a supporting midfield role with Benjamin Nygren also playing off Camilo Duran. It just did not work.

With Naderi passed fit, unsurprisingly, McInnes’ side was unchanged from seven days previously at Ibrox.

Daizen Maeda was back at the place he called home for four years. What O’Neill would have given for his battling qualities in recent times.

McCowan’s first involvement was a slack pass to Naderi. The German threaded the ball through to Djeidi Gassama who took a heavy touch and lost a fine chance to strike first.

Manny Fernandez’s strength eased Duran off the ball in their first joust. In their second, the Colombian’s pace drew a booking for the Rangers defender.

Celtic's beaten players are a picture of frustration at full-time after offering little hope to fans

It was typically feisty. Referee John Beaton next dipped into his pocket to show yellows to McInnes and Celtic coach Mark Fotheringham following a heated verbal exchange.

Celtic did have the ball in the net when Auston Trusty slammed home a volley, although he already knew that Liam Scales was offside.

There was a little more aggression from O’Neill’s players than was witnessed a week ago. That wasn’t difficult. Still, Rangers won the vast majority of the second balls. Naderi’s hold-up play allowed the visitors to gain plenty of territory.

The basics began to look beyond O’Neill’s players, typified by Liam Scales sending one ball straight out of play while under no pressure.

O’Neill was incensed when Dujon Sterling left a bit on Nygren while clearing his lines. Beaton wasn’t interested.

Celtic lacked imagination. The final ball which O’Neill had identified as the missing ingredient in the last two matches was again conspicuous by its absence. The same could be said of composure and bravery on the ball.

Rangers should have been in front before they made it count. Gassama sped away from Colby Donovan and pulled the ball back to the edge of the penalty box. Dan Neil’s shot was weak and easily saved by Viljami Sinisalo. The Finn also easily plucked James Penrice’s header from the sky.

Rangers boss Derek McInnes and Celtic coach Mark Fotheringham tussle on the touchline

Celtic’s most promising moment arrived when they moved the ball from right to left at pace. Nygren found McCowan, who rolled the ball into Tierney’s path. A rising strike slapped the top of the bar. O’Neill would quickly rue that moment.

The manner of Rangers’ opener said everything about the lack of Celtic’s defensive mettle. Penrice’s corner was nodded clear by Scales. Kim Minsu was allowed to shoot from the edge of the box because no one in green and white charged out to meet him.

When Sinisalo dived to his left to palm the shot away, Naderi was first to react. A smart low finish silenced Parkhead.

It could have been worse for the champions at the break. McCowan gave the ball away and watched Gassama take a delightful first touch before clipping the post. Kevin Kelsy’s follow up was blocked.

McCowan was replaced by Kasper Hogh at the break. Celtic restarted positively. Mika Baur’s cross was met at the back post by the head of Donovan. Ivor Pandur pulled off a reflex save.

So fragile were Celtic, though, that a second Rangers goal early in the second half would have sealed it.

Penrice dashed into the box and tried to steer his left foot shot beyond Sinisalo. The Finn did just enough.

When Kim was able to ride three challenges and let fly, O’Neill looked even more exasperated. While the Korean’s shot flew just wide, Celtic were living dangerously.

Kasper Hogh came off the bench for Celtic but got little change out of Olwethu Makhanya

A routine ball over the top exposed Scales. Naderi did Callum McGregor for pace. On the stretch, Kelsy couldn’t convert the cross.

James Forrest replaced the ineffective Nygren. Celtic continued to huff and puff. McGregor, so often the difference in these games, was caught on the ball time and time again and was eventually booked. Tierney, the other mainstay, increasingly looked lost and was subbed.

Olwethu Makhanya found the net after a half-cleared corner only for VAR to spot that his ball juggling on the edge of the box had been a little too literal.

What was striking, although by no means surprising, was how devoid of ideas Celtic looked as the clock ticked down. Sideways passes and aimless crosses were as good as it got. They looked absolutely clueless. It’s a recurring theme.

Sports.title: Tottenham outcast Richarlison takes to social media to send pointed message to club just hours after Spurs' latest Premier League defeat
Sports.content:
Tottenham outcast Richarlison takes to social media to send pointed message to club just hours after Spurs' latest Premier League defeat

Exiled striker Richarlison has been making his presence known amid Tottenham's poor start to the new Premier League season, posting on Instagram hours after their defeat to Aston Villa.

Richarlison was set to depart north London this summer but a move never materialised, and the Brazilian has now been kept out of Tottenham's first-team squad.

In the latest twist to what is turning out to be a protracted saga, Richarlison took to social media on Saturday within hours of Tottenham's 3-2 defeat to Villa to post videos of himself training.

He captioned the video of him undertaking drills: 'The focus remains'. His second post was another video of him undergoing sprint training, accompanied by the caption: '35.4km/h - I broke my record'.

Richarlison's future in north London has become increasingly uncertain after a proposed transfer to Brazilian side Vasco da Gama fell through last week.

He hasn't made a matchday squad in the top flight since the opening-day defeat to Brentford, while he was also left out of Roberto De Zerbi's squad for their away loss to Liverpool in the third round of the Carabao Cup earlier this week.

Richarlison took to social media on Saturday within hours of Tottenham's defeat to Villa to post videos of himself training

De Zerbi has stood firm on Richarlison's absence, saying on Monday: 'At the start of this season, I spoke to him (Richarlison) many times to convince him to stay and he didn't want to

Earlier this week Richarlison shared a screenshot of a social media post about his omission and accompanied it with the message 'Why?' and a tearful sad-faced emoji

His absence has been compounded by Tottenham's lack of goals this season, with Spurs scoring only their first two league goals of the campaign against Villa on Saturday through Conor Gallagher and Jan Paul van Hecke. However, they came too late to influence the result as Tottenham lost 3-2.

On Tuesday, Richarlison shared a screenshot of a social media post about his omission and accompanied it with the message 'Why?' and a tearful sad-faced emoji.

De Zerbi has stood firm on Richarlison's absence, however, saying on Monday: 'At the start of this season, I spoke to him (Richarlison) many times to convince him to stay and he didn't want to.

'I can't go every day to pray for him to stay.

'What I have done at the beginning of this season has been to speak with him and to propose an extension of the contract. If he said, 'no thank you,' I finished my job.

'I know what happened in the last 45 days. It's not right if I explained. It's not my behaviour. The relationship, the problem is between the player and the club.'

Richarlison also had a proposed £35million deadline-day transfer to Everton collapse after the forward failed to agree personal terms with the Toffees.

He was subsequently left out of Spurs' Premier League squad amid a dispute between him and the club over the remaining nine months of his contract, according to BBC Sport.

Richarlison, Spurs' top scorer with 11 Premier League goals last season, remains in north London and trains with De Zerbi's squad, except when they are undertaking tactical work.

The 29-year-old signed for Tottenham from Everton in 2022 for £60million.

Sports.title: Inside Burnley's shocking decline under Alan Pace's ALK: The humiliating sponsor fiasco, why highly-respected CEO quit the Clarets, club staff aghast at changes behind the scenes and the 'ominous shadow' of debt leaving supporters terrified
Sports.content:
Inside Burnley's shocking decline under Alan Pace's ALK: The humiliating sponsor fiasco, why highly-respected CEO quit the Clarets, club staff aghast at changes behind the scenes and the 'ominous shadow' of debt leaving supporters terrified

The threat of mutiny has long been simmering away at Turf Moor. And earlier this month, as Burnley threw away a lead against Bristol City, extending a barren run at a ground in which they have now not won a league game in nearly a year, the fury of a despairing fan base finally boiled over.

Boos thundered around the stadium. Clarets striker Armando Broja got into an angry confrontation with a disgruntled fan in the car park. No one was immune to the ire, and certainly not owner and chairman Alan Pace who bore the brunt of the chanting.

You expect he may well suffer it again if Burnley flounder against Derby on Saturday as they return to Turf Moor rooted to the foot of the Championship with one league win in the last 328 days and none since February. The last time they were in this division they won promotion with 100 points. How far away those days feel now.

Not just because of the dismal football they are having to endure, and the precarious position that’s put them in, but for the ever-growing list of questions for which they are so rarely given answers.

Why did the club wait until relegation before sacking Scott Parker? Why did they wait 71 days to appoint Nicky Hayen and start pre-season without a manager? Why did they sell top scorer Zian Flemming on deadline day with no replacement lined up, and why did they only receive £20million for a player with 11 top-flight goals in a summer when Premier League clubs spent £3.5billion?

Why did they have to drop shirt sponsor Finotive One, a self-titled ‘trading ecosystem’, on the eve of the season? And why, after all that, has the club’s chief executive James Holroyd just left his position after little more than a year in charge?

Pace promised an ‘exciting journey’ when he bought the club in December 2020. That’s certainly one way of putting it. And all of this against the backdrop of that leveraged buy-out, one akin to Manchester United under the Glazers, that used Burnley’s own money to turn a once debt-free organisation with £80m in the bank into one with £13m cash in the coffers, according to the last accounts, and £142m of debt casting an ominous shadow.

No wonder it’s starting to turn toxic.

Burnley owner Alan Pace (centre) has been the subject of fan ire at recent games amid worries about the Clarets' performance on and off the pitch

Nicky Hayen's side slumped to a 2-1 defeat at home to Bristol City a fortnight ago. They have not won a league game at Turf Moor in 2026

Holroyd’s arrival was seen as a huge coup for the club, a man steeped in experience having spent 14 years at Manchester United following another 14 years at adidas.

One former colleague described him to Daily Mail Sport as ‘incredibly serious and incredibly methodical about his work’. A man who spent the best part of three decades working for just two companies was out of his third one after just over a year.

Burnley confirmed his departure to Daily Mail Sport and said that Holroyd had ‘decided to step down to pursue a new challenge’. He will continue to work at the club as part of their Burnley In The Community department but is no longer involved on the commercial side of the business.

‘It's been an honour and a privilege to serve this great club,’ said Holroyd. ‘There's a pride and a resilience that runs through Burnley that you feel from the moment you arrive. That's what makes this such a difficult decision, but it's why I'll keep supporting the incredible work being done by BFC in the Community.

'I want to thank Alan and the board for the opportunity to serve this club, and the staff and supporters for making me feel truly part of the Claret family.'

Daily Mail Sport understands the embarrassing and expensive Finotive One fiasco, where the club dropped their shirt sponsor after just 42 days despite a star-studded launch that featured investor and former NFL star JJ Watt, England cricket legend Jimmy Anderson and Arnold Schwarzenegger, and replaced all purchased shirts free of charge, played a part.

Burnley refused to confirm the reason why the sponsorship ended but it’s understood Finotive One failed to meet its payments.

Sources also told Daily Mail Sport that difficulties had arisen in Holroyd and Pace’s working relationship and the Finotive One debacle did nothing to ease matters. A parting of the ways was decided to be best for all concerned.

The club dropped their shirt sponsor after just 42 days despite a star-studded launch that featured investor and former NFL star JJ Watt (right)

Holroyd has been replaced on an interim basis by Amy Wells, who was head of HR, and director of strategy and transformation Nathan Kavanagh.

Sources suggested Holroyd found the chairman too hands-on, a complaint echoed to Daily Mail Sport by other former members of staff, with one saying employees often felt they were not trusted to get on with their job.

Most of the staff who were in place when Pace's ALK took over are no longer there, many leaving within a year, leading to a sense among those close to the club that they cannot recognise the one they once knew.

‘These were local people, where the club meant everything to them, and one by one you saw them leave,’ said one former member of staff.

There’s a feeling that the sense of community and togetherness that forged a spirit able to take Burnley into Europe has been eroded.

Pace has spent money, and appointed two good managers in Vincent Kompany and Parker, but fans struggle to connect to an ever-revolving door of players they see as mercenaries as the club bounces between the Premier League and the Championship. None of them they see as personifying the famous ‘Legs, Hearts, Minds’ motto emblazoned on Sean Dyche’s request on a wall at the training ground.

The overwhelming sense among the fanbase now is that the last two promotions have papered over the cracks and the fissures are growing too wide to fix.

Manager Hayen is already under pressure and facing questions about his future and whether he’s been told defeat by Derby could spell the end. ‘Not at the moment,’ he said. ‘They didn't tell me this can be my last game. It can be, I don't know.’

Kyle Walker addressed staff this week to tell them that the players were doing everything they could to fix things.

Manager Nicky Hayen is already under pressure and facing questions about his future and whether he’s been told defeat by Derby today could spell the end

Midfielder Reo Hatate looks pained during Burnley's draw at Wrexham last week

So much of it, though, comes back to the money. The £142m debt from the most recent accounts for the 2024-25 promotion season, the interest on bank loans of up to 12 per cent, the £36m of net interest payments over the last five seasons when there was none before the takeover.

The £9.5m taken in ‘management fees’ under the current ownership, ones that jumped from £1.5m to £4m after relegation. The transfer debt of £95m that was just £3m four years ago and takes the club’s total gross debt to nearly a quarter of a billion. The near £40m sale of incoming transfer fees to London-based firm Fasanara Capital. And why Velocity Capital, ALK’s investment arm, still owes the football club around £81m.

Under the previous ownership, made up of local businessmen, Burnley were famously debt-free, cash rich, and one of the most profitable clubs in Premier League history. Dyche worked miracles on a budget as he established the Clarets in the Premier League and took them into Europe.

Now, according to respected finance blog Swiss Ramble, Burnley’s external debt of £142m last year was the fourth highest in England behind only Tottenham and Everton, who have built new stadiums, and the Glazers’ United.

‘There’s a few of us who have been querying the leveraged buyout model of Alan Pace for a few years,’ football finance expert Kieran Maguire tells Daily Mail Sport.

‘It’s reliant on Burnley regularly being in the Premier League for the broadcast cash flows, when its matchday income is only seven per cent of total revenue.

‘The concerns are that the club has £75m of short-terms loans, £30m of long-term loans, has sold players but has sold the transfer instalments from the sales and owes £94m in unpaid transfer fees. Under those circumstances they will struggle to borrow more and, if they do, will have to pay punitive interest rates.

‘It therefore could come down to whether or not Alan Pace has (a) the cash and (b) the desire to provide funding himself.’

Kyle Walker addressed staff this week to tell them that the players were doing everything they could to fix things

Sources suggested outgoing CEO James Holroyd found Pace too hands-on, a complaint echoed to Daily Mail Sport by other former members of staff

In response to questions about Burnley’s financial position, the club told Daily Mail Sport that the latest set of accounts, due to be submitted to the Premier League by October 31, ‘will give a more accurate picture of the current position’.

Those accounts are expected to show a fall in both debt and how much is still owed by Velocity to the club.

The management fees, meanwhile, are understood to be payments to non-full-time Burnley employees, such as consultants, for their services. The increase is thought to be due to performance-related bonuses.

The worry for Burnley, especially after such a torrid start to the campaign, is what happens if they don’t go up again this time. They are only getting two years of parachute payments instead of three as they came straight back down last season.

The £35m settlement Everton were forced to pay for breaking financial rules in the season Burnley were first relegated was a lifeline, but it remains uncertain whether the Clarets will ultimately receive it after the Toffees appealed against the decision.

Concerns have been raised, too, about whether Burnley will become a side dish as Pace and ALK expand their multi-club model. They have already purchased Spanish side Espanyol and are believed to be eyeing up Club Leon in Mexico.

In the most recent meeting between the club and its independent supporters association, the group was told, according to the latest newsletter, that ‘while EPL TV money is still available to the club, we will remain the priority’.

‘The question does remain what happens in the circumstances where the club is not quickly re-promoted to the EPL and the parachute money comes to an end,’ the newsletter continued.

There’s a feeling that the sense of community and togetherness that forged a spirit able to take Burnley into Europe under Sean Dyche has been eroded

Burnley have not been outside the top two divisions in more than a quarter of a century. They may well no longer exist had they not beat Leyton Orient on the final day in 1987 to stay in the Football League. Supporters worry that their status as a modest town club, surrounded by big cities, will make it even harder to fight their way back up.

‘There’s a feeling that we could be the next Leicester,’ said one source. The deeper fear, of course, is whether they could also become another Bury and be the first Premier League team to go bust.

The club, for now, are not in immediate danger of that and plans are said to be in place should the worst happen. But the longer Burnley remain outside the top flight and, heaven forbid, fall through the divisions, the more difficult it will be to keep on paying the piper.

Sports.title: England set to rest Jofra Archer, Josh Tongue and Gus Atkinson for T20 Australia tour as new coach Stephen Fleming sets out ambition to lead Test side to world No 1
Sports.content:
England will use a second-string bowling attack during the Twenty20 section of their upcoming tour to Australia in a bid to keep their Test artillery fresh for Stephen Fleming's debut series in South Africa in December.

In a first sign of how England's job share between Fleming and limited-overs coach Brendon McCullum will work, plans have been drawn up to rest Jofra Archer, Josh Tongue and Gus Atkinson from the five T20 matches Down Under.

Although the trio will travel to Australia for the three one-day internationals taking place between 13-18 November - a year out from the World Cup in southern Africa - they are likely to be offered a period of rest before hooking up for an official warm-up fixture between 9-11 December, ahead of three Tests in South Africa.

It would mean Sonny Baker, Saqib Mahmood and Jamie Overton taking on greater seniority for a team that returned to the top of the Twenty20 rankings in completing a 3-0 whitewash of Sri Lanka at Emirates Old Trafford on Saturday.

'Right through the schedule we will look at what the priorities are and how we are able to manage the key players and personnel so that English cricket has the best opportunity to succeed in those times,' McCullum said, of trying to balance resources leading up to next summer's Ashes and the World Cup.

'How do we make sure we have got the best players available for that stuff? We will see, probably the fast bowlers in particular given a bit of a freshen up leading into that Test series, so therefore the T20s may be an area where we can introduce some new talent, which will be important for us as well, to keep growing our talent base in that space.

Plans have been drawn up to rest Jofra Archer (left) and Gus Atkinson (right) from the five T20 matches down under

It is a first sign of how England's job share between England's new Test coach Stephen Fleming (right) and limited-overs coach Brendon McCullum (left) will work

'We will work it out. We will do what we think is right to ensure everyone has the best opportunity to succeed and that will include, at times, having to sit guys out.'

Despite McCullum's talk of drafting in new talent, 38-year-old Richard Gleeson remains amongst the most effective English pacemen in the shortest format while Brydon Carse, 31, also enjoyed a good Hundred competition. His availability will depend on the outcome of a Cricket Regulator probe into a late night incident in Derby last month.

Meanwhile, Baker, who at 23 is at the other end of the career spectrum, took the man-of-the-match award in Manchester after completing a series analysis of 11.5-2-44-6 and was 'walking a foot taller on the back of it,' according to McCullum.

England will now focus on moving further up the one-day standings by winning a three-match ODI series versus the Sri Lankans starting in Chester-le-Street on Tuesday. Harry Brook's team are currently seventh, one place behind their opponents.

Fleming marked his unveiling as England coach on Saturday by setting himself the goal of toppling Australia as the world's No 1 Test team.

Speaking at Emirates Old Trafford, the 53-year-old nominated emulating the unique achievement of Andy Flower in taking an England team to the summit - staying there for 12 months from August 2011 - as the primary goal of a job he began with a tour of county cricket earlier this week.

'I would love to be in charge of the No 1 Test team in the world. That would be my aspiration,' Fleming said.

'The marquee events - the Ashes - are something I can't wait for. As a New Zealander, I have watched and loved the Ashes all my cricketing life, so to be part of that is an absolute highlight. I can't wait for that.'

'I would love to be in charge of the No 1 Test team in the world. That would be my aspiration,' Fleming said

Those five matches next June and July represent Fleming's first home series in charge, and he will hope to have narrowed the 24-point chasm by then between the Australians and an England side currently languishing in mid-table - the 3-0 whitewash of a poor Pakistan earlier this month, overseen by captain Joe Root and interim head coach Marcus Trescothick representing a first series win since 2024.

Fleming's family and business commitments meant he was slow out of the blocks, after being appointed in July and some will even argue it's a false start, as he will honour his contractual obligations as a commentator with Sky in his homeland for four T20 matches between New Zealand and India next month before heading to South Africa for his first assignment this December.

As a coach it is T20 that he is associated with, following 18 years in charge of Chennai Super Kings at the Indian Premier League, but he was 'kissing coaches' heads' at four County Championship fixtures this week, reacquainting himself with the English domestic game, having captained Nottinghamshire to the title in 2005, and was quick to remind people of his influence on New Zealand's cricket as a player.

'My DNA was based on Test cricket. I am inherently a red ball lover, and that was where I learned strategy, leadership, captaincy, the nuances of the game,' he said.

'If anything, I moulded myself into the white ball world based on man management and strategy and leadership.'

One of the relationships he developed at Chennai was with Ben Stokes, and although the pair caught up at Chester-le-Street on Thursday, Fleming was quick to dismantle suggestions of England's ex-captain launching a sensational comeback against Australia next summer.

'My view – when a player decides to retire it's a big decision and I have the utmost respect for that decision so that's where it sits,' he said.

Stokes was, however, along with Fleming's compatriot and close friend McCullum, the subject of praise for creating a template for Test cricket in this country to which he will look to add pragmatism.

Of comparisons in style to McCullum, Fleming said: 'I'll bet on the favourite and he'll bet on the longest odds possible.'

Adding: 'It depends which timeline you want to talk about but for me, the way they changed the nature of Test cricket was quite remarkable. I have a huge amount of respect for the courage that took. Obviously the last 12 months it hasn't evolved as they would have liked, or the fans would have liked, but as a lover of cricket I was very impressed with how the team went about it.'

Among the changes Fleming says he would like to instill, creating a new 'identity' for the team, is greater discipline both on and off the field, vowing to bowl overs quicker in a bid to avoid World Test Championship points penalties and improve image following a spate of alcohol-related incidents.

Unable to comment on the news that Carse has avoided charges following a police investigation into a Derby nightclub incident due to an ongoing secondary probe by the Cricket Regulator, Fleming did offer guidance on the conduct he expects within the squad he inherits.

'If you want an example, a great example of how to behave as an international cricketer, Joe Root is it,' he said.

Sports.title: 'Brutal, searing and punishing heat' - Babb on playing for Ireland at USA '94
Sports.content:
While none of the home nations qualified for the 1994 World Cup, the Republic of Ireland did.

It was a second successive appearance at the tournament for the Boys in Green, who were again led by 1966 World Cup winner Jack Charlton.

At Italia '90, the weather had been hot - but at USA '94, it was a different kettle of fish altogether.

The iconic image of Charlton launching an open bottle of water in the direction of Andy Townsend and Tommy Coyne always provides a reminder of that.

Image: Jack Charlton led the Republic of Ireland at Italia '90 and USA '94

He clashed with FIFA over their policy that bottles could not be thrown to the players on the pitch, so took to throwing the contents instead before FIFA later relented and allowed water bags to be thrown.

"They trust me to do what is right for them and I will continue to do it," Charlton said. "We have been right in pursuing this matter and FIFA's change of heart proves that."

Charlton was rarely seen without his white baseball cap that summer. Steve Staunton famously even wore one during the national anthem before the second group game against Mexico.

One of the players in the Ireland squad that summer was Phil Babb. The defender, then 23, had just completed his second full Premier League season at Coventry.

He made his international debut in a 0-0 friendly draw with Russia in March 1994, then played in the next four friendlies leading up to the tournament.

Image: Phil Babb played in all four of the Republic of Ireland's games at the 1994 World Cup

Nothing was set in stone, but he knew he would at least have a decent chance of being included in Charlton's 22-man squad, so started to physically prepare himself.

"A coach at Coventry asked me if I wanted to do anything specific - we ended up doing 12-minute sessions in a sauna!" Babb recalls, with a smile.

"We were doing burpees, press-ups, just trying to acclimatise to that intense heat. We did about six sessions - but I wouldn't recommend it for anyone now!

"I was a fit lad and had played pretty much all the Premier League games Coventry had played that season. I adapted to the heat pretty well, but I know some of the older lads really struggled."

Babb started alongside Paul McGrath in the heart of defence for Ireland's tournament opener at Giants Stadium in New Jersey.

Image: Ray Houghton's stunning strike earned a shock 1-0 win over Italy

That Saturday, they shocked an Italy side that featured Paolo Maldini, Franco Baresi and Roberto Baggio. John Aldridge's stunner sealed a memorable 1-0 win.

It was an achievement made all the more impressive by the fact the Azzurri went on to finish as runners-up - but also given the fact it was played in temperatures exceeding 30C.

"When we walked out onto the field, about two hours before kick-off, you could tell it was going to be absolutely roasting," he recalls.

"You could tell that straight away and we didn't stay out long. I just checked the grass to see which studs I wanted, then I went straight back in. I know some of the lads were walking around and taking the atmosphere in, but I thought: 'This is too hot'.

"I didn't go out for a warm-up with the rest of the lads, either. I stayed in the changing room. It was built for NFL, so they had a 40m sprint track. I warmed up in there and waited until we went out. It was brutal, it was searing, it was punishing.

"It affected everyone's game. You were saturated after just 10 minutes walking onto a pitch, so you had to conserve energy at the right times.

"Recovery was very basic and there was very little ball work because of the demands of the actual games and the fluids you lose. When you're that dehydrated, it's quite difficult. You want a drink, but you don't feel hungry and that is a key part of the recuperation."

Image: Babb, whose Ireland were knocked out by Dennis Bergkamp's Netherlands, joined Liverpool later that summer

Thirty-two years on from that tournament, football has evolved exponentially.

Sports science has taken on a key role in the game and, this summer, is likely to play into the way teams approach games tactically due to the heat. A slower tempo is expected in many.

Charlton was not prepared to facilitate the same in 1994, though.

"We only played one way, so if you tried to go off-piste, Jack would certainly let you know!" adds Babb.

"We had one style of play, with a lone striker. If it wasn't Tommy Coyne, it might have been Niall Quinn up there and we'd be putting long balls up to him, with either willing runners out wide or the midfield bombing on.

"That was the Irish way back then. Tommy ran tirelessly, to the point where he actually collapsed with heat exhaustion on the plane home.

"I think Jack's sports science was a barrel of Guinness in his room and he'd call the lads in and have a pint! I'm sure there's a high calorific content in that, so maybe he was ahead of his time!"

In spite of that, Babb's memories of the tournament are largely positive.

"I enjoyed it, I have to admit! I'd rather play in the searing heat than a wet Tuesday night in Hull," he says.

"I was a fit lad and it was quite easy for me playing alongside Paul McGrath, who was imperious in that tournament. I learned a lot from him and how he conserved his energy.

"I felt I got stronger because I got used to it. I guess our 0-0 draw against Norway would probably attest to the heat and the style of play.

"It all comes down to the individual. Footballers are supreme athletes now and they leave nothing to chance, so I think they'll cope a lot better than we did in the mid-90s."

The methods may have moved on since Charlton was throwing water onto the pitch, but Babb's memories from USA '94 provide a reminder this World Cup will be a battle against more than just the opposition.

Sports.title: Ogbene earns Republic of Ireland draw with Canada
Sports.content:
Chiedozie Ogbene's equaliser ensured the Republic of Ireland continued their good run of results as they drew 1-1 with World Cup co-hosts Canada in Montreal.

Canada went ahead in the 24th minute from an own goal by defender Jake O'Brien, heading a failed clearance into his own net from Stephen Eustaquio's corner.

Ireland were then awarded a penalty in the second half after Cyle Larin - who signed a two-year deal with Southampton earlier in the day - took out Jamie McGrath.

Canada goalkeeper Maxime Crepeau saved Troy Parrott's initial attempt, but Ogbene was on hand to slam home the rebound and tie the game in the 60th minute.

Image: Ireland's Jake O'Brien heads the ball into his own net

Ireland, who failed to qualify for this summer's World Cup, went close to a winner but Crepeau denied a charging run from Mason Melia late on.

The Orlando City goalkeeper missed out on the 2022 World Cup in Qatar after breaking his leg while playing in the MLS Cup final.

Canada, managed by former Leeds boss Jesse Marsch, officially open the World Cup on June 12 in Toronto against Bosnia and Herzegovina, before facing Qatar on June 18 and Switzerland on June 24.

They remain without captain Alphonso Davies, who is still nursing a hamstring injury he sustained while playing for Bayern Munich.

Sports.title: Republic of Ireland edge past Qatar in friendly as both sides end with 10
Sports.content:
Captain Nathan Collins headed the Republic of Ireland to a 1-0 friendly victory over World Cup-bound Qatar as both sides were reduced to 10 men.

Collins ensured Ireland got the better of a side managed by his former Wolves boss Julen Lopetegui with an early header.

However, just how the evening might have panned out had Jack Moylan not been dismissed as half-time approached, a sparse crowd inside the Aviva Stadium will never know.

Heimir Hallgrimsson's side, whose hopes of making it to the World Cup finals were dashed in heartbreaking fashion in March when they lost their play-off semi-final to the Czech Republic on penalties, were in complete control until Moylan's premature exit.

Qatar substitute Almoez Ali suffered the same fate 12 minutes from time.

Image: Jack Moylan was sent off before half-time at the Aviva Stadium

The game was played out against the backdrop of ongoing unease at the forthcoming Nations League clashes with Israel, and play was interrupted on several occasions during the first half as 'Stop the Game' protesters among a crowd of 28,981 repeatedly hurled tennis balls on to the pitch.

Ireland will now head for Montreal and their friendly against World Cup co-hosts Canada on June 6, while Qatar continue their preparations for the finals - they launch their Group B campaign against Switzerland in San Francisco on June 13 - against El Salvador in Los Angeles on the same day.

The Republic took the lead with just five minutes gone when, having been fouled by Ayoub Al-Oui wide on the left, Moylan curled the resulting free-kick on to the head of Collins, who glanced the ball effortlessly past 'keeper Mahmoud Abunada.

Image: Qatar's Almoez Ali was also sent off

There was a brief interruption after the protesters made their presence felt for the first time as Qatar's Pedro Miguel underwent treatment for injury, but once order had been restored, Troy Parrott whipped a first-time shot wide after being picked out by Seamus Coleman.

The Qataris simply could not get anywhere near Hallgrimsson's men and a mid-half drinks break did little to improve matters for the visitors with Abunada having to field Jayson Molumby's deflected 24th-minute shot from distance.

Lopetegui could not hide his frustration on the sideline and only the bravery of defender Ahmed Fathi denied Chiedozie Ogbene a second goal as he attempted to latch on to Liam Scales' header back across goal.

But the home side's night took a turn for the worse on the stroke of half-time when Northern Irish referee Jamie Robinson deemed Moylan's challenge on Jassem Gaber worthy of a red card, much to the Lincoln frontman's clear astonishment.

Image: Former Wolves and West Ham boss Julen Lopetegui is now in charge of Qatar

With defender James Abankwah having replaced Dara O'Shea at half-time, the 10 men found themselves under pressure for the first time on their return, although Coleman very nearly caught Abunada off his line with an audacious 52nd-minute attempt from the right wing.

Edmilson Junior dragged a long-range effort wide two minutes later after Molumby went down in midfield under Fathi's challenge and it took a fine 71st-minute reaction save by Caoimhin Kelleher - his first of the night - to keep out Yusuf Abdurisag's deflected shot.

However, Qatari hopes of salvation were dashed with 12 minutes remaining when Ali struck out at Molumby off the ball on several occasions and was also sent off.

Sports.title: Parrott out of luck as Republic of Ireland draw with North Macedonia
Sports.content:
Troy Parrott had two goals disallowed as the Republic of Ireland played out a stalemate against North Macedonia on the night on which they had hoped to book a trip to the World Cup finals.

Five days after their dreams came to an end for another four years in Prague, Ireland drew 0-0 with the Macedonians in a friendly encounter neither side wanted as the Czech Republic and Denmark fought for the big prize.

Even a third successive home victory for the first time since the 2015-16 campaign would have provided scant consolation for Thursday night's disappointment but Heimir Hallgrimsson's men had to make do with a disappointing draw.

AZ Alkmaar striker Parrott came closest to breaking the deadlock as 37-year-old defender Seamus Coleman received a standing ovation from a crowd of 39,560 at the Aviva Stadium when he was replaced during the second half of what could yet prove to be his final appearance for his country.

Nevertheless, the squad will reconvene for a series of friendlies at the end of the season ahead of next season's Nations League campaign and later Euro 2028 qualification having restored a measure of pride and established a momentum they hope will serve them well when they return to competitive action.

The hosts went on to the offensive from the off, although they were unable to find the final ball to allow either Parrott or Chiedozie Ogbene to threaten.

John Egan could not direct an 11th-minute corner at goal and Ogbene saw his snapshot deflected over three minutes later, but goalkeeper Caoimhin Kelleher had to parry Enis Bardhi's 21st-minute free-kick after it flicked off the defensive wall, with Bardhi volleying high over after the resulting corner had been only half-cleared.

Macedonia keeper Stole Dimitrievski saved Parrott's 23rd-minute header comfortably after Dara O'Shea and Finn Azaz had sparked a concerted attack, and Azaz failed to make the most of a free-kick two minutes later after he had been tripped just outside the penalty area.

Parrott was played into a promising position by Knight nine minutes before the break, only to miss the target by some distance.

The in-form striker - he scored his sixth goal in three games in Prague - might have done better again two minutes later after Azaz's clipped pass had caused problems for the Macedonian defence but he snatched at his attempt and fired high and wide.

Parrott twice had the ball in the net as time ran down but an offside flag stalled his celebrations on each occasion.

Ireland were unfortunate not to take the lead with 52 minutes gone when Azaz accepted Seamus Coleman's pass and found Parrott, who turned smartly before shooting against the upright.

Azaz curled an effort just wide and Tihomir Kostadinov denied Parrott a clear run on goal as the hosts began to turn the screw but it was veteran Coleman's 61st-minute departure as

Hallgrimsson made changes which attracted the biggest cheer of the night to that point.

Wholesale changes did not help the flow of the game, which rather petered out as the whistle approached, although Ireland substitute Johnny Kenny passed up a glorious opportunity to win it at the end with a weak shot at the keeper.

Sports.title: Szmodics out of hospital and 'on the mend' after collision
Sports.content:
Republic of Ireland forward Sammie Szmodics has been released from hospital in Prague after being knocked unconscious during Thursday's World Cup play-off defeat by the Czech Republic.

The 24-year-old, who is currently on loan at Derby from Ipswich, was hurt in a collision with defender Stepan Chaloupek just two minutes after his introduction as an extra-time substitute at the Fortuna Arena, sparking concerned medics to rush to his aid.

Szmodics was carried from the field on a stretcher and taken straight to hospital, where Ireland head coach Heimir Hallgrimsson later revealed he would spend the night under observation.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Danyal Khan looks back on the heartbreaking result for the Republic of Ireland who lost their World Cup qualifying play-off against Czech Republic on penalties

A Football Association of Ireland spokesperson said on Friday morning: "Sammie Szmodics was transferred to hospital yesterday having sustained a head injury during extra time of the play-off against Czechia.

"Following further tests and a period of observation, he has been safely discharged from hospital and will continue his recovery under the care of the Republic of Ireland and Derby County medical teams."

Szmodics, who Hallgrimsson confirmed would have taken a penalty in the shoot-out which Ireland ultimately lost 4-3, took to social media to express his thanks to those who had helped him.

He posted on X: "Gutted the way it ended. Fans and boys immense all evening!! Appreciate everyone's messages. And thank you to the medical staff who acted so quickly to help me. On the mend."
