World.title: Nigeria: Tinubu Meets Macron for Private Dinner in Paris
World.content:
According to Mr Onanuga, the dinner reflected the longstanding relationship between Nigeria and France.

President Bola Tinubu met French President Emmanuel Macron on Thursday for a private dinner at the Élysée Palace in Paris.

It is the latest in the series of meetings and engagements between Nigeria and France since Mr Tinubu assumed office in 2023.

The president's Special Adviser on Information and Strategy, Bayo Onanuga, disclosed the meeting in a post on X on Friday. He also shared photographs of the two leaders at the French presidential palace.

Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn

PREMIUM TIMES reports that the meeting took place while Mr Tinubu was in France during the second leg of his three-week annual leave in Europe.

He arrived in Paris on Monday after spending the first part of his leave in London.

According to Mr Onanuga, the dinner reflected the longstanding relationship between Nigeria and France.

In the post, he wrote, "French President Emmanuel Macron received President Bola Ahmed Tinubu for a private dinner Thursday night at the Élysée Palace, reflecting the enduring relationship between Nigeria and France and their shared commitment to strengthening bilateral cooperation."

President Tinubu, in a separate post about the meeting, also said his conversation with Mr Macron reflects both countries' mutual interest in maintaining good relations and strengthening the existing partnership.

He also thanked the French president for his hospitality and friendship.

"It was a pleasure to share a private dinner with President Emmanuel Macron at the Élysée Palace in Paris. @EmmanuelMacron

"Our conversation reaffirmed the strong friendship between Nigeria and France, as well as our shared commitment to deepening cooperation and building a mutually beneficial partnership between our two nations," he wrote.

Photographs released from the dinner showed Mr Tinubu and Mr Macron together at the Élysée Palace, with another image showing Mr Tinubu, Mr Macron and France's First Lady, Brigitte Macron.

However, details of the interaction or any potential agreement between the two leaders were not provided.

World.title: Africa: Hub Unconference to Tackle Ai's Growing Influence in Africa
World.content:
The Hub Unconference is set to return for its 12th edition in Harare next week, bringing together young Africans to debate the growing influence of artificial intelligence (AI) and digital technologies on society.

The two-day event, scheduled for 24 and 25 September at Harare Gardens, will run under the theme "Unruly Algorithms" and bring together students, creatives, journalists, policymakers, technologists and other digital enthusiasts.

Organisers said the gathering would examine how digital systems are influencing information, education, creativity and civic participation across Africa.

Rather than focusing solely on explaining artificial intelligence, this year's edition aims to explore how young Africans can influence and shape the technologies increasingly affecting their lives.

Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn

Hub Unconference Coordinator Takudzwa Musakasa said the organisers wanted to shift the conversation towards action and participation.

"We didn't want this year's edition to be just about what AI is doing to us, we wanted it to be about what we are going to do about it," Musakasa said.

He said the "Unruly Algorithms" theme would encourage young Africans to understand the systems influencing their lives, question how they were developed and take part in shaping their future.

The programme will feature panel discussions, masterclasses, debates, live podcasts, creative pop-ups and interactive showcases, with speakers from several African countries.

Among the speakers are Angela Kilisungu and Nkumi Mtingwa from Tanzania, Uganda's Antonio Kisembo and Samuel Eibu, Malawi's Willson Chivhanga, and Zimbabweans Darlington Chugumbu, Linda Mujuru and Joice Svotwa.

The programme will also feature a Canva masterclass led by Nicole Njanjari, as well as pop-up sessions involving organisations including Friendship Bench, Magitare Trust and Defend Defenders.

Participants from Uganda, Malawi, Tanzania, South Africa and Zimbabwe are expected to discuss ways African countries can strengthen control over their data and use it to promote transparency, civic advocacy and locally driven innovation.

Musakasa said bringing people from different sectors into the same space was central to the event's approach.

"We're bringing students, creatives, journalists, technologists and policymakers into the same space to question these systems, learn practical skills and imagine what a digital future shaped by us could look like," Musakasa said.

Close 

The organisers said the conference would provide an opportunity for participants to explore practical ways of engaging with emerging technologies while considering their wider social and civic implications.

The Hub Unconference is free to attend, although participants are required to register through the Shoko Festival website.

The event will take place alongside the country's annual urban culture festival, the Shoko Festival.

World.title: Guinea: Guinea Bans France 24, Withdraws Jeune Afrique Correspondent's Accreditation
World.content:
Dakar — The Committee to Protect Journalists calls on Guinean authorities to reverse Thursday's ban on France 24 after a presenter called President Mamadi Doumbouya a "putschist president" and to reinstate the accreditation of the pan-African weekly Jeune Afrique's Guinea correspondent Diawo Barry.

"By prohibiting France 24 from broadcasting and Jeune Afrique's Diawo Barry from working, Guinean authorities have shown their ruthless determination to silence independent voices and to intimidate other media outlets into self-censorship," said Moussa Ngom, CPJ's Francophone Africa representative. "Authorities must immediately reverse these decisions and refrain from further actions that erode press freedom and the public's right to information."

In its September 17 decision, the regulatory High Authority of Communication (HAC) said it had banned France 24 because it had failed to comply with its order the previous day "to immediately cease using terms deemed derogatory to the dignity of the Head of State and to make the required editorial corrections." The HAC also withdrew press accreditation for all the French state-owned channel's correspondents, special correspondents, and contributors in Guinea.

On Monday, a France 24 presenter used the word "putschist" while commenting on Doumbouya's visit to Ivory Coast.

Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn

Hours after the HAC's September 16 notice, France 24 added an online correction to the video's description, saying that Doumbouya had been "mistakenly labeled a coup leader."

"Having seized power in a coup on September 5, 2021, which overthrew President Alpha Condé, he was subsequently elected President of the Republic following the presidential election of December 28, 2025," the correction said.

France 24 told Agence France-Presse news agency that it had also apologized and corrected the error on air.

Also on September 16, the HAC revoked Barry's accreditation as Jeune Afrique's correspondent on the grounds that his coverage of news in Guinea did not meet the requirements of objective, neutral, balanced reporting.

The Guinean satirical newspaper Le Lynx, where Barry is publishing director, suggested that Jeune Afrique's September special report on Guinea, "Democracy under surveillance," had "ruffled feathers."

Jeune Afrique said that the HAC's decision had been handed down "without prior consultation" and was "not based on any specific allegation" to support its "vague" accusations.

Since Doumbouya took power, the HAC has introduced long-term and indefinite bans on numerous critical outlets and reporters. The whereabouts of journalist Habib Marouane Camara, who was seized by uniformed men in 2024, and of exiled journalist Mamoudou Babila Keita's elderly father, Elhadj Adama Keita, who was kidnapped in 2025, remain unknown.

Close 

CPJ's calls to request comment from the HAC went unanswered.

World.title: Nigeria: Niger State Imposes 24-Hour Curfew After Suspects Die in Custody
World.content:
The Niger State Government has imposed a 24-hour curfew across Minna, the state capital, as tension rises over the deaths of about 37 suspected illegal miners in the custody of the Nigeria Security and Civil Defence Corps (NSCDC).

The curfew takes effect immediately after Juma'at prayers on Friday, the government announced.

The government has also ordered the suspension of all mining activities in the state until further notice.

The directives are part of the state government's measures to address the prevailing security situation and restore safety across the state.



The government advised residents to remain indoors and comply fully with the curfew and other security directives until further notice.

The government also cancelled an All Progressives Congress (APC) rally scheduled for Minna on Saturday and suspended the NSCDC State Commandant, Suberu Aniviye, and his team.

Governor Mohammed Bago announced the measures during a press briefing in Minna on Friday.

He said the curfew was necessary to prevent a breakdown of law and order and to allow the government to manage the situation while investigations continue.

Background to the curfew

The deaths occurred after the NSCDC detained suspects arrested in connection with mining activities in the Ema Ushishi area of Niger State.

More than 37 detainees reportedly died while in custody, although the exact number and cause of the deaths have not been officially established.

The bodies were later moved to a mortuary, a development that heightened tension among youths and residents in Minna.

The incident triggered public concern and fears of possible protests or violence, prompting the state government to cancel the APC rally and impose the curfew.

Mr Bago described the deaths as tragic and unacceptable and said the government had begun steps to establish what happened.

He announced the constitution of a committee of inquiry to investigate the incident and determine the cause of the deaths.

Cause of death not established

The governor cautioned against concluding the forensic examinations, medical assessments, and autopsies.

He said possible causes being considered included suffocation caused by overcrowding in the detention facility and exposure to hazardous substances allegedly linked to illegal mining.

"There is no official root cause of these deaths yet. It is too early for anybody to conclude the root causes," Mr Bago said.

He said the state government was compiling a register of the deceased to identify and contact their families.

Mr Bago assured the victims' relatives that the government would engage with them and provide the necessary support during the investigation.

NSCDC commandant suspended

The governor announced the immediate suspension of Mr Aniviye and his team to allow for an impartial investigation.

He said the suspension was not a declaration of guilt but a measure to ensure that the investigation was conducted without interference.

The governor said the Director-General of the NSCDC, who is currently outside the country, had delegated his deputy to represent him in engagements concerning the incident.

He added that the state government had already met with the senior NSCDC official.

'We will probe deeply'

Mr Bago pledged that the government would investigate the incident thoroughly and ensure that those responsible for any wrongdoing were held accountable.

"Lives of human beings are lives of human beings. Such an unjust government will not tolerate any injustice, and we are going to make sure that we probe this thing deeply until we get to the root of this," he said.

He urged residents, particularly youths, to remain calm and obey the curfew.

Close 

"We are calling on all the youth to please stay away from violence. It is not going to bring about those who have died. It will rather cost us a lot at the end of the day," he said.

Mining suspended

The governor also ordered the closure of activities at the illegal mining site in Ema Ushishi.

He expressed concern over mining operations conducted without adequate technology, safety equipment and protective gear.

According to him, such practices expose miners to dangerous conditions and may have contributed to the incident.

The state government said it would continue to work with the NSCDC, the police, the State Security Service and other relevant agencies to establish the facts.

Mr Bago commiserated with the families of the deceased and declared three days of mourning in the state.

He said the cancellation of the APC rally was intended to allow the state to mourn the victims and focus on restoring calm and completing the investigation.

World.title: Algeria: Algeria Shifts Towards English As French Loses Ground in Schools
World.content:
Primary school pupils in Algeria are in for a change this year when, for the first time, the national curriculum will focus on English over French. The move follows a general trend across former French colonies in North Africa that are now prioritising English.

Algeria's 2026-27 school year kicks off next week with a change: a shift away from its usual focus on French as a second language.

Introduced in primary schools alongside French in 2022, from now on English will be the first foreign language children study.

Algerian education minister Mohamed Seghir Saadaoui announced in July that English classes would begin in the third year of primary school, when children are around 8. French lessons will follow a year later.

Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn

"In third year, only English will be taught," Saadaoui said.

Colonial baggage

The reform is part of a broader shift towards English in Algeria, where French remains closely tied to the country's colonial history.

In a paper published earlier this year, Algerian linguist Fadhila Leroul of the Mouloud Mammeri University of Tizi-Ouzou says the change can be explained not only by English's status as a global lingua franca, but because in the political context of former French colonies cutting ties from France, it steers Algeria "beyond the colonial legacy attached to French".

Algeria's history with France is long and tightly knit. Algeria was under French rule from 1830 to 1962, and was formally incorporated into France in 1848.

The French language was imposed everywhere from administration to formal education, but French was not accessible to just anyone. Arabic remained the language of the majority, while French was for Europeans and those with access to education.

According to Abu Bakr Khaled Saad Allah, an Algerian professor and researcher on higher education, this division made language deeply bound up with questions of national identity. Algerian writer Kateb Yacine, who wrote in French, once described the language as a "war trophy" taken from the former colonial power.

How a Nigerian town came to speak 'street French'

Following its independence, Algeria pursued policies to make Arabic the official national language. Arabic has been the country's primary language ever since, but for decades French remained prevalent in academia.

Algiers began toying with the idea of pushing English in the early 1990s, when primary school students were given the choice between English and French as a second language.

The plan was shut down and English was taken off the syllabus until 2019, when the minister of education put forward a plan to promote the use of English in universities. In 2022, President Abdelmadjid Tebboune announced that English would be introduced in primary schools.

The move coincided with a weakening of Algeria's relations with France. The relationship between the two countries has been tense since 2021 and, despite a period of rapprochement in 2023, worsened in 2024 after France declared its support for Morocco's sovereignty over the disputed Western Sahara.

The last word: why half of the world's languages could vanish this century

Regional shift

Both Morocco and Tunisia also took pains post-independence to cut ties to their former colonial power.

Morocco was a French protectorate from 1912 to 1956. Under Paris, French was the only language used for instruction. When Morocco got its independence, it steered the country towards policies of Arabisation to ensure Arabic once again took a central place.

The Moroccan government progressively introduced Arabic into primary education, but French remained the language of higher study, particularly in mathematics and science.

In the 2000s, the kingdom began to move towards a more multilingual model that supported both Arabic and French. At the same time, English was cementing its dominance as a global language - particular with younger generations.

One 2021 survey of 15-25-year-olds, commissioned by the British Council, found 40 percent of respondents believed English was the most important language to learn, compared to only 10 percent for French. As one participant said: "Everyone is turning to the English language because of its dominance on the internet."

By 2023, the Moroccan government began introducing English in public schools, where before it had been limited mainly to private institutions.

Close 

French overtakes Arabic to become world's fourth most spoken language

Tunisia was also a French protectorate from 1881 to 1956. The colonial rulers soon established a public education system that prioritised French, and it became the language of administration and economy. Those seeking access to higher opportunities therefore became bilingual in both French and Arabic.

After its independence, unlike Morocco and Algeria, Tunisia did not seek to cut out French from education and daily life. While it also pursued a policy of Arabisation, it maintained strong links with French education. The language of its former colonisers remained important in science, medicine, higher education, business and government.

But in contrast to its neighbours, Tunisia introduced English early on after independence as a foreign-language option in schools. Decades on, young people are increasingly choosing it.

In a 2020 Afrobarometer survey, around 68 percent of Tunisian respondents said English was the most important language for young people to learn. Only some 13 percent chose French.

World.title: Christine Taylor’s ‘Hey Dude’ salary was far lower than castmates remembered
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

Christine Taylor is looking back at her early Hollywood career — and revealing that her "Hey Dude" salary was far lower than her castmates remembered.

During an appearance on "The Secret World of Alex Mack" actress Natanya Ross’ "We’re Still Here, Babe" podcast Wednesday, Taylor — who played Melody Hanson on Nickelodeon’s western comedy series from 1989 to 1991 — said she earned approximately $3,500 per episode by the show’s final season.

"By the time ‘Hey Dude’ ended, we had this discussion amongst our castmates, and everyone seemed to think [that] by the last season, we were making $5,000 an episode," Taylor said.

"No, we were making $3,500 an episode, I’m pretty sure, because they would bump us up $500 every season," she added.

Taylor said all of the cast members earned the same amount, despite her co-stars’ shared belief that they were making $5,000 per episode.

"Everyone in their brain was like, ‘$5,000.’ I was like, ‘No way, no way. That would have … no, it did not happen,’" she recalled.

The actress said she was careful with the money she earned while working on the popular children’s series. She also credited her family with helping her financially as she moved to Los Angeles and pursued acting.

JENNIE GARTH ADMITS ‘SCARY’ FINANCIAL SPIRAL AFTER ‘90210’ FAME

Taylor remembered budgeting closely, using laundromats and monitoring her spending during the early stages of her career.

The actress went on to appear in "Saved by the Bell," "Blossom" and "Robin Hood: Men in Tights" before landing her breakout role as Marcia Brady in "The Brady Bunch Movie."

‘BRADY BUNCH’ STAR SHARES THE SIMPLE WORD THAT SAVED HER FROM HOLLYWOOD TRAPS

Taylor also revealed that she was asked to lose 10 pounds before playing the iconic character in the 1995 film.

"Of course, I was embarrassed when that ask came my way," she said, adding that the request reflected the attitudes of the 1990s and "would never happen today."

FORMER DISNEY STAR DYLAN SPROUSE SAYS ACTING AS A KID WAS ‘CHILD LABOR’

Taylor later starred alongside her husband, Ben Stiller, in films including "Zoolander" and "DodgeBall." The couple married in 2000, separated in 2017 and later reconciled. They share two children, Ella and Quinlin.

GET ENTERTAINMENT SCOOP DELIVERED RIGHT TO YOUR EMAIL BY CLICKING HERE

Taylor’s experience is part of a broader pattern in Hollywood, where a recognizable television role does not always guarantee financial security. Several former television stars have revealed that their salaries and residual checks were dramatically different from what audiences assumed.

JODIE SWEETIN SHARES SHOCKING 'FULL HOUSE' RESIDUAL CHECK AMOUNT DESPITE SHOW'S MEGA SUCCESS

"The Sopranos" star Drea de Matteo recently said she was forced to find alternative income after acting work slowed down. The actress revealed that she turned to OnlyFans after facing financial difficulties and a lien on her home.

During an appearance on Jamie Kennedy’s podcast, de Matteo said she earned enough through the platform to pay off a $75,000 lien within 75 minutes of posting a bikini photo. She also said she sometimes earned approximately $100,000 per month.

LIKE WHAT YOU'RE READING? CLICK HERE FOR MORE ENTERTAINMENT NEWS

"I was not — people think I’m made of f---iii money," de Matteo said. "Everyone sees me coming, they’re like, ‘Here comes that rich b---- from ‘The Sopranos.’ And it’s like, no, I’m not at all."

More recently, "Married... with Children" star Ted McGinley revealed that he receives extremely small residual checks from some of his popular television projects, despite starring in long-running shows.

In aninterview with Page Six, McGinley — who also found fame on "Happy Days" and "The Love Boat" throughout the 1970s, ’80s, and '90s — said he's holding on to a "whole stack" of checks each worth a total of one penny.

"I’ve been getting residuals all the time," said McGinley, who admitted the checks become smaller and smaller as the years go by.

CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

While McGinley doesn't bother to cash the small checks, he can't get himself to toss them either. The actor said he more than likely has a total of $2 worth of checks.

World.title: Obama criticizes Trump on approach to AI, escalates warning for stronger regulation
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

Former President Barack Obama criticized President Donald Trump's approach to artificial intelligence on Friday, calling for stronger federal regulation as the technology rapidly advances and concerns grow over safety, jobs and human control.

"The challenge we have is that, obviously, we have a president currently that has said that’s for losers," Obama said during an appearance at Colgate University in Hamilton, New York. "So we’ve got a gap of at least a couple of years, where things are moving really fast, and we have an administration that is not capable of or willing to — I would argue both — putting together a serious regulatory framework."

Obama's remarks expanded on a warning he issued last week, when he privately urged Democrats to make AI a central political issue.

DEMOCRATS EMBRACED AI’S GROWTH BEFORE TRUMP CAME ALONG — NOW THEY WANT TO SLOW IT DOWN

RNC member and Humans First Chairwoman Amy Kremer told Fox News Digital last week that policymakers should recognize AI’s risks without handing greater control to Washington or the technology companies themselves.

"You don't have to agree on politics to recognize reality: AI is moving incredibly fast, and policymakers need to understand both the opportunities and the very real risks that come with it," she said.

"Where I likely disagree with President Obama is on what government should do about it. The answer isn't handing Washington bureaucrats more control, and it certainly isn't allowing Big Tech to write the rules that govern itself," she said.

"We need guardrails that protect Americans while allowing American innovation to lead the world. That means protecting children, workers and our national security, while making sure China doesn't win the AI race," she continued.

AI 'DOOMERS' RISK KNEECAPPING US VS CHINA, BUT EX-PENTAGON VET SAYS BOTH EXTREMES MISS THE MARK

The debate shifted again Saturday when Trump announced the creation of an "AI Force" and said he plans to appoint an AI czar, while reiterating that his administration would resist efforts to slow development as the United States competes with China.

"We will not in any way hinder or stifle the Growth of this incredible Industry," Trump said in a lengthy Truth Social post.

Obama, speaking during Colgate’s Family Weekend, argued that relying on companies’ financial incentives and potential liability was insufficient to manage the risks posed by increasingly capable AI systems.

"[The] government has to be regulating this!" Obama said. "I heard one of Donald Trump’s main advisors on this make the argument that, ‘The market will take care of it. These companies will solve the safety issues because they have every incentive to do so — if it turns out to be dangerous, people will just sue them, and they’re worried about financial liability.’ That’s not how we treat airlines! Or drug companies, or food companies."

Obama's characterization of the administration came as the White House has pursued its own AI policy framework, though one focused heavily on encouraging development and limiting regulations it considers burdensome.

The Trump administration unveiled a national legislative framework in March addressing child safety, free speech, workforce issues and energy costs while calling for a consistent national approach to AI policy.

TRUMP’S DATA CENTER PUSH FRACTURES CONGRESS AS LOCAL ANGER EXPLODES: 'GRASPING AT STRAWS'

Trump also signed a national security directive in June ordering agencies to accelerate adoption of advanced AI while requiring systems used in national security settings to be "robust, steerable, controllable" and subject to clear lines of accountability.

The disagreement has intensified as executives inside the AI industry themselves call for additional safeguards. Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei urged companies last week to slow the pace of improvements to frontier models, while OpenAI CEO Sam Altman and Elon Musk expressed support for greater caution.

CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

Fox News Digital reached out to the White House for comment, but did not immediately hear back.

World.title: California animal rescue operator charged with felonies for alleged 'inhumane and unsanitary conditions'
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

A California animal rescue operator is facing up to 24 1/2 years in state prison after being charged with 35 felonies and misdemeanors for alleged cruelty to animals, as she is accused of leaving roughly 300 animals living in severe squalor.

Christine De Anda, 57, operator of the "Rock ‘N’ Pawz" rescue, faces 12 felony counts of animal cruelty, two felony counts of grand theft of labor, and 21 misdemeanor charges ranging from failure to provide care to operating an unlicensed kennel, according to the Los Angeles County District Attorney's Office.

Prosecutors requested that her bail be set at $914,500 ahead of her arraignment at the Antelope Valley Courthouse.

FLORIDA MAIL CARRIER ACCUSED OF SNATCHING PETS ON ROUTE, TRAPPING 100-PLUS CATS AND DOGS IN ‘HOARDING’ HOUSE

"For someone who calls herself an animal rescuer, there’s a fundamental responsibility to protect and care for the animals entrusted to her," Los Angeles County District Attorney Nathan J. Hochman said. "Instead, purported rescuer Christine De Anda allegedly left these animals to suffer or die from starvation, dehydration, untreated injuries and painful urine and fecal burns in filthy conditions."

"After repeated citations and warnings, Ms. De Anda continued taking in animals she could not care for, leaving hundreds to endure prolonged suffering," Hochman added. "These animal victims cannot speak for themselves and look to us to protect them. My office will hold their victimizer fully accountable for her inhumane actions."

The charges stem from a March 20, 2026, search warrant executed by Los Angeles County Animal Care and Control (DACC). Investigators removed more than 300 animals — primarily dogs, but also cats, a pig, a rabbit, a goose and two goats — in what DACC Director Marcia Mayeda called the "largest companion animal search warrant and rescue operation ever conducted" in the department’s history.

117 DEAD DOGS FOUND AT ANIMAL RESCUE, MANY WITH GUNSHOT WOUNDS AS INVESTIGATORS PROBE FOR ANSWERS

"More than 300 animals were removed from severely inhumane conditions," Mayeda said. "Animals were living in and saturated with their own excrement, had serious untreated illnesses and injuries, were emaciated, and were forced to live in small crates without adequate room to properly lie comfortably. Our teams have worked tirelessly to stabilize them, provide the medical care they needed, and help them recover."

At least one cat was found dead from starvation and dehydration at the start of the investigation, authorities said.

FLORIDA MAN ALLEGEDLY KILLS FAMILY'S KITTENS IN FRONT OF TEENAGE DAUGHTER AS FORM OF PUNISHMENT: OFFICIALS

"Sadly, despite all efforts, we were unable to save every animal due to the extent of their illnesses and injuries," Mayeda added. "DACC is deeply grateful for the support of the Society for the Prevention of Cruelty to Animals Los Angeles, Pasadena Humane and Kern County Animal Services for assisting us with this rescue and the Los Angeles County District Attorney’s Office for its commitment to pursuing justice for these animals."

The L.A. County DA's Office shared a video on YouTube of the animals at the shelter, showing the conditions that led to the charges.

CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

Prosecutors say De Anda continued to take in an increasing number of animals despite years of citations and warnings regarding her inability to care for them. She is accused of violating multiple county codes, including operating an animal kennel without required land-use approval, maintaining unsanitary conditions and having structures with unpermitted construction, plumbing, electrical and grading work.

World.title: Rutgers' Greg Schiano crashes out on official after costly penalty in tough loss to USC
World.content:
Rutgers was very, very close to pulling off an all-time upset against No. 12 USC on Saturday.

If it wasn’t for an ill-timed Pick Six in the third quarter and a questionable illegal substitution penalty, the Trojans may have been under the microscope a bit more Sunday morning. In the midst of the Scarlet Knights’ defeat, head coach Greg Schiano had one of the wilder crash outs of the year.

USC had the ball and was trying to drive down the field to get another score that likely would have sent more of the fans in Piscataway, New Jersey, home early. The referees called a play dead over an inadvertent whistle that set up another third-down play. It would have been 3rd-and-7 from USC’s own 28-yard line. But Rutgers was called for an illegal substitution that moved the ball up a few more yards.

It was one of the best games Rutgers played all season after being trounced by UMass to start the year and then suffering a defeat against Boston College. The Scarlet Knights had 460 total yards in the loss. Quarterback Dylan Lonergan had three touchdowns and two interceptions.

World.title: Mississippi gov trolls Lane Kiffin, LSU after Ole Miss defeats Tigers in coach's return to Oxford
World.content:
Mississippi Gov. Tate Reeves got the last word on Saturday night after Ole Miss defeated LSU in Lane Kiffin’s highly anticipated return to Oxford.

The Tigers climbed back into the game in the third quarter, scoring two touchdowns to bring the game to within three points. LSU tied the game with a field goal early in the fourth quarter. But Rebels quarterback Trinidad Chambliss scored on a 14-yard run with 6:14 left. Ole Miss added a two-point conversion to go up eight points.

THE CRAIG CARTON SHOW–UNFILTERED, UNAPOLOGETIC AND UNMISSABLE. DOWNLOAD HIS DAILY PODCAST NOW!

Ole Miss held on for the 32-24 victory.

Reeves added insult to injury with a post on X.

"What does a $54 million buyout for the old coach, a $91 million contract for the new coach, and a $50 million roster get you?" he wrote. "An a-s whipping in Oxford, Mississippi!"

The governor was referring to Kiffin’s departure from Ole Miss to LSU and the way the Tigers’ roster was constructed in the offseason.

World.title: Trump says new arch will also deploy drones, position snipers and store ammo
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

President Donald Trump said Sunday that his planned triumphal arch near the Arlington Memorial Bridge will be converted into a military complex capable of housing drones, deploying snipers and storing ammunition.

"At the strong request of the United States Military, and for National Security purposes, I have agreed to convert the magnificent Triumphal Arch … into a top grade Military Complex/Triumphal Arch," Trump wrote on Truth Social.

TRUMP REVEALS ARC DE TRIOMPHE-STYLE MONUMENT FOR AMERICA’S 250TH ANNIVERSARY

Trump said the 250-foot structure would have the "rapid ability" to deploy large numbers of drones, as well as snipers positioned on the roof and plaza areas. He also said the complex would store "large quantities of sniper ammunition."

"There will be no facility like this anywhere in the World," Trump wrote.

The monument, inspired by Paris’ Arc de Triomphe, is intended to welcome visitors crossing the Memorial Bridge from Arlington National Cemetery into the nation’s capital. The proposed structure would be clad in granite and topped with three golden statues.

FROM THE GILDED OVAL OFFICE TO A NEW BALLROOM: A LOOK AT TRUMP'S WHITE HOUSE PROJECTS

The project has drawn criticism from preservationists, lawmakers and veterans, who argue that it could disrupt views of the Lincoln Memorial and Arlington National Cemetery. Opponents have also questioned whether the project requires congressional approval under federal law.

The National Capital Planning Commission has approved the site and preliminary plans, but the project still requires additional review. Construction was previously expected to begin this month.

The arch is one of several major construction and renovation projects Trump has pursued in Washington.

TRUMP GAVE THE OVAL OFFICE A GILDED MAKEOVER – AND COVERED THE COST HIMSELF

The administration has also begun work on a 90,000-square-foot White House ballroom. The sprawling addition, announced last July, will accommodate approximately 650 seated guests and follow the White House’s classical design.

The White House currently lacks a formal ballroom, and the new structure is expected to replace the East Wing. Then-White House press secretary Karoline Leavitt said the ballroom was estimated to cost $200 million and would be financed by Trump and private donors.

CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

The ballroom is not the only update.

Trump has introduced gold accents in the Oval Office and Cabinet Room, lined the "walk of fame" with portraits of former presidents, including a photo of the autopen representing former President Joe Biden’s time in office, added stone pavers to the Rose Garden lawn and installed two 88-foot flagpoles.

The White House did not immediately respond to Fox News Digital's request for additional comment.

World.title: Waltz delivers blunt warning to nations defying Iran sanctions, touts Greenland deal
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

UNITED NATIONS, NEW YORK: President Donald Trump will return to the United Nations this week seeking greater international cooperation in confronting Iran, even as his administration moves to reshape the global institution hosting world leaders, U.S. Ambassador to the U.N. Mike Waltz told Fox News Digital in an exclusive interview ahead of the gathering.

US presses allies to enforce Iran sanctions ahead of the UN General Assembly

With the U.S.-Iran war entering its seventh month, Trump is expected to address the General Assembly on Tuesday and meet Gulf leaders whose countries have been directly affected by the conflict.

The gathering comes as Washington seeks to intensify economic pressure on Tehran, European allies confront Russia's ongoing war in Ukraine, and the administration faces questions about whether its push to reduce the U.N.'s size and spending risks diminishing the organization's ability to respond to international crises.

BESSENT WARNS IRAN'S OUTSIDE BACKERS TO 'STAY AWAY' AS TRUMP SEEKS TO 'ASPHYXIATE' TEHRAN'S ECONOMY

Waltz outlined what Washington expects from its partners on Iran: full enforcement of sanctions against Tehran, with consequences for countries that fail to comply.

"They will reinforce that message, but importantly, it's all of these countries actually enforcing the sanctions and what they're going to hear is there will be consequences for friend and foe," Waltz said. "The president is doing this for the future security of the world."

European and Asian allies have largely resisted Trump's requests for assistance in the Iran conflict, which began with U.S. and Israeli strikes in February, Reuters reported on Sept. 18. The war has also disrupted energy markets, with Iran obstructing shipping through the Strait of Hormuz and its Houthi allies tightening their grip on a critical Red Sea shipping corridor.

Waltz said the administration intends to make sanctions enforcement a central part of its diplomatic push during UNGA.

"The Iranian economy continues to crater," Waltz said, pointing to the country's currency, inflation and the U.S. naval blockade. "One way or another, the president has been crystal clear on our goals here that Iran cannot and will not have a nuclear weapon."

His remarks follow a Sept. 17 U.N. Security Council vote in which Russia and China blocked an effort to continue independent monitoring of international sanctions on Iran.

Trump is also expected to meet Gulf leaders to discuss the conflict and regional security. Waltz said the administration wants to hear directly from its Gulf partners about their concerns, describing the collective meeting as an important diplomatic opportunity.

JEFF BARTOS SAYS UN REFORM IS NO LONGER AN 'OXYMORON' AFTER $570M IN CUTS

A UN the Trump administration wants to change — but not abandon

The Iran conflict is unfolding against a broader debate over the future of the United Nations, an institution Trump has repeatedly criticized and his administration has sought to substantially reform.

On Sept. 16, the United States paid $725 million toward the U.N.'s regular budget and another $102 million for peacekeeping operations. The payments reduced Washington's outstanding debt and averted the immediate risk of losing its General Assembly voting rights in 2027. However, the U.S. still owed approximately $1.312 billion to the organization's regular budget, according to the U.N.

Asked why American taxpayers should continue funding an organization the administration has repeatedly criticized for what it considers anti-American bias, Waltz pointed to efforts to reduce spending and redirect the institution toward its original mission.

"The president is clear about getting the U.N. back to basics and helping it realize its potential," Waltz told Fox News Digital.

He said the administration had secured more than $1 billion in budget reductions, with roughly 3,000 headquarters positions being cut and a reduction of approximately 25% in peacekeeping personnel.

"We have the U.N. on a diet," Waltz said.

But Waltz also made clear that the administration does not intend to abandon the United Nations.

"There's got to be one place in the world where everyone can come together and put diplomacy first and can actually talk," he said. "We don't ever want to see a U.N. in Beijing or Moscow or Brussels."

"If we just walked away, you'd have 192 countries talking without us," Waltz added.

Gaza offers one example of how the administration intends to use the U.N. while limiting direct American military involvement. Waltz pointed to the U.N.-endorsed Board of Peace and the planned International Stabilization Force, which is intended to support security and a postwar transition in Gaza. The ambassador said he does not want American troops deployed there, arguing that international security operations should allow other countries to share the burden. The U.N. Security Council endorsed the Gaza peace plan and authorized the stabilization force in November 2025.

The State Department said Sept. 18 that Secretary of State Marco Rubio will be in New York from Sept. 20–23 to meet foreign counterparts, advance U.S. security and economic priorities and continue the administration's campaign for U.N. reform.

WALTZ CALLS OUT IRANIAN DIPLOMAT AT UN FOLLOWING DRONE STRIKES ON BAHRAIN AND KUWAIT

Greenland agreement adds another dimension to allied diplomacy

Trump arrives in New York days after announcing a new security agreement with Denmark and Greenland aimed at expanding the American military presence in the Arctic while restricting adversaries from establishing bases or making sensitive investments on the island.

The agreement falls short of Trump's earlier ambition to acquire Greenland, which remains an autonomous territory within the Kingdom of Denmark. Denmark and Greenland have stressed that the arrangement will not compromise the island's sovereignty or right to self-determination. Additional details of the agreement have yet to be made public.

Waltz told Fox News Digital that the deal reflects the Arctic's growing strategic importance as melting ice opens new shipping routes and increases access to energy and mineral resources.

"It's incredibly significant," Waltz said, pointing to Russia's Arctic military capabilities and the potential for new shipping routes to transform global trade.

"It took some tough tweets, maybe some tough language," he said. "We now have an agreement with our ally Denmark."

The agreement comes as European governments confront overlapping security challenges involving Russia's war in Ukraine, Arctic defense and uncertainty over transatlantic security arrangements, while Washington seeks greater allied cooperation in its campaign against Iran.

TRUMP ARRIVES AT NATO SUMMIT AS IRAN RIFT LOOMS ABOVE ALLIANCE TALKS

World leaders converge on New York

The U.N. expects 73 heads of state and 45 heads of government, along with 49 ministers, 11 vice presidents and one crown prince, to attend High-Level Week, U.N. spokesperson Stéphane Dujarric told reporters Friday.

Member states have submitted approximately 1,000 requests for bilateral meetings, while about 168 events are scheduled alongside the official proceedings.

The 81st General Assembly's General Debate begins Tuesday and runs through Sept. 28.

Beyond Iran, world leaders are expected to address Russia's invasion of Ukraine, the future of Gaza, international security and the U.N.'s ability to respond to emerging global challenges.

Waltz described the administration's approach with a slogan inspired by the president's political branding: "Make the U.N. great again."

CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

But the immediate diplomatic questions facing Washington are more concrete: whether allies will increase pressure on Iran, whether Gulf leaders can agree on a path toward ending the conflict and whether the administration's push for a leaner U.N. can coexist with its efforts to use the organization to address international security challenges.

World.title: Electric Mercedes motorhome targets 621-mile range
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

If you think you've seen some wild RVs, this one may reset the scale. Professional truck driver and content creator Tobias Wagner, better known online as Elektrotrucker, is preparing to drive around the world in a specially converted Mercedes-Benz eActros 600. A full Bliss Mobil living module sits behind the cab, turning this electric truck into a rolling home. Wagner plans to make the entire journey on battery power.

Mercedes-Benz Trucks says the route will cover about 28,000 miles through more than 30 countries over roughly one year, with a goal of no more than 80 charging stops. According to Mercedes, the trip would be the first known circumnavigation of the globe in a fully battery-electric truck. What really caught my attention is how far Wagner hopes to go between those stops. Here's how this massive electric motorhome works and why its 621-mile range target could be the toughest part of the trip.

100 KODIAK DRIVERLESS TRUCKS ARE HEADED FOR PUBLIC ROADS

NEW! 🩺 Free CyberGuy LIVE class: Get Better Healthcare With AI Saturday, September 26 at 11 a.m. ET / 8 a.m. PT

Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson will show you five practical ways AI can help you organize your health history, remember important appointment details, understand complicated medical information, research prescriptions and prepare smarter questions for your doctor. No technical experience is needed.

Save your free spot at CyberGuyLive.com

This electric Mercedes motorhome started as a long-haul truck

Underneath the living quarters sits the Mercedes-Benz eActros 600, a battery-electric truck built for long-distance commercial freight. Its three lithium iron phosphate battery packs provide a combined installed capacity of 621 kWh. Mercedes normally designs the truck to travel about 310 miles under specific fully loaded long-haul test conditions.

Wagner's expedition truck has a very different job. Instead of pulling a heavily loaded commercial trailer, it carries a custom living module. Mercedes also modified the truck with single rear tires and expedition equipment. Those changes help reduce weight and rolling resistance compared with a traditional freight configuration.

The finished expedition vehicle reportedly has a maximum weight of about 34,170 pounds. Power comes from Mercedes' electric axle and four-speed transmission. The eActros 600 produces about 536 horsepower continuously, with peak output reaching roughly 805 horsepower. That's a lot of muscle for a vehicle carrying its own kitchen and bed.

Could it really travel 621 miles on one charge?

This is where the project gets especially interesting. Wagner and Mercedes believe the lighter expedition setup, combined with careful hypermiling, could potentially travel as far as 621 miles on a single charge. That would be roughly double the range Mercedes quotes for a fully loaded eActros 600. Mercedes says the lighter expedition vehicle should significantly exceed the eActros 600's normal long-haul range. How close he gets will depend on road conditions, temperature, speed and terrain.

Why the 621-mile target could become important

Wagner wants to travel about 28,000 miles while stopping to charge no more than 80 times. That works out to an average of roughly 350 miles of driving per charging stop, although the actual distances will vary considerably along the route. Some stretches could become much more challenging.

The expedition will cross regions where high-powered truck charging remains difficult to find. The latest route includes Central and East Asia, Australia, the United States and several countries in Latin America. That's where stretching the truck well beyond its normal freight range could become useful.

ROBOTAXI PIT STOPS COULD POP UP NEAR YOU

Charging a 621-kWh battery takes serious power

Eventually, even this giant battery has to plug in. The eActros 600 supports CCS2 fast charging at up to 400 kW. Mercedes says that level of charging can take the battery from 10% to 80% in about 70 minutes under its specified conditions. Mercedes has also demonstrated Megawatt Charging System technology at up to 1,000 kW, which can cut charging times dramatically on compatible equipment.

Wagner's expedition setup has also been prepared for different charging systems around the world. It includes charging connections positioned on both sides of the truck. The project also has adapters designed for charging infrastructure in China and North America. That flexibility could prove essential once the truck leaves Europe. Mercedes revealed another important backup. Wagner has equipped the truck with his own Alpitronic DC charging station. That lets him charge from AC connections at up to 43 kW in special situations when conventional high-powered truck charging is not available.

The back of the truck is a fully electric home

Bliss Mobil added a roughly 13-foot expedition module behind the cab. Inside, Wagner gets a U-shaped dining area along with a kitchen. A bathroom sits toward the rear. There's also a drop-down bed that stores above the dining area when he wants more room during the day. The camper can sleep as many as four people. Wagner will have considerably more room because his primary travel companion is his dog, Krümelix.

The living module also follows the electric theme. It uses a separate 400-Ah lithium battery supported by 1,000 watts of solar power. That system handles equipment such as the induction cooktop, refrigerator and air conditioning. It also powers other onboard systems without relying on diesel or propane. The motorhome reportedly carries about 106 gallons of fresh water. A multistage filtration system helps Wagner manage water during extended stretches away from traditional campgrounds.

The camper can operate separately from the truck

Bliss Mobil designed the expedition module as a largely self-contained unit. Its electrical and plumbing systems sit within the camper rather than depending on the truck itself. That approach allows Bliss Mobil modules to move between compatible truck chassis.

Wagner's module does have a 24-volt connection to the eActros. That means the living area can draw energy from the truck's main battery when necessary. Still, the expedition has an obvious reason to conserve that electricity. Every bit of power used inside the camper could otherwise help move a nearly 17-ton vehicle farther down the road.

There's an electric motorcycle riding on the back

A giant expedition truck can handle plenty of roads, but there will always be places where its size becomes a problem. Wagner has another electric solution for that. A motorcycle carrier on the back holds a Honda WN7 electric motorcycle. When the road becomes too tight for the eActros, Wagner can leave the motorhome behind and continue on two wheels. The motorcycle uses a 9.3-kWh battery and produces about 67 horsepower. It's a useful backup for a trip designed to reach places far beyond normal highway rest stops.

TOYOTA JOINS HYDROGEN TRUCK ALLIANCE PUSH

Nearly $800,000 buys one very unusual motorhome

None of this comes cheaply. A price sheet displayed with the vehicle broke down the cost of the eActros 600 truck, Bliss Mobil camper and additional equipment. The total is approximately $796,600 including tax based on the exchange rate used at the time. Call it nearly $800,000. The Honda electric motorcycle wasn't included in that figure.

Of course, this also isn't a production RV you can configure at your local Mercedes dealership. Wagner's vehicle is a specialized one-off expedition build created around a commercial electric truck. We've seen other companies rethink how electric vehicles fit into camping. The CyberTrailer takes a different approach, using solar power and an onboard energy system to support off-grid travel.

The around-the-world trip starts Sept. 20

Mercedes-Benz Trucks says Wagner will officially depart from IAA Transportation 2026 in Hanover, Germany, on Sunday, Sept. 20. From there, the trip is expected to last about a year. Mercedes says Wagner will travel through around 30 countries on five continents while putting battery-electric truck technology through real-world conditions well beyond familiar European freight routes. Mercedes says the planned route may still change as the trip progresses. The vehicle may be built for an extraordinary adventure, but the results could tell us something much bigger about electric transportation.

What this means to you

You probably won't be putting an $800,000 electric expedition truck in your driveway. Still, this trip could answer questions that eventually affect far more ordinary electric vehicles. Range is only part of the EV equation. Reliable charging becomes even more important when you leave major highways or travel through areas with limited infrastructure. Wagner will be testing both. If the eActros can consistently travel well beyond its standard commercial range, engineers will get another example of how vehicle weight and driving technique can change battery performance.

The charging side may prove equally revealing. A vehicle can carry an enormous battery, but long-distance travel still depends on finding equipment powerful enough to recharge it. Wagner's onboard charging equipment gives him another option when high-powered public chargers are unavailable, but slower charging could add considerable time to the trip.

We have already seen experiments that attack the charging problem from another direction. One electric road project is testing technology that can transfer power to vehicles while they drive. Wagner's trip takes the opposite approach. He is bringing a huge battery and finding out how far today's infrastructure can take it.

Kurt's key takeaways

I love a good road trip, but this one takes the idea to another level. What fascinates me most isn't simply whether Wagner can squeeze 621 miles out of this massive battery. I want to see what happens when he leaves the easy charging routes behind and has to make this technology work across more than 30 countries. That's where this trip could get really interesting. A giant battery and impressive range numbers are great, but you still need a working charger when you pull in. If Wagner can circle the globe with roughly 80 charging stops, that's a pretty strong demonstration of how far electric trucking has come. And if he gets stranded looking for power along the way, we'll learn something from that, too.

World.title: Ed Sheeran calls situation in Gaza ‘unjustifiable’ in first concert since Macklemore controversy
World.content:
Demonstrators shouted “Free, free Palestine” in unison as motorists honked their horns in support.

Robert Boucher, 73, a retired surgeon, said he was there to take a stand for freedom of speech.

“The action that’s been taken by the stadium owners and folks who oppose Macklemore and what he represents and the comments that he’s made, that’s really an unjustifiable attempt to squelch free speech,” Boucher said.

The Philadelphia resident asserted that his criticism is of the Israeli government and its treatment of civilians in Gaza, not a stance against Jewish people.

“We’re here to specifically support our right to say the things that we’re saying and to not be labeled as antisemites or anti-Israel,” he said.

Gwen Myrick, 51, of West Philadelphia, said she supports Macklemore’s stand.

“I am here in support of Macklemore,” she said. “Because that is how a movement is born — standing up for the people who are brave enough to stand up.”

Robert Boucher, a retired surgeon, asserted that criticism of the state of Israel for its treatment of civilians in Gaza is not a stance against Jewish people. Nicole Acevedo / NBC News

The protest followed a weeklong controversy that began after Macklemore voiced support for Palestinians. He accused Robert Kraft, owner of the New England Patriots and Gillette Stadium, of organizing a boycott among stadium owners in response, an allegation Kraft did not deny.

In a statement, Kraft, a staunch supporter of Israel and Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, said the decision was not intended to stifle Palestinian advocacy or diminish Palestinian suffering but to ensure a “welcoming environment” at Gillette Stadium in Foxborough, Massachusetts. Macklemore had been scheduled to open two “Loop” tour dates there later this month.

Sheeran said previously that the company promoting his tour made the final decision to drop Macklemore because it held the rapper’s contract.

Messina Touring Group did not respond to multiple requests for comment from NBC News. The promoter told Rolling Stone that it had been informed that multiple venues “will not allow a concert to take place with Macklemore on the lineup,” resulting in his removal.

Macklemore had been scheduled to open Saturday’s show in Philadelphia. Instead, the protesters outside Lincoln Financial Field repeated some of the same pro-Palestinian remarks that Macklemore said led to his removal.

Adi Chattopadhyay, who said he helped organize the demonstration, said Sheeran could halt criticism by donating money to Palestinian-related causes.

“Send that money to families in Gaza,” he said. “Will he support the innocent people of Gaza who have been bombarded? Will he actually do something?”

Macklemore has pledged to donate $1 million, which he said represented all of the net earnings from Sheeran’s tour, to six organizations supporting Palestinians. Kraft later pledged $2 million toward causes supporting people impacted by the war in Gaza to match a similar donation made by Sheeran.

On Saturday, Sheeran told fans at his show that he’s spoken to “people across the spectrum to work out how to make a contribution that helps victims of these terrible times.”

Sheeran, right, said previously that the company promoting his tour made the final decision to drop Macklemore, left, because it held the rapper’s contract. Getty Images

‘I just really came for Ed Sheeran’

Despite the controversy, fans inside the stadium said they were excited to watch Sheeran’s performance, and weren’t bothered by the lack of opening acts.

Friends Karen Mossop, 59, and Karen Macort, 62, said they were there to experience only one artist — Sheeran.

Mossop defended Sheeran and said he just “got caught up in a really negative campaign.”

“Because he’s a really nice guy, he didn’t realize the ramifications of what would happen,” she said.

Mossop also questioned the professionalism of the artists who dropped out.

“It’s a shame that the opening acts quit,” she said. “They’re supposed to be professionals, and they should have acted professionally.”

Alexandria Rasa, 27, of neighboring New Jersey, said she was excited to experience her second Sheeran concert.

“I just really came for Ed Sheeran,” Rasa said. “I don’t really care about his opening acts, so that didn’t really affect me.”

Friend Hannah Luster, 26, also of New Jersey, was focused on the task at hand — basking in the music.

“[I’m] definitely going to enjoy it, probably going to take a video or two,” she said.

Fans inside the stadium said they were excited to watch Sheeran’s performance and weren’t bothered by the lack of an opening act. Heather Barry / Getty Images

Dale Dietrich, 46, and his friend, Jeanine Fusik, 47, were hoping that Taylor Swift, who has been known to join Sheeran onstage, and vice versa, might appear with him Saturday night.

“Ed needs to be rescued,” Dietrich said, referring to fallout from Macklemore’s departure, “and there’s probably one person that can really do it.”

Sheeran did not appear to need saving once the show got underway, though. But he did address the absence of his normal “B stage,” saying it was missing “because I was afraid of what might happen if I stood in the middle, and I will admit that.”

Sheeran spent much of his time onstage as a one-man band — a style fans will recognize from past performances — letting his vocals, instruments and loop pedal command the stadium crowd. But he also got some backup after calling a friend for last-minute help.

The fill-in musicians — a drummer, keyboardist, bassist, guitarist and violinist — had three days to learn the songs, Sheeran said, and he thanked them for their support.

He seemed most grateful to the audience at Lincoln Financial Field.

“Today has honestly been the best show of my life” he said. “I’ve felt so much love from you guys, and I am so grateful.”

The concert ended with fireworks and a crowd on its feet.

Nicole Acevedo reported from Philadelphia, and Dennis Romero from San Diego.

World.title: Trump says his proposed arch will include a military complex housing drones and snipers
World.content:
President Donald Trump said in a Truth Social post Sunday that he would convert plans for a Washington, D.C.-area “Triumphal Arch” to those for “a top grade Military Complex/Triumphal Arch” at the request of the U.S. military, citing “national security.”

The new plan, he said, is to “house, store, and have the rapid ability to use large numbers of drones, plus Snipers, on both the roof and plaza areas, and additionally have and hold large quantities of sniper ammunition in storage.”

Reached for comment, a Pentagon spokesperson said the department has “nothing additional to provide beyond the post.” The White House declined to provide additional information.

His post marked a significant change in plans that had already been in progress, as the Trump administration had announced earlier this month that it was preparing to break ground in the coming weeks.

A model of President Trump's planned "Triumphal Arch" at the Great American State Fair in Washington, D.C., on July 2. Joe Raedle / Getty Images file

The president’s announcement was also the second time he has framed a controversial construction project as a national security endeavor. Trump previously argued that the White House ballroom construction was necessary for national security and tied the project to an underground military complex.

The ballroom, too, has faced legal pushback, though the Supreme Court ruled at the end of August that the administration could move forward on ballroom construction indefinitely. The National Trust for Historic Preservation sued over the ballroom, arguing that Trump did not have the unilateral ability to undertake the project. The Supreme Court, though, ruled that the trust likely did not have proper standing to bring the case forward.

In early April, the White House argued to a federal appeals court that the project, including the ballroom, was “necessary to ensure the safety and security of the White House and its grounds.” Weeks later, a gunman stormed a security checkpoint at the White House Correspondents’ Association dinner, prompting the president to issue renewed calls for a White House event space. The annual dinner is hosted by the White House Correspondents’ Association, not the White House.

Artist renderings and diagrams of the new White House East Wing and ballroom, briefly posted on the National Capital Planning Commission's website, on Feb. 17. Jon Elswick / AP

The proposed 250-foot arch project, which would sit in a roundabout between the Lincoln Memorial and Arlington National Cemetery, has faced legal challenges from veterans and historians. The project area sits on the Potomac, across from Washington.

The arch proposal has already passed key hurdles, though it’s unclear how Trump’s announcement could affect the prior approvals. In April, the project obtained approval from the Commission of Fine Arts, which is now composed of the president’s allies after he fired previous members. In July, the National Capital Planning Commission, which is led by Trump appointees, approved the preliminary site and building plans. The arch, which would sit a few miles from Reagan airport, also passed the Federal Aviation Administration’s air safety standards last week, with the administration announcing that it “would not pose a hazard to aircraft.”

Rep. Don Beyer, D-Va., whose district includes Arlington National Cemetery and is adjacent to the proposed site, slammed Trump’s plan in a post to X.

“Putting a drone launching site directly in the landing path for DCA is a stupid, dangerous, and unworkable idea,” he said in the post.

The project appeared poised to move forward imminently. Interior Secretary Doug Burgum announced on Sept. 3 that the administration was preparing to start excavation work “over the next two-week period.” U.S. District Judge Tanya Chutkan ordered the Trump administration to provide 48 hours’ notice before it starts “any activity” on the arch, other than work to determine whether there are archaeological resources on the proposed site.

Trump has made Washington-area construction projects a key priority during his second term. Besides plans for the ballroom and arch, the president also moved to renovate the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool, added a White House helipad and pushed to fix fountains in the capital.

Following the renovation of the Reflecting Pool, chunks of the pool’s new coating floated to the surface and the water turned green with algae. Trump also repeatedly claimed, without evidence, that vandalism led to the damage.

World.title: Princess Diana’s brother says King Charles ‘gaslit’ him in dispute over book claims
World.content:
Princess Diana’s brother, Charles Spencer, has accused King Charles of gaslighting him after Buckingham Palace pushed back at his claims about the monarch’s conduct.

Buckingham Palace released an unusually forceful statement Wednesday ahead of the release of a memoir by Spencer, which charts the breakdown of then-Prince Charles’ marriage to Princess Diana, and the fallout from her death in a Paris car crash in 1997, one year after the royal couple finalized their divorce.

In an initial excerpt released ahead of publication, Spencer recalled a heated phone call with Charles amid a disagreement about funeral arrangements, claiming that a furious Charles had told him Diana would “soon be forgotten.”

“While we do not comment on books as a matter of principle, His Majesty is mindful that the pain of fraternal grief can cloud reason, affect judgment and color memory in ways others do not recognize, even many years after such a loss,” the palace had responded.

In an interview with Britain’s Mail on Sunday newspaper, Spencer said: “It is not every day you wake up to find you’ve been gaslit by the king.”

“It was astonishingly provocative and below the belt because it was essentially trying to say I’d lied without the king being able to deny what I’d said,” Spencer added.

“Gaslighting” is a form of manipulation where the manipulator is trying to get someone to question their own reality, memory or perceptions.

In a further interview with the BBC that aired Sunday, Spencer said he told close friends and family at the time about what Charles had said “because it was so monstrous.”

He also appeared to indicate that Charles and Diana’s sons, heir to the throne Prince William and his brother, Prince Harry, were aware of his allegation before the memoir was published.

“I don’t like to talk about what I’ve been speaking about to William and Harry, but this will not be a surprise to them, I will tell you that. These words will not be a surprise to them,” he said.

There has been no public comment from William or Harry on Spencer’s memoir.

Spencer, an earl whose aristocratic family has generational ties with Britain’s royal family, denied that the book, published after years of silence, was motivated by money or score-settling. “I have a duty, as an eyewitness to history, in the final season of my life,” he told the BBC. “I wanted to just put things down that were true.”

He added: “This is not a threat, it’s a fact: I know lots of things about the king which I chose not to include in the book, because they were not relevant. I’m a historian. ... I wanted to give the context.”

Spencer’s book, “Swan Song: Diana, My Sister,” is due to be released publicly on Tuesday.

In other excerpts from the book, published in advance by the Daily Mail newspaper, Spencer writes that Charles sounded “giddily elated” and “like a lottery winner” when they spoke by phone immediately after Diana’s death, adding: “I suspect the prince’s first reaction must have been to think more of how this event might free him to marry the woman he loved, rather than appreciating the loss of one he did not.”

He also speaks about his sister’s mental health and recounts conversations with her, saying she had told him how “things became very difficult indeed in the marriage early on.”

The book also includes an allegation that Diana suspected Charles was “in love with” a member of royal staff during their marriage, separate from his relationship with the now-Queen Camilla, though Spencer says he has no evidence that was true.

Since its initial statement, Buckingham Palace has remained silent on the further allegations in Spencer’s book. The palace again declined to comment Sunday.

Prince Harry, who quit as a working royal six years ago amid a reported rift with senior royals, has remained close to the Spencer family, with his own memoir “Spare” thanking “my mother’s siblings for their love, support, time, and perspective.”

Of his relationship with Harry, Spencer said: “There’s this perception in the media that I’m on Harry’s side. Well, I’m on my deceased sister’s sons’ side, both of them, and if either of them wanted anything, then I’d be equally there for them. I never get involved in one camp or the other, except as a benign figure, I hope.”

The royal family continued to undertake public duties this week even as Spencer’s book has dominated the headlines, with Charles also meeting with senior figures in AI at a summit in Scotland.

World.title: Is it too early to panic in the NFL? These teams don’t want to find out
World.content:
“My message is just echoing ‘don’t change, don’t flinch, don’t blink,’” Cowboys quarterback Dak Prescott said. “This is a long year. We have to stick together.”

Two seasons ago, the Rams were one of three teams that started 0-2 and still made the playoffs. But as the Rams, the preseason Super Bowl favorite, prepare to face the Giants (1-0) on Monday, they have already lost more than their first game. Pass-rushing star Myles Garrett will miss at least four games after he underwent surgery last week to combat swelling in his left knee. The un-retirement of Aaron Donald will help absorb the loss of Garrett along the defensive line, but Donald won’t be an every-down player.

The Rams’ vaunted offense managed just 190 yards in its first performance against the San Francisco 49ers, as well.

“The big area of focus improvement will be in regard to the pass game and some of the different things that we can do collectively,” coach Sean McVay said. “It always starts with me.”

The Rams are one of five teams this season — joining the Broncos, the Packers, the Cowboys and the Washington Commanders — that already have one division loss. Of that group, NFC East rivals Washington and Dallas find themselves in the most precarious situations. When they play each other Sunday, one will leave 0-2 in its division.

“It’s another division game,” Cowboys pass rusher Rashan Gary said. “Understanding that, we know we just went 0-1, and we can’t do that going into this week. The urgency is up, for sure.”

The Patriots have been here before. Last season they responded to their 0-1 start by losing only two more times over the next four months en route to a Super Bowl appearance. The bounceback was helped, however, by playing the easiest schedule in 26 years.

It will be more difficult to keep this latest season-opening loss from snowballing into something bigger. The Patriots’ next three opponents all made the playoffs last season, starting with Sunday’s matchup against the Pittsburgh Steelers — whose defense sacked New England quarterback Drake Maye five times and forced five turnovers when the teams met last season. An injured ankle will sideline the Steelers’ top offseason acquisition, receiver A.J. Brown, for at least the next four games.

World.title: American dream of owning a home out of reach for many as mortgage rates soar (again)
World.content:
The average interest rate on a 30-year fixed mortgage soared to 7.2% this week, its highest in a year and a half. Coupled with home prices near record highs, it’s putting the American dream of owning a home further out of reach for millions.

“We don’t want to buy this big, beautiful house only to just sit in it, staring at each other, stressing about a mortgage payment every month,” said Alexandra DeCandia, who teaches biology at Georgetown University.

DeCandia and her husband, Edward Schrom, both 33, are looking for their first home in the Washington area. They hope to start a family and want to buy a home before they do.

“It’s something that’s a huge decision and one that will impact us, as well as our future family,” DeCandia said. “It’s very stressful to try to figure that out in this shifting landscape.”

Mortgage rates were on a downswing earlier this year, hitting 5.99% in late February. But ever since the U.S. and Israel attacked Iran on Feb. 28, they have skyrocketed.

Mortgage interest rates are heavily influenced by the yield on 10-year Treasury bonds, which has been rising as oil prices soar and drive up the cost of goods across the economy.

And mortgage rates could keep rising. The Federal Reserve this week hiked its key interest rate in an effort to get a handle on inflation — and it suggested it may raise rates again this year. Higher rates can drive up borrowing costs across the economy.

Meanwhile, the average home price nationwide is near a record high, at $429,100 as of August.

One bright spot for homebuyers, however, is inventory. There were 1.62 million unsold homes on the market in August, according to the National Association of Realtors.

That’s equal to 4.9 months’ supply, which is measured as the time it would take at the current pace of sales to sell all those homes. That is the highest level in more than a decade, and it gives prospective homebuyers more room to negotiate prices.
