But when they said their goodbyes at the airport, her middle sister, Shawnessy Luke, noticed something was off.

"I remember it like it was yesterday," Shawnessy Luke said. "The way he hugged her. And I think that’s strange. That’s prolonged. And I knew something was going on."

Shawnessy Luke believed her sister, Vienna, when she began to open up. (Allison Luke)

Shawnessy Luke describes herself as a person with great intuition and "like a dog with a bone." She waited until she and Vienna Luke got back to their parents' home to ask questions. She was doing her laundry in the family’s narrow utility room when she insisted that her sister explain.

"She definitely pulled it out of me," said Vienna Luke. "I did not volunteer."

Vienna Luke told her sister what happened in the days leading up to the drinking game, facts that were accepted in court: How Sewell had held her hand, how he called her up from her basement bedroom to watch a lightning storm and then massaged her back, and how he told her he loved her.

Then she shared how Sewell proposed she get drunk, and how she couldn’t remember much more than that.

"In my moral compass brain, the minute I heard those things, I was like, I don’t need to know anymore, I believe you," said Shawnessy Luke. "We’ve got to tell someone about this because [...] whatever happened to you [...] was wrong."

Shawnessy Luke says she insisted they tell their mom and dad.

Middle sister Shawnessy Luke has stuck by her sister's side through all the steps of the investigation. 'I'm here in support of her going through this process. That's my goal. That's the only reason I'm here.' (Ben Nelms/CBC)

The night in question had happened in June 2007, about 10 years before the #MeToo social movement. As Vienna Luke told her parents about Sewell holding her hand and massaging her back, she stopped short of sharing the most damning memory of all — that she woke up to Sewell removing her underwear. She felt like her parents didn’t know how to handle what she was saying, and didn't have the vocabulary at the time to talk about sexual assault.

"I knew that I couldn’t share more," she said.

Her father called Sewell right away. She didn’t overhear their conversation, but she recalls her father handed her the phone and she found herself suddenly on the line with Sewell.

Vienna Luke pleaded with Sewell to tell his wife what had happened, hoping her oldest sister would take her side. She still doesn’t know if that happened, only that her oldest sister has continued to stand by her husband and is still married to him today.

Her parents declined to be interviewed for this story. In a victim impact statement filed in court, they wrote: "Our effort to uncover the full story was unsuccessful. Lacking information and clarity, we had no path forward. We felt uneasy about what we knew, but did not pursue this matter further."

Years of numbing

In the years that followed, the Luke family struggled with the divide created by that night: Vienna’s oldest sister and Sewell on one side, Shawnessy and Vienna Luke on the other, and their parents trying to walk a line between all three of their daughters.

"It was easier to take Justin for his word," Vienna Luke said. "He was the one that knew what happened. He got to write the story."

Vienna Luke in 2014, seven years after the horrible night. 'I was just a robot,' she said. 'I was going through the motions of what I thought I was supposed to be doing.' (Allison White)

With no clarity about what had actually happened and that one horrific memory of him removing her underwear replaying in her head, Luke says she spent years feeling like a robot trying to numb her pain.

She also moved out of her parents' house and moved to Vancouver, got a job, and met a man who she credits for showing her how to love herself again.

When they started a family, Luke says something inside her started to shift. She knew she’d have to tell her children the truth someday, and something about birth reconnected her to her body.

"My body wasn’t just laboring," she wrote in her journal. "[It was] waking up."

Twelve years after the assault, and weeks after she delivered her second child, Luke called up her sister Shawnessy.

"Hey, I’m ready to deal with this," she said.

So the two sisters made a list.

The sister detectives

Together, they wrote down all the names of people they suspected had soured on Sewell after he had disclosed to his wife and friends two extramarital affairs five years earlier.

Shawnessy Luke's first call was to one of those ex-lovers, a female veterinarian who had worked at Sewell's clinic.

Justin Sewell's veterinarian clinic in Fort St. John, B.C. (Matt Prepost)

In a recording of that phone call shared with CBC and in court testimony, the woman said she and Sewell were discussing previous sexual experiences when he said something shocking.

"So what he told me was that he put ketamine in [Vienna’s] drinks," the ex-lover revealed during a phone call Shawnessy Luke recorded. "But he didn’t know how much was enough to like, make her forget."

The sisters say this new information validated a hunch they had come to believe: that Vienna Luke had been drugged.

It also gave her a little piece of evidence to march into the Vancouver Police Department and report.

'I do my job for the victims'

Vienna Luke's file was transferred up to the small RCMP detachment in Fort St. John. Against all odds, it landed on the desk of Sgt. Joëlle LaChance, a female officer with a special commitment to cases that many officers would simply dismiss as too hard and too old.

"My whole life I have been a champion for the underdog," she said. "Being able to stand up for the victim … it's why I do my job."

'Being able to stand up for the victim — it's why I do my job,' said RCMP Sgt. Joëlle LaChance. (submitted by Joëlle LaChance)

LaChance said she knew Sewell — with his stellar reputation in the community, had a lot to lose. So instead of going directly to the veterinarian to question him, she called on other RCMP units for help, including the undercover unit.

Together, they hatched a plan.

Court records show Sewell had emailed Vienna Luke several times in the years since the night of the drinking game, asking her to accept that he had changed and hoping that the extended family could be together again.

Luke showed the police those emails. Together, they crafted back emails that suggested there could be a possibility for family reconciliation, but first Luke would need the whole truth and they’d have to meet face-to-face.

They pitched Sewell on a plan to fly to Vancouver to meet Luke.

Unbeknownst to Sewell, Luke would be prepared.

Vienna Luke carried this piece of paper with her into the undercover operation at YVR airport. Her notes came from training with the RCMP. (Vienna Luke)

For weeks, she trained, preparing to grill him for the facts. She spent a couple of days in a hotel room, sitting across from an undercover RCMP officer who role played with her. The officer worked to get her comfortable asking tough, direct questions, using words like "vagina" and "ejaculate" — specific terms that would be necessary for charges to be laid.

"This isn’t a trained hitman," the undercover officer said. "She’s very polite, very soft-spoken. And I knew that was exactly the opposite of what we were going to need to do."

Something changed for Vienna Luke when she became a mother. 'My firstborn, [...] my constant reminder that I am lovable,' she wrote in her journal. 'My second child, [...] you showed me a bravery I didn't know I had.' (Ben Nelms/CBC)

On the day of the sting at Vancouver airport, everyone involved held their breath. RCMP had laid the groundwork, but as soon as the tape started recording and Sewell walked in, it would be entirely up to Luke to get the truth.

For the plan to work, Luke would need to be both victim and hero. The RCMP believed it was the best chance at bringing charges. Luke knew it was her only chance to get answers.

"You think I'm exactly the same," Luke remembered thinking. "You think I'm gonna play your same little game, but we've got a new game and I'm writing it."

An extraordinary encounter – and as much truth as she’ll ever get

In the recording, Sewell sits down across from Luke and quickly tries to take control. He claims pornography and a culture that objectifies women is part of why he assaulted her that night.

"Okay, but you’re not actually telling me what happened," Luke replies. "Let’s get back to the night and what actually … happened."

The undercover officer who had spent time coaching Luke for this moment felt proud.

"Take control of that conversation," he said in an interview while listening back to the recording. "Don’t just accept a two-minute fluffy bullshit answer."

An excerpt from the transcript submitted in court of the surreptitious recording between Vienna Luke (VL) and Justin Sewell (JS). (CBC)

Luke persists, peppering Sewell with questions seeking specific details, seemingly undeterred by the fact she’s learning this information about the worst night of her life for the first time.

On tape, Sewell confesses to drugging her, removing her clothing, masturbating and ejaculating twice on her body, and taking 30 photos, including ones where he is spooning her naked body and one where his penis is near her face.

As Luke prepares to wrap up, she lobs an open ended question.

"Is there anything that I’m not asking?" Luke said.

"No reason for me to disclose this. But I took pictures of you at other times," Sewell replied.

His response allowed the RCMP to recommend another charge, this one for voyeurism.

A rare conviction in a historic sexual assault

On the morning of April 26, 2022, Fort St. John RCMP arrested Sewell as he left his home for work.

LaChance said this case was a big deal for the small Fort St. John RCMP detachment. 'People didn't believe we could do it,' she said. 'I believed with Vienna as the agent that we could do it because she was showing the strength and wanting to have justice.' (Tom Summer/CBC)

Sewell pleaded guilty to one count of sexual assault and two counts of voyeurism — one for the photos he took of her the night he assaulted her and one for times he had watched her through her bedroom window. Crown agreed to stay a charge of administering a drug with intent to commit a sexual assault.

In the courtroom, Luke’s mother, father, and Sewell’s supporters listened to the recording from the airport.

A provincial court judge sentenced Sewell to house arrest. Crown appealed and the Court of Appeal judges determined the lower court judge had overstated the mitigating fact of Sewell’s confession.

They issued a sentence of 33 months less a day in prison for his crimes.

Luke asked the court to remove the publication ban on her name — something that is standard in cases of sexual assault to protect the victim’s identity.

As she began to tell friends and acquaintances her whole story, that she was the unnamed victim, she says she realized how important it was to her that she could also say she was the secret agent.

Vienna Luke is telling her story for the first time publicly in a new CBC Podcast called Agent Layla. (Vienna Luke)

"It took this … experiment of the police saying, 'Hey, how about you go undercover as yourself' for me to realize, whoa, look at the advocate I can be for myself," she said.

"I was Agent Layla. That's me."

The CBC podcast Personally: Agent Layla is available wherever you get your podcasts.

World.title: The tangled what-ifs of Alberta separation — from trade and treaties to currency and disaster costs
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

It’s the big things that might spring to mind first when pondering the consequences of Alberta separation — the potential impacts to the gross domestic product, jobs, wages, debt and such.

This week’s major report by the University of Calgary’s School of Public Policy laid out these figures in sharp relief, with a series of outcomes ranging from modest long-term benefits to massive long-range detriments (and short-term pain in any scenario).

But beyond the headline figures contained in the government-commissioned summary report, we find a series of the U of C academics’ technical papers.

They underpin predictions of an independent Alberta’s debt load and potential job losses by diving into the many complex factors a breakaway republic named Alberta would have to contend with.

When you form a whole new country from the rib of an existing one, there’s a tonne to consider, from tariffs and multilateral agreements to currency, interest rates and treaties — both international and Indigenous.

Or even seemingly smaller (but still billion-dollar) factors, like public-sector pension obligations, and who pays for the aftermath of major floods and wildfires, the kinds of disasters Alberta knows all too well.

So without further ado, here’s a glimpse at the report’s analysis of some of the other challenges of Alberta independence, in the event that the public’s current pro-unity majority shifts dramatically, and opts for independence in two successive referendums, beginning with the one on Oct. 19.

Trade-offs

Owing largely to oil pipelines, Alberta’s trade south of the border is more valuable than its exports to the rest of Canada, the School of Public Policy report notes.

Because of that, the authors suggest it may be most expedient for a new country to strike a direct deal with Washington, rather than try to inject itself into the already rocky talks around the Canada-U.S.-Mexico Agreement (CUSMA).

However, it notes that while the current U.S. administration might offer terms that are beneficial to an oil-producing neighbour, the report adds: “As much as the U.S. depends on Alberta oil and gas exports, Alberta depends on making those exports more, and the U.S. administration knows this.”

Danielle Smith and Donald Trump: future trade dealmakers? (Danielle Smith/X)

Meanwhile, joining CUSMA — does it become CUSAMA? ACUSMA has a certain ring — would provide largely tariff-free access to its big customers, including Mexico. “However, the process could be lengthy,” the report states, a familiar refrain throughout.

Also, ratification to Alberta’s benefit might run into pushback from Democrats in the U.S. Congress, given their historic opposition to the Keystone XL pipeline.

And while Alberta separatists might be wary of global bodies like the World Economic Forum (WEF) and World Health Organization (WHO), they’re more likely to need to get their new country into the World Trade Organization (WTO), World Bank and International Monetary Fund.

“Without membership in these institutions, a separate Alberta would not receive most-favoured-nation tariff rates, making it subject to the same tariff rate as, for example, North Korea,” the report says.

And there’s a wait for that.

The fastest any country has ever gotten into the WTO is three years, and five to seven is more like the “best-case-no-active-opposition” estimate, the report says.

But will there be no opposition? Other countries with their own secessionist movements might be wary of offering a quick embrace of a breakaway ex-Canadian republic.

And domestically, even if there’s a deal reached between Alberta and Canada, the regulatory differences and hiccups of interprovincial trade could get exacerbated when there’s a harder border. There’s a risk “the border ‘thickens’ considerably, in similar fashion to the U.K.’s border with [European Union] countries after Brexit,” the report says.

Money talks

The report notes that the currency question was a major preoccupation during separation debates in Scotland and Quebec.

The dilemma is massive: stick with the loonie, try a Euro-style shared dollar, or strike off with a new Alberta form of money?

While sticking with the Canadian dollar is easiest and quickest, it keeps Ottawa in control.

“A separate Alberta would still be subject to Bank of Canada interest-rate decisions and it would remain reliant on fiscal policy to deal with Alberta-specific shock,” the report states.

A separate Alberta could choose to keep this coin as its legal currency, but it keeps monetary policy control in Ottawa if that's the case. (Paul Chiasson/The Canadian Press)

An Alberta-Canada monetary union, like in Europe, might most resemble the current situation. “It is not obvious, however, that the RoC [rest of Canada] would see great benefit to entering a formal monetary union with a separate Alberta.”

Alberta bucks as legal tender? It’s the most common solution for new nations, the report states.

“The exchange rate for a separate Alberta would likely be quite volatile, as it would largely reflect the price of oil,” it says. “This could cause problems for non-commodity exporters, who would see their export revenues become more volatile in domestic currency terms.”

Of high interest

On top of the big debt Alberta would assume as its share of Canada’s current federal liabilities, the cost of servicing that debt would be greater. Alberta already has to pay higher rates than Canada on interest payments, with a slightly higher credit rating than the country as a whole — a premium currently worth around 0.46 percentage points, the academics’ paper states. The volatility of the fossil fuel economy may make it tough to boost a standalone Alberta’s credit rating, but the study points out that oil-reliant Norway, which has a similarly sized population, has a solid rating — thanks in part to its massive sovereign wealth fund.

However, it adds: “a short-term increase in rates is likely unavoidable” for a new country.

Indigenous treaties

The report actually devotes little specific analysis to the question of First Nations rights, given the lack of international comparators of secession that involves Indigenous land claim matters, and the high degree of uncertainty. (It’s not even certain that courts would allow a secession referendum to go ahead in the first place, given the ruling that blocked a petition for a straight leave-or-stay question.)

Roughly one per cent of Alberta’s land mass is covered by First Nations reserves, over which Ottawa has exclusive legislative authority. But 100 per cent of the province’s territory is covered by Treaties 6, 7 and 8 — agreements to which Alberta is not a signatory. Figuring out longstanding land and rights issues in a separate Alberta would be a “focal point” of separation negotiations, the report says.

Treaty 8 Grand Chief Trevor Mercredi speaks as First Nations chiefs, band councillors and elders gather in March to call on Premier Danielle Smith to end the separation debate. (Jason Franson/The Canadian Press)

“Given the fraught history of Indigenous-settler relations, as well as those with Métis communities, negotiations over treaties, territory, rights and finances will be delicate, complex and protracted. The agreement of all actors cannot be presumed.”

That might be an understatement. Conflict seems highly predictable, given treaty grand chiefs’ vows to strenuously fight separation , and their call for police to investigate Alberta’s premier for treason for planning October’s vote.

In our defence

An independent nation must defend itself, and starting a military would be one of the biggest costs for a separated Alberta. But the $8.3 billion estimate that the School of Public Policy calculates for a transitioning province could be just the start of it.

Would Alberta want to join with Canada, the U.S. and Europe in their continental defence pact, NATO? If so, there are targets Alberta would have to meet — spending two per cent of its total annual economy on defense in the short term, and five per cent by 2035.

Alberta’s GDP is proportionately larger than Canada’s. The school’s report estimates the two per cent target would cost around $10 billion annually, while next decade’s benchmark would run about $25 billion.

That’s a lot of Alberta Air Force jets!

How's the beef?

Alberta’s lucrative agriculture and food trade — hello, cattle country — relies on the Canada Food Inspection Agency’s oversight.

A separate Alberta could hire the province’s former federal inspectors and mimic Canadian policies, but “convincing international buyers these moves are acceptable would be complicated, costly and time-intensive,” the study warns.

Given that overseas product exports would still need to ship from Canada’s coastal ports and piggyback on Canada’s existing supply chains, Alberta officials would have to persuade other countries it was safe to intermingle Alberta-inspected meat or grain with Canadian product in transport.

Would other countries, including Canada, immediately trust Alberta's food-safety inspection system? (Ben Nelms/CBC)

“In the short term, a separate Alberta would likely have to ‘rent’ inspection services from the Canadian government, adding to costs and ceding control of agriculture, processed food and livestock policy to Ottawa,” the report states.

“There are few if any gains imaginable from this scenario, only costs.”

When disaster strikes

The federal government has a long history of playing financial backstop after climate disasters like wildfire and floods. That’s meant a lot of massive cheques cut to Alberta for various non-insurable rebuilding needs.

Ottawa paid around $2.8 billion for damages in the 2013 southern Alberta floods , and ultimately $385 million for the 2016 Fort McMurray wildfire . The wildfire in Jasper National Park — that’s another dicey transfer negotiation in itself — has led to $900 million in federal payments thus far.

Only British Columbia has received more in federal Disaster Financial Assistance Arrangements than Alberta, the report notes.

“A separate Alberta would lose the ability to have such costs borne largely at the national level and would instead need to cover them entirely on its own.”

World.title: Canada's 'Railway City' wants passenger trains back. Like in much of the country, it's not so simple
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Wil Zufelt stands among the remnants of what was once one of Canada's busiest railway hub. He says St. Thomas, Ont., needs to save what's left of its railway history before more of it disappears.

To an outsider, the 3.2-hectare sea of grass surrounding the Elgin County Railway Museum in the heart of St. Thomas, Ont., might look like an urban park. That's not what Wil Zufelt sees.

To him, it's an enormous open wound.

"You say green space," he said. "We're actually sitting in the middle of a brownfield site that was left behind from the railroads."

Built in 1913, the hulking red-brick building was once the Michigan Central Railway Locomotive Shops, where locomotives were maintained and overhauled by a staff of 400 workers. It's one of three survivors of a sprawling railway complex that once had 112 buildings.

The old building is now a museum, but it can't welcome visitors. It's literally crumbling. The city engineer ordered it closed after finding its walls were bowing and its ceiling was unsafe.

'Pay attention to what we're losing'

"People need to wake up," Zufelt said. "Pay attention to what we're losing."

The former Michigan Central Railway Locomotive Shops sit on 3.2 hectares of former railway lands in St. Thomas, Ont. Built in 1913, the building is now home to the Elgin County Railway Museum, but is closed to the public because of structural concerns. (Patrick Morrell/CBC News)

Zufelt heads Railworks, the organization behind three of St. Thomas's surviving railway landmarks. He's launching a campaign to raise $8 million to save and restore the former locomotive shops.

The goal is to turn the old locomotive shops into not just a museum, but an active gathering place at the centre of a redeveloped downtown.

"I want it to be more than alive. I want it to be the centre of St. Thomas," he said. "That's what success is, is putting a heartbeat back in the core and then you have your arteries and everything pumps out from the middle."

By 1914, eight railways converged on St. Thomas, bringing more than 100 trains through the southwestern Ontario city every day. Its location made it a major hub for American rail traffic between Detroit and Buffalo and between New York and Chicago. The cross-border connection was so important, at one point, St. Thomas even had a U.S. consulate.

Today, the community that calls itself the "Railway City" has no rail connection at all.

Tracks that snake everywhere and nowhere

The railways are long gone, but their remains are scattered across the city — empty lots filled with rubble from where railway buildings once stood, abandoned shunting yards, railway spikes that turn up like seashells on a beach and tracks that snake everywhere and nowhere.

The old London to Port Stanley Railway runs past a restored station in St. Thomas before it abruptly ends — disappearing into the grass of a residential neighbourhood.

A section of railway track ends abruptly in St. Thomas, Ont., where a missing connection has been under a federal order to be restored by CN since 1990. Across Canada, communities looking to revive passenger rail are confronting what remains after decades of decline. (Colin Butler/CBC News)

The missing connection was the subject of a 1990 federal transport order requiring CN to replace the missing diamond at its own expense once the line reached CN tracks. But the physical connection was never completed.

Today, part of the former route is blocked by a parking lot enclosed by a fence.

The Canadian Transport Agency told CBC News the order remains in effect and CN's obligation would still apply if the physical connection were made.

CN did not respond to a request for comment by publication time.

What St. Thomas tells us about Canada's railways

St. Thomas is an unusually stark example of what happened in communities across Canada as the railway era receded, according to Thomas Blampied, a historian who studied Canada's railway history at the University of Toronto.

The former Canada Southern Railway Station in St. Thomas, Ont., is one of the surviving landmarks from an era when the city was one of Canada's busiest railway centres. The 1873 building is one of three remaining historic railway buildings in a community that once had 112. (Colin Butler/CBC News)

"Cars started to eat away at passenger revenue from railways and trucks started to take some of the freight traffic," he said.

As passengers moved to cars and freight moved to trucks, railways abandoned increasingly unprofitable routes. They didn't simply stop running trains. Much of the infrastructure was removed with them.

"Do we keep the infrastructure — so the track, all the signals, all the crossing warnings — do we keep it all intact?" Blampied said. "Increasingly, the answer was no."

In some cases, the rails were sold for scrap, in many cases, he said, "it made economic sense to completely withdraw."

But even where the railway lines survived, the network changed.

Canada looks to bring passenger rail back

Anthony Perl, a transportation policy expert at Simon Fraser University, said railways removed passing tracks and other infrastructure once passenger trains disappeared, reshaping the network around the needs of freight.

The Northern Ontario tourism sector are hoping the return of the Northlander passenger train will help bring more people to the region. (Submitted by Ontario Northland)

"We had a great streamlining, or right-sizing, or value engineering, pick your term — of the national rail infrastructure in Canada as passenger trains went away," Perl said. "To optimize it for long, slow freight trains."

He said that matters now because Canada is trying to put passenger trains back on a network that, in many places, was either removed or rebuilt for another purpose.

In Ontario, the province is preparing to restore Northlander passenger service between Toronto and northeastern Ontario, more than a decade after it was cancelled. The federal government meanwhile, is developing Alto, a new high-speed passenger railway between Toronto and Quebec City that would run largely on its own tracks.

Other communities are pushing for passenger rail to return, including on Vancouver Island, in Alberta between Calgary and Banff and in Cape Breton.

The power of owning the tracks

But Canada's railways have something airlines and trucking companies don't: control over the infrastructure they use.

Abandoned freight cars sit on overgrown tracks in a former shunting yard in St. Thomas, Ont., one of the remnants of the city's once sprawling railway network that linked major North American cities. (Colin Butler/CBC News)

"No one is going to build an alternative set of rails across this country under any circumstances," Perl said. "That's why they make the call on whether to put in or take out tracks in particular places."

In St. Thomas, CN has yet to restore the missing connection between London and Port Stanley.

"Even when the Canadian Transportation Agency orders them to do something they don't want to do," he said, "it can take quite a while, if ever, that they will go along with it because they have the ownership of that infrastructure."

Perl argues that kind of power has deep roots in the railway business and points to language the industry has given us.

"To 'railroad someone' is to take advantage and treat someone unfairly or unjustly," he said. "You don't see that with too many other industries."

World.title: From 'The World’s Greatest Lover' to 'The Happy Jogger': The people who walked across Canada before Terry Fox
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

When Terry Fox set off to run across the country, he inspired millions with his dream of curing cancer and his call for others to pick up where he left off after a recurrence of his own illness forced an early end to his Marathon of Hope in August 1980.

Fox may be the most famous person to attempt to cross Canada on foot, but he wasn’t the first.

This weekend, as millions of people around the world prepare to take up Fox’s torch and run to raise money for cancer research, here are the stories of some other cross-Canada trekkers.

One of the earliest, Percy Beresford Greathead, planned to walk not only across Canada but around the world.

Born in England in 1862, Greathead led a colourful life. He was educated in Belgium, lived in the West Indies, South and Central America, and moved to Winnipeg to work as a translator after being mistaken for Jack the Ripper in Whitechapel.

On March 2, 1895, he left Vancouver carrying nothing but a clean pair of socks, a revolver, and some chewing tobacco.

On his solitary travels through the wilderness, he evaded a wild cat by jumping off a cliff, landing safely in moss and brush below. Awakened one night by a grizzly, he put a bullet in its head and ate it the next morning for breakfast.

Greathead had his closest shave when a train came barreling towards him on a narrow railway bridge over a ravine.

At Bear Creek in the Rocky Mountains, Beresford Greathead was forced to leap over the side of a railway bridge and dangle over the ravine to let a train pass — at least, according to Greathead. (Travel, May 1897/Google Books)

“Quick as chained lightning,” he said, “I swung myself over the side and hung there suspended in space until the train had passed by…. I doubt not that during that time some of my hair turned grey.”

He arrived in Halifax on March 27, 1896, and marked his achievement by emptying a bottle of water he had filled from the Pacific Ocean into the Atlantic.

The one problem with Greathead’s incredible story is that he was the only person telling it, and he may not have been a reliable narrator.

An Ontario newspaper announced his arrival in Ottawa in September 1895, only to publish a follow-up a month later calling him a “fakir and fraud” who had run out on his debts in Winnipeg after serving a prison sentence for forgery.

Later cross-country walks were monitored more closely.

Billing himself as “The World’s Greatest Lover,” Burnest Heard pushed an oil drum in front of him the whole way to prove he didn’t hitchhike.

When Charles Burkman and Sid Carr set out to walk from Halifax to Vancouver in 1921, the Halifax Herald offered to sponsor them in return for the right to publish their daily updates from the road.

The publicity attracted others with a taste for adventure, and soon the 1921 walk turned into a race.

Father-son duo Jack and Clifford Behan reached Vancouver first, on June 11, but young married couple Jennie and Frank Dill, who left Halifax a week after the Behans, finished the hike most quickly.

The Dill’s 134-day time was declared “a world’s record” by the Herald and created a sensation, not least because it had been achieved by a woman.

Frank, in fact, credited Jennie with setting the pace. Before they left Halifax, she had reportedly told him not to worry about the walk “because if he got tired, I’d pick him up and carry him.”

Soon, cross-Canada hikers began using their journeys to raise awareness of social issues.

George Hincks and Marshall McDougall pictured in the Calgary Daily Herald on April 21, 1923. (Calgary Daily Herald)

In 1923, nearly sixty years before Fox’s Marathon of Hope, two other leg amputees walked to advocate for Canadians with disabilities.

Calgarians George Hincks and Marshall McDougall had lost their legs to battlefield injuries during the Great War. Hincks said they were trekking from Calgary to Ottawa "to prove that an amputation case has as much stamina as the average citizen who has not lost a faculty."

Cross-Canada walkers from Greathead onwards financed their journeys by selling picture postcards of themselves or giving talks along the way.

Hincks and McDougall used their lectures to describe how disabled Canadians were shut out of the job market. Hincks himself had been unemployed for three years, and, according to historian Eric Story, the men placed the onus on their able-bodied audiences to overcome their prejudices and stop judging by appearances.

Hiking on crutches eventually rubbed their feet, hands, and underarms raw, and the pair were forced to call off their walk in western Ontario. Hincks, like Fox, stopped in Thunder Bay.

Four decades later, Ken Weldrick also crossed the country for disability rights.

Calling himself “The Happy Jogger,” the 23-year-old child welfare worker ran from Vancouver to St. John’s to raise awareness and funds for Canadians with intellectual disabilities.

“The Happy Jogger” Ken Weldrick rubs his bare feet on Jan. 22, 1975. His winter run across the Prairies would land him in hospital for two months with frostbite to his face, hands, and feet. (Winnipeg Tribune/University of Manitoba)

“In the larger cities like Toronto and Montreal,” he said. The associations for people with intellectual disabilities "have a lot of money, and the patients can get the care they need. But in the other parts of the country, there are not enough funds coming in.”

Weldrick mostly slept outdoors and followed a routine of running for half an hour, resting for five minutes, then running again.

Undertaking the trip in the middle of winter, he was hospitalized in Manitoba for two months after suffering serious frostbite to his face, hands, and feet. He lost all his toenails as a result.

By the time he reached St. John’s on July 1, 1975, supporters had pledged about $7,000 directly to local charities for people with intellectual disabilities.

There are people walking across Canada right now. Though it may be a pastime almost as old as Confederation, the prospect of crossing this great continent on foot hasn’t lost any of its appeal.

World.title: Why Prince Harry and Meghan face more challenges after their return to the U.K.
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Public or private? Personal or officially royal?

In ways, it can get confusing — there was Prince Harry, smiling for the cameras that often capture his comings and goings as he arrived at a charitable event Thursday night in London.

His attendance at an awards ceremony connected to the Invictus Games, which he founded for wounded and ill service members, garnered headlines. Media reports noted that it was his first appearance in public since he and Meghan, Duchess of Sussex, returned to the U.K. from California with their two children late last month.

Still, in the past few days, it has also been made clear — via a letter from Buckingham Palace — that he and Meghan remain non-working members of the Royal Family.

"In short, their position is akin to ​private citizens with commercial and charitable interests," the letter stated.

The missive from the palace and all the media attention it garnered in recent days are a stark reminder that issues that arose when Harry and Meghan stepped back from official duties in 2020 remain front and centre with their return to Britain.

WATCH | Prince Harry and Meghan returning to Britain: Harry and Meghan moving back to the U.K. | Duration closed caption 2:06 Prince Harry and his wife Meghan are moving back to the United Kingdom with their children, Buckingham Palace has confirmed. The couple will remain non-working royals and live as private citizens.

The letter affirms that King Charles agrees with his late mother, Queen Elizabeth, that there can't be members of the Royal Family “who are half in and half out, especially in the 21st century,” Toronto-based royal historian Carolyn Harris said in an interview.

At the beginning of Elizabeth’s reign, she was “quite inclusive” in terms of bringing in members of her extended family to carry out royal duties, Harris said.

But times — and public expectations — have changed.

“In the current climate, when there's a lot of scrutiny of how taxpayers’ money is being spent … the emphasis now is on a small, streamlined Royal Family and for there to be a clear divide between those who are working members of the Royal Family and those who are not,” Harris said.

The letter — particularly the timing of its release — seemed to catch Harry and Meghan off guard, and was seen by some royal observers as a “brutal put-down” for the couple.

Prince Harry visits Ninestiles School in Birmingham, England, to launch an Invictus Games education program on Friday. (Aaron Chown/Reuters)

The line “has been drawn in the sand quite clearly,” Chandrika Kaul, a professor of modern history at the University of St. Andrews in Scotland, said in an interview.

“The palace … has issued statements very clearly saying that if Harry and Meghan wish to do whatever they wish to do in terms of charity work or other engagements, they're doing so in their own capacity as private individuals,” she said.

“They are not representing the Royal Family or the monarchy.”

Harris sees parallels between Harry and Meghan’s return to the U.K. and their departure six years ago.

“As in 2020, Harry and Meghan might have thought making a major life change is going to lead to certain decisions unfolding in their favour, and instead there are challenges.”

Six years ago, one initial challenge was whether Harry and Meghan might, as they seemed to hope, essentially be part-time working royals while also pursuing private, commercial interests. The answer from the Queen ultimately was a clear “No.”

Prince Harry, right, arrives to attend the inaugural Invictus Spirit Awards in London on Thursday. (Aaron Chown/AFP/Getty Images)

This time, one challenge has been around security, an issue that has been of particular concern and spawned a previous, unsuccessful legal challenge from Harry. Now, however, the U.K. government committee that oversees tax-funded security for public figures and royalty will reconsider the level of police protection for the couple.

Earlier this week, word also emerged that Harry and Meghan’s children, Prince Archie, 7, and Princess Lilibet, 5, were changing schools, reportedly because of security concerns raised over traffic and the length of the commute from their home.

“Prince Harry may be hoping that a decision will be made in his favour regarding security now that they are back in the United Kingdom,” said Harris.

“But there is a long history of Harry and Meghan making a major life change, but the details are still to be arranged, and that can lead to tensions on all sides.”

Overall, says Kaul, attention and reaction to Harry and Meghan’s return has been “relatively muted.”

“It has been noticed and covered and discussed on national mainstream media, but … the popular media haven't gone berserk over the impact.”

She also sees the potential for Harry to carve out a new identity now that he’s back in the U.K.

“There has always been and there continues to be a great deal of public affection and regard for Harry. I don't think that's ever gone away.”

The King and AI

King Charles, centre front, poses with attendees during a conference he hosted of leaders from the artificial intelligence sector and government at Dumfries House in Cumnock, Scotland, on Thursday. (Jonathan Brady/AFP/Getty Images)

Inside the restored 18th-century Palladian country house that serves as the home of his charitable foundation, King Charles signalled both the hopes and risks that surround a very 21st-century concern.

“AI is already showing its immense capacity to improve and save life — for example, in the field of life sciences and medicine,” Charles told leaders of some of the world’s leading AI firms who accepted his invitation to come to Dumfries House in southwestern Scotland on Thursday.

“Yet, those who have created these technologies are now increasingly warning that AI risks developing darker capacities — perhaps even to take life. In this regard, if I may say so, there seems urgency in adequately considering the existential dangers of such technologies falling into the wrong hands, and being used in potentially catastrophic ways.

“Surely, we need sufficient means of control before it is all too late?”

Charles’s convening of AI leaders is in keeping with both longstanding interests the monarchy has had in technology and his own efforts to bring people together on issues of the day.

“There's always these intersections between royalty and new technology, whether it's Queen Victoria embracing photography and then right at the end of her reign, film, or Queen Elizabeth II embracing video conferencing during the COVID-19 pandemic,” Harris said.

WATCH | King Charles warns of risks of AI: King Charles warns AI leaders of 'existential dangers' | Duration closed caption 3:43 King Charles hosted executives from AI companies OpenAI and Anthropic, as well as chipmaker Nvidia and the Google DeepMind AI research laboratory, in Scotland, and urged them to apply safeguards to their products 'before it is all too late.'

But there was more than that at play on Thursday, Harris suggested.

“For King Charles III, it's clear that he sees his role as King is to bring people together in the hope that solutions to complicated issues may be found.”

Charles does that from a unique position, Harris suggested.

“It's part of that unifying role of the monarch, the ability to bring people together. Anyone who receives an invitation to Buckingham Palace is likely to accept.”

Kaul also saw the focus on AI as a reflection of some of Charles’s longstanding interests and perspectives.

“It testifies to the King's lifelong commitment not just to technology, but to this kind of harmonious balance between nature and human beings and his deep interest in civilization and the continuation of culture.”

King Charles, left, walks with Google DeepMind chair Demis Hassabis, centre, and Nvidia chief executive Jensen Huang, right, to a meeting to discuss artificial intelligence at Dumfries House in Cumnock, Scotland, on Thursday. (Getty Images)

Charles’s actions also reflected an effort to bring people together in a way that differed from how his mother might have approached issues of the day.

“I think there is a greater sense that it is Charles who's driving the agenda,” Kaul said.

“The Queen's way of handling it was always to clearly weigh up the issues, but … particularly in her later years, [she] seemed to … put the royal mark of approval on an agenda rather than necessarily take a leading role in pushing an item onto the agenda.”

In his speech on Thursday, Charles posed two questions:

“First, how can we harness the benefits of AI, with safety at its heart? And, second, how can we build international co-operation and consensus to achieve this, so no nation is left behind, but the human race is left in place?”

Humanity, he said, “must remain sacred.”

“The decisions taken at this formative time will shape the world inherited by future generations. And so, the task before you is not merely to advance technology, but to ensure that it remains firmly in the service of humanity, community and the natural world. As we embrace what is new, we must not lose what is timeless.”

Coming together to prevent suicide

Prince William, left, and television presenter and former gymnast Gabby Logan, right, attend the launch of a suicide prevention toolkit on World Suicide Prevention Day at Hill Dickinson Stadium in Liverpool, England, on Sept. 10. (Shirlaine Forrest/Reuters)

Prince William was doing some convening of his own the other day on one of his key charitable priorities when he met with star athletes and leaders of sports organizations.

Along with Catherine, Princess of Wales, William was on hand at the Everton Football Club to launch a suicide prevention initiative.

“Sport creates belonging. It creates identity. It creates connection. And those connections matter,” William said.

“When somebody is struggling, often it is not a professional who first notices. It is a friend. A coach. A colleague. A teammate. Someone who sees a change. Someone who asks if everything is all right. Someone who starts a conversation. And that conversation could make all the difference.”

The suicide prevention toolkit launched by William aims to help people across sport have “the confidence to recognize warning signs, start supportive conversations and connect individuals with help before they reach crisis point,” Kensington Palace said.

In the initiative, Harris saw a reflection of the interests of several members of the Royal Family.

“We see a bit of Prince Philip's influence in terms of the interest in sport, but also William and Catherine, and at one time Prince Harry as well, were all very concerned with mental health and mental health initiatives.”

There is also the concern William’s mother, Diana, Princess of Wales, had in marginalized people and making “them feel loved and accepted,” Harris said, along with the concern his father, King Charles, has had in youth and opportunities for them.

A brother's claim and a palace response

Prince Philip, left, Prince William, Prince Harry, Charles Spencer and Prince Charles walk behind the coffin of Diana, Princess of Wales, in London on Sept. 6, 1997. (Reuters)

The response came quickly, by royal standards.

Not long after the first headlines emerged online Wednesday about claims the brother of the late Diana, Princess of Wales, is making in a book to be released this coming week, Buckingham Palace had a statement of its own.

In a published excerpt of Swan Song: Diana, My Sister, Charles Spencer claims that King Charles said his former wife would soon be forgotten after her death.

Spencer says he told Charles that Diana would not have wanted their sons, William and Harry, then 15 and 12, to walk behind her coffin in the funeral procession. He claims Charles told him: "Rest assured, we'll forget her soon enough." He also accuses Charles of having "contempt" for his ex-wife.

The palace responded later Wednesday with a statement of its own.

"While we do not comment on books as a matter of principle, His Majesty is mindful that the pain of fraternal grief can cloud reason, affect judgment and colour memory in ways others do not recognize, even many years after such a loss," it said.

British newspapers, shown Friday in London, reported on Buckingham Palace's reaction to Charles Spencer's upcoming book about his sister, the late Diana, Princess of Wales. (John Phillips/Getty Images)

Harris sees parallels in that statement to another high-profile reaction from the palace.

“In common with Queen Elizabeth II's statement that ‘recollections may vary’ after Harry and Meghan were interviewed by Oprah Winfrey, King Charles III is refusing to allow Earl Spencer to have the last word on circumstances concerning the Royal Family,” she said.

“The King has his own memories of the days following Diana's death and they are not the same as those of Earl Spencer.”

Diana died after a car crash in Paris in 1997.

Nearly 30 years after her death, she continues to captivate and draw headlines, and says Harris, her legacy continues to be debated and contested.

“Diana combined glamour with vulnerability and people from a variety of social and cultural backgrounds saw themselves in aspects of her experiences even though she was born into the aristocracy and married a prince,” said Harris.

“Recent films, television series, plays and novels have revived interest in Diana for a new generation who remember the princess through popular culture portrayals rather than historical events.”

Royally quotable

"The shock of witnessing these fires around the world in recent months reminds us forcibly of the mounting pressures that prolonged heat and drought are placing upon our precious Earth.”

— King Charles, in a message where he expressed his admiration for those who helped tackle wildfires across the U.K. this summer.

King Charles, centre, meets community leaders, firefighters, volunteers and landowners during a visit to the Cairngorms National Park in Aviemore, Scotland, on Wednesday. (Andrew Milligan/Getty Images)

Royal reads

Enslaved African people were seared with hot metal brands bearing the royal crown , according to research by historians who have documented the monarchy’s centuries-long involvement in Britain’s slave trade. [The Guardian]

Prince William has launched a community fund to revive a village in southwestern England. [The Independent]

The Princess of Wales visited the cancer hospital where she was treated for the illness and praised the "incredible" care she received. [Sky News]

The Duchess of Edinburgh tried her hand at polishing gemstones at a local family jewellery business in Zambia on the second day of her tour of the African country. [Daily Mail]

Prince George posed for a portrait in his new school uniform after arriving for his first day at Eton College accompanied by his proud parents, the Prince and Princess of Wales. [Daily Mail]

Prince Harry and Meghan's highly publicized return to England got the full Saturday Night Live UK treatment — and in true British fashion, the welcome was served with a distinctly chilly reception. [CBC]

Lost or long-discarded items revealing glimpses of the behind-the-scenes life of Buckingham Palace staff over decades have been uncovered during the restoration of the monarchy’s HQ. [The Guardian]

World.title: Protection for women who defy the Mafia is changing in Italy. Does it go far enough?
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

35 years after Italy established its witness protection program, CBC’s Megan Williams explores the heavy personal toll endured by women who spoke out against the mafia — including investigative journalist Federica Angeli, who has lived under armed police guard for 13 years.

The women who defied the Italian Mafia — and the price they paid

"Take a map of Italy, tear Sicily from it and throw it away."

That was the advice the late anti-Mafia prosecutor Paolo Borsellino gave a young Piera Aiello in 1991, when she came to him to say she was ready to tell all about the Sicilian Mafia family she had married into.

Aiello's husband had been gunned down in front of her in the pizzeria they ran together. He was the abusive son of the local Mafia boss, and Aiello had been coerced into marrying him as a teen. Still, she wanted his killers caught.

"I have already decided," she recalls telling Borsellino about her decision to testify. "I just need to pack my bags."

Three days later, Aiello left Sicily with two suitcases — one filled with clothes, the other with toys for her three-year-old daughter.

The following year, Borsellino was killed, along with five members of his police escort, in a Mafia car bombing in the Sicilian capital of Palermo.

Piera Aiello spent nearly three decades living under another identity to keep her safe, after testifying about the Sicilian Mafia family she had married into. (CBC)

Aiello would spend most of the next three decades living under another identity, which kept her safe from the Mafia.

But cut off from her Sicily and her old life, building a new one was lonely and arduous.

"I couldn't find work, and I had to support my daughter," she said, explaining how she found work in the countryside harvesting olives, eventually saving enough to open a small business.

Aiello's early years in protection reveal a less visible aspect to Italy's long fight against organized crime: what happens after someone speaks out. For women, the rupture can be both practically and emotionally tougher.

A new Italian law extending protection from organized crime — and providing social, economic, educational and psychological help — to children and the adults caring for them, often their mothers, is designed to address some of those gaps.

Memorial to Paolo Borsellino and body guards killed in Palermo, Sicily, in 1992. (Megan Williams/CBC)

Limits of protection

Liberi di scegliere — the "Free to Choose" bill — became law in July and entered into force on Aug. 9.

Sen. Vincenza Rando spent years pushing for the law and working with women who wanted to break away from Mafia families. Many of them, she says, fall outside the categories around which Italy's traditional protection system had been built.

"Women who are neither justice witnesses nor co-operating witnesses, I call them 'cultural collaborators.' They leave that environment and build a culture of legality," Rando said.

They may not be informants or have any useful intel about a murder, a drug shipment or an extortion racket. Their act of rebellion, she says, may simply be deciding that their children will not grow up inside a Mafia family and culture.

Rando says some leave homes flush with cash, only to end up with nothing. Others need a new identity just to sign an employment contract without being traced. Their children are forced to change schools and friends, thrust into a life with entirely different moral codes.

"If you move somewhere where nobody knows you and you cannot even say who you are, who can you talk to?" Rando asked. "Who can you safely tell your story to?"

Italian Sen. Vincenza Rando spent years working with women who wanted to break away from Mafia families. (CBC)

Under the new legislation, people under the age of 25 and relatives who care for them may be relocated outside their home region, provided with education and psychological support and, where necessary, given new identities.

Critics say the law gives the state too much power over family life, allowing for the separation of children from parents, which could be seen as punishing children for their parents' crime.

But Rando and supporters say the law prioritizes keeping mothers and children together when the mother breaks with the criminal group.

Aiello supports its aims, but worries short-term intervention will not be enough to permanently break the cycle. She says longer-term support through education and job training is essential.

"What does it mean for the State to take responsibility for them for two years?" Aiello asked. "It means nothing."

For Aiello, the lesson from her own experience is that protection has to mean more than physical safety: it also has to provide the tools to build an independent life.

The 'privilege' of never walking alone

Anti-Mafia prosecutor Nino Di Matteo has spent most of his career seeing the cost of protection from the inside.

He has lived under police escort since 1993, at times under Italy's highest level of security. His two children were born while he was already under protection; within days of leaving hospital, he recalls, they too were travelling in an escort car.

Reporters wait on outside a special bunker court in Caltanissetta, Sicily, on Jan. 19, 2023, during mafia boss Matteo Messina Denaro's trial for the 1992 Palermo bombing that killed anti-mafia Italian magistrate Paolo Borsellino. (Miguel Medina/AFP/Getty Images)

Now based in Rome, he says people outside Sicily sometimes perceive police protection as a mark of status, which he says irritates him.

"People can tend to see the protected person as privileged," Di Matteo said. "From that point of view, I would rather not be 'privileged.' People should perhaps think about the sacrifice involved in never being able to take a walk alone."

Di Matteo is equally wary of a lot of the mythology surrounding the Mafia itself. He points to the media's focus on its most cinematic elements of violence and overt criminality — "the so-called military Mafia" — rather than the white-collar Mafiosi who appear to be part of legitimate businesses and cultivate relationships with political and institutional power.

Books for sale at the anti-Mafia museum, called the Museum of the Present, in Palermo, Sicily. (Megan Williams/CBC)

And he says women's roles in that world have also frequently been misunderstood.

"Women have always played a fundamental role, for both good and bad," Di Matteo said.

Some wives and mothers are the family enforcers of the Mafia identity of husbands and sons. Others have rebelled against it — often painfully breaking away — to become justice witnesses and campaigners.

"For a woman I imagine it may be even harder," Di Matteo said of criminal organizations built heavily around kinship. "Especially when speaking out means accusing your own son, your own blood."

When Mafia threats reach your family

Federica Angeli came to protection by a very different route.

An investigative journalist in Ostia, Rome's gritty seaside district, Angeli spent years reporting on local criminal clans and their grip on parts of Ostia's lucrative beachfront economy.

In 2013, during one investigation, Mafia boss Armando Spada discovered the hidden camera she was carrying. Angeli says he detained her upstairs in a room, placed a gun between them and made clear that he knew where she was most vulnerable.

"You have three children. What shall we do?" Angeli remembers him saying to another man. "Shall we start with the youngest one, the one with the pretty eyes?"

A month later she witnessed an attempted double murder near her home. She testified and was placed under police protection.

Investigative journalist Federica Angeli in Ostia near Rome. Angeli spent years reporting on local criminal clans and their grip on parts of Ostia's lucrative beachfront economy. (Megan Williams/CBC)

For 13 years, armed escorts have followed Angeli through ordinary life: work, dinner out with friends, a day at the beach, family outings. She says friends stopped inviting her over because security officers first had to inspect their homes. Restaurants meant being seated according to security requirements. Spontaneity vanished.

Angeli chronicled her ordeal in the memoir A mano disarmata (Unarmed), later adapted into a feature film. In 2016, Italian President Sergio Mattarella made her a Knight of the Order of Merit of the Italian Republic.

But despite the public recognition, the beachfront clean-up in Ostia has sometimes generated resentment: Angeli says she hears residents complain that some establishments worked better under Mafia-linked operators. Other criticism aimed at her is more gendered.

"As a woman, and as a mother, I was heavily criticized for my choice," she said. "Everyone said, 'You put your children in danger,'" who for five years were placed under protection, too, due to threats.

But she rejects the idea that there is one correct maternal response.

"There is no handbook for being the right mother," she said of the decision to denounce organized crime. "But I wanted to free my children from having to bow to the Mafia."

Piera Aiello wanted the same thing for her daughter when she left Sicily.

She built a new life near Rome, and in 2018, she was elected to parliament — Italy's first sitting justice witness — after a long battle to regain her real name. She sat on the Antimafia and Justice committees, where she pushed for stronger witness protections.

And, this summer, more than three decades after Borsellino told her to tear Sicily from the map, she moved back to her beloved island.

"I kept that crumpled piece of Sicily in a drawer," she said, "And I picked it up and glued it back on."

World.title: Alberta researchers investigate how zombie parasites take control of ant brains
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

In the southeast corner of Alberta, the Cypress Hills are a dramatic sight rising out of a sea of prairie.

Look down, and you’ll see another drama playing out.

Ants are clasped onto plants and shrubs throughout the Cypress Hills Provincial Park against their will, waiting to be accidentally swallowed up by an unsuspecting herbivore.

The culprit is the parasite Dicrocoelium dendriticum, a worm with an incredible ability to zombify its host.

According to researchers at the University of Calgary and University of Lethbridge, this parasite sits alone in the hall of fame of parasite manipulations because it is able to turn its control on and off — something not seen elsewhere in the world of zombies.

Zombies are everywhere

Zombie parasites are quite common in nature, says Cameron Goater, a parasitologist and professor emeritus at the University of Lethbridge.

“Almost every taxon [species] of hosts on the tree of life contains parasites or are infected with parasites that lead to manipulation,” said Goater.

The goal is often to get from one host to the next. Take the famous Cordyceps fungus popularized in the video game franchise turned hit HBO show The Last of Us. Infected ants climb plants and die so that the fungus can burst out and rain spores down on unsuspecting ants.

Or the horsehair worm that drives crickets to commit suicide by jumping into water so the worms can emerge and mate.

These examples and nearly all others in the animal kingdom end in the host's death, but Dicrocoelium is different because the nature of its life cycle incentivizes keeping the host alive.

Dicrocoelium has what parasitologists call a complex life cycle involving multiple hosts. The final host is a grazing mammal like elk, deer or cattle. Adult worms live in their livers, and their eggs are pooped out and eaten by snails.

A cross section of an elk liver infected with Dicrocoelium. The white spots are inflamed bile ducts containing an adult worm. (Cameron Goater)

In snails, the egg divides into hundreds of larval forms called cercaria. These are packaged in mucus and coughed out as a slime ball. (That is the official term.) Slime balls are then eaten by ants, and all but one cercaria go to the abdomen, while a single "brainworm" cozies up next to the ant's brain.

This is where the challenge begins.

“The problem is the final host almost never ingests ants,” said Goater. “In many cases, things like deer and elk and cattle actually avoid ants.”

So, it helps to have a brainworm that compels the ants to climb plants where they can be accidentally eaten.

In this CT scan cross section of an infected ant, the small orange area is the brainworm, found below the ant brain. The round grey balls in the abdomen are encysted parasites waiting to be ingested so they can travel to the liver. (Daniel Martín-Vega)

But this solution is risky. Ants clinging to vegetation are exposed to predators, they can’t eat and, importantly, they are extremely susceptible to dehydration.

“The solution to that problem is to detach from a plant and go back to the nest,” said Goater. “That's where this on-off switch comes from.”

For the rest of their lives, these ants climb plants and cling on so long as the temperature is below approximately 19 C.

How can a parasite inside an ant know what temperature it is outside and adjust its mind control in response?

“That's exactly the kind of question that keeps us awake at night,” said Goater, “because it seems that the mechanisms that run that might be something completely new.”

How to take over a mind

The first step to understanding this phenomenon is to look at the genes being expressed during and after the clinging behaviour, and comparing this with uninfected ants.

“We've gone inside the brain of the ant to try and determine what those changes are from the ant perspective,” said James Wasmuth, a parasitologist at the University of Calgary. “And we see a lot of changes in different biochemical pathways when it's doing the zombie behaviour.”

While it appears the ant is not sensing the environment in a normal way when it’s under parasite control, it is difficult to pinpoint one change that is driving behaviour, said Wasmuth.

According to Shelley Adamo, an insect neurobiologist and professor emeritus at Dalhousie University, this is to be expected.

“When I first got into this business, the assumption everyone had was there was a magic bullet,” said Adamo.

However, the more scientists learn about these systems, they realize that’s not the case.

“Evolution rarely does the grand redo,” Adamo said.

Parasites like Dicrocoelium work by tapping into existing systems, which are themselves extremely complex.

“We rely on chemicals for communication from one nerve cell to another; it's not hardwired,” Adamo said.

This gives the parasite ample opportunity to interfere, gradually evolving ways to nudge these systems to their benefit. The result is a plethora of subtle changes culminating in the precise manipulation.

Solving that puzzle requires many careful experiments where some genes are suppressed or not to see if the manipulation remains.

Ants infected with the parasite Dicrocoelium dendriticum cling to plants against their will so they can be eaten by grazing mammals. (Andrew Hurly)

However, Adamo is excited by the first steps taken by the Alberta researchers toward identifying potential molecules involved like adenosine.

"That molecule is interesting because it's also involved in immune systems as well as neural systems," said Adamo.

According to Wasmuth, adenosine regulates stress and feeding, as well as sleep.

“A massive increase in adenosine pathways induces sleep in other animals. So, we think that the worm is somehow controlling the invertebrate sleeping,” said Wasmuth, “but we don’t actually know.”

Along with adenosine, certain biochemical pathways related to smell, metabolism and circadian rhythms appear to be altered, Wasmuth said.

No magic bullet but lots to learn

Understanding how a parasite changes behaviour means deciphering the chemical code behind the behaviour.

“These parasites have tapped into a really vital clue about how brains work because they can subtly alter something that causes a behavioural shift which is quite dramatic,” said Adamo.

Humans are equally susceptible, says Adamo.

“If you take drugs, for example, you can alter the way your brain perceives things."

This is the gift and curse of animal brains: they are extremely plastic and can learn throughout their lives, “but the weak side is that you are also open to manipulation if somebody knows the chemical code,” said Adamo.

Why Cypress Hills?

Goater believes Dicrocoelium can teach us about the consequences of humans manipulating nature.

This parasite was introduced to Canada likely from importing sheep and other animals from Europe decades ago, says Goater.

So why don’t we see it nationwide?

“This is what we call an anthropogenic introduction of a parasite or disease, because humans brought it in, and almost certainly the way we manage the landscape influences transmission as well,” Goater said.

“We do a lot of things in that park that really benefit transmission, and one of them is we control fires and that leads to high snail densities, high ant densities,” Goater said. The park is also managed for cattle grazing, which likely contributes as well.

Humans may have inadvertently created the perfect conditions for this parasite in Alberta, which according to Goater is pretty amazing given its complex life cycle.

“When it moved over and colonized these unique areas, it had to jump into a new species of snail, into a new species of ant and then to a new species of grazer,” he said.

Understanding the conditions that allowed all those factors to line up, said Goater, can inform how we deal with all sorts of emerging diseases.

World.title: Not just lemonade stands: How a new wave of 'kid-preneurs' are making their own money
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

LISTEN | Lots of kids across Canada are becoming entrepreneurs: Cost of Living 8:17 Why more kids should run lemonade stands

At six years old, Jayden Karlee Castillo started running a business selling toys in front of her house.

Three years later, she’s still at it, even adding new products to her lineup and taking them to more customers.

In July, Castillo joined the first Kids Markets event held in Millarville, Alta., near Calgary, selling a variety of items including bracelets, earrings and 3D-printed toys she makes herself, as well as hand sanitizers and squishies she sources from wholesalers.

So far she's saved hundreds of dollars for a trip to Japan and the Philippines, and has something else planned, too.

“I really wanna treat my parents to a good dinner,” Castillo told CBC’s Cost of Living.

The Kids Markets initiative, which gives children ages five to 17 a chance to sell their own products, isn’t the only program helping young entrepreneurs take their ideas to market.

Kids Markets saw an average of 16 youth-run businesses at each of their market events since they began in June this year. (Kids Markets Calgary)

In B.C., kids can sell their products through BizKids Market, while in Toronto there’s an annual marketplace called Kid2Kid. There’s also Children’s Business Fair in Brandon, Man., along with similar initiatives across the country .

Jodi Letkiewicz, an assistant professor of finance at California State University, says kids have been starting their own small businesses for generations, but there’s been a noticeable uptick in recent years.

“There’s always been kid-preneurs out there … but now it’s sort of exploded.”

Why are there more kid entrepreneurs?

Lemonade Day Calgary, an initiative that supports kids to operate their own lemonade stand, drew a record 792 young participants this year. That’s up from 164 when the U.S.-born program launched in Calgary in 2023, says Chantelle Little, who brought the initiative to Canada.

According to Letkiewicz, who researches how kids learn about money, there’s no single reason why more young people are getting interested in entrepreneurship, but social media has made it easier for children to see others their age running their own businesses.

Through accessible platforms such as YouTube, kids can also learn how to start a business, while AI tools can help with everything from coming up with an idea and creating a business name and logo to researching customers, setting prices, building a website and doing basic bookkeeping.

Jodi Letkiewicz is an assistant professor of finance at California State University. She studies how parents influence their children's financial knowledge and behaviour. (Submitted by Jodi Letkiewicz)

For some kids, the rising cost of everyday life may also be putting money more firmly on their radar, says Letkiewicz. They’re becoming more aware of what things cost, and curious about ways they can earn some money of their own.

“If you think about how often we're talking about the cost of living now, whether it's at the dinner table, the parents talking with friends about something, or they hear it on the news on a radio [in the] car … they're absorbing that information,” she said.

A good foundation for the future

Another reason may be childhood itself: kids can be curious, creative and willing to take chances, without the same fear of failure that can come with age.

“They might have a fire for something,” said Letkiewicz. “You don’t want to put that out.”

That’s the case for Calgary’s Atley Ma. When he was nine years old, Ma seized an unquenchable opportunity.

“We had been filling our own Soda Stream canisters just because it was more cost effective at home, and we started doing it for friends and family, and then I kind of realized, ‘why not do it as a business?’”

Atley Ma, also known as SodaKid, started running a business when he was nine years old. He says the many different rewards he gained along the way have been invaluable. (Submitted by Atley Ma)

It grew into a thriving operation called SodaKid. Now 18, Ma has earned enough to cover university tuition for his engineering degree.

Ma credits his success not only to word-of-mouth recommendations, but to the unique advantages of being a kid.

“You're a little bit cuter and a little bit smaller than everybody else selling the same thing that you're selling,” he said.

And kids stand to gain more than just some extra cash, says Ross Levine, an economist and senior fellow at the Hoover Institution at Stanford University. They also “learn an enormous amount” from handling the ins and outs of running a small business, he says.

“They are acquiring quite a bit of skills [including] financial literacy, how to solve problems, how to co-ordinate with other people, and what a balance sheet is,” he said.

Those skills served Chantelle Little of Lemonade Day Calgary well. She’s been an entrepreneur for 18 years, ever since she sold pop at a golf course as a child. Today, she is the founder and CEO of Tiller, a digital marketing agency, and credits her childhood experience with where she is now.

“I didn’t really realize I was running a business per se, but looking back, that’s where I really got my first taste of sales,” she said.

Chantelle Little smiles next to young entrepreneurs who came up with creative ideas to sell lemonade. (Lemonade Day Calgary)

‘The world is your oyster’

Family support is another important part of kid entrepreneurship, says Letkiewicz.

“It’s all about resources, like what resources are available to you, in your family, in your community,” she said.

Sisters Emery and Hannah Hynes, who run a soap and candle business in London, Ont., told CBC London their mom covers the cost of a table at a farmer's market.

“We’re really grateful that our mom has invested a lot and helped us a lot with money and paying for it,” said Hannah. “It’s really nice we get to do things like this because we really enjoy it.”

Ma says building a website for SodaKid helped him discover his interest in computer engineering.

Now, he hopes another young entrepreneur will eventually take over SodaKid and grow it further.

“The world is your oyster at that young age,” said Ma. “You have so much possibility, and it teaches you hard work, organization, people skills, and if nothing else, you make a little money on the side.”
