World.title: From the archive: How do I know it’s a ‘no’? A comprehensive guide for foreigners
World.content:
The goal of our “From the Archive” series is to revisit popular stories that capture the unique history and culture of life in Mexico. This Sarah DeVries article — originally published in November 2024 — is a humorous look at why Mexicans won’t say “no,” and how to know when they’re telling you “no” without actually saying it.

Mexicans are famous for their polite social graces and good humor. Unfortunately, they’re also known for a strong aversion to saying “no” or saying anything negative at all.

But what one sees as polite omission, another might take as flat-out lying. Being polite while also communicating what you mean can be a tricky balancing act; it’s true. And for those of us from more direct cultures, it’s downright opaque. Why would someone just not say what they mean?

Nothing is as simple as it seems, I suppose. Still, there are plenty of recognizable broad strokes we can examine here.

A lesson in keeping the negative to yourself

An impressive example of this tendency came years ago when I lived in Querétaro. I’d been working at a language school then — the kind that says they’ll help with immigration papers but never do. It was someone’s birthday, and teachers and students alike all went out to a bar to celebrate. It was a good time!

The next day, the director of the school told us teachers that one of the students wouldn’t be coming to class that day; there’d been an issue with his car. What was the issue? Someone had broken into it and stolen his car radio and CD player!

And when had this happened? It wasn’t when we were inside the bar, no. It happened at the school before we all left. He’d given some of us a ride, even, and had said nothing about his missing equipment.

It’s been almost 20 years, and I’m still shocked he kept that in.

He didn’t want to say anything about it because he didn’t want to ruin the evening before it had even begun. I myself would have been physically incapable of not saying anything. Just, wow.

Now that I’ve been here a while longer, I’ve seen more examples. People simply seem loath to talk about things that will make people gloomy. What for? We can get sad all on our own, after all.

So the first rule of communication, then, is to not disappoint. That is, of course, if you want the person you’re talking to to feel good. I’d personally rather be momentarily disappointed than later be sitting around like a dummy waiting for someone who’s not going to show, but that’s on me, I guess.

So knowing that “no” is a “no-no word” here, how might you decipher what people mean when they give you an answer?

Words that actually mean ‘no’: a guide for foreigners

Well, that’s just what I’m here to help you with! Below is a list of “actually, that might mean ‘no'” words and phrases.

‘Gracias’

This one is tricky. I sometimes have to stop myself from pedantically saying, “Um, that’s not one of the options for a yes or no question.” I can tell you from experience that challenging someone’s politeness in this way makes you look like an ass.

The way I’ve personally gotten around this is to pause comically and ask, “¿Gracias ‘sí’ o gracias ‘no’?” That will usually get a grin and an actual answer, which, by the way, is almost always “Gracias, no.” Remember that you can use it, too! It’s especially helpful when you’re wandering through a market and merchants are offering their wares. It also usually works if the “market” is coming to you in the form of individual sellers! An emphatic “muchas gracias” will usually transmit the idea that, while you are very grateful for the offer, you will not be purchasing a bottle of perfume on that particular day.

‘A lo mejor sí’

“A lo mejor” is a phrase that means “probably” or “likely.” It’s important to note, then, that all interpretations leave some wiggle room for it maybe not working out. If it doesn’t actually work out, well, they haven’t lied! There was always a chance.

This is, to me, one of the more dismissive ways to say no, a kind of “uh-huh, sure” version. In Mexico, this kind of dismissive “doing what you can to leave the conversation already” is called “dar el avión” (to … give the plane?). And when you “das el avión,” it’s often detectable. There are two likely outcomes of this, then. One is that the other person sighs, gives up and goes on their way. Another is that they get frustrated: “¡No me des el avión!” If that happens, you’d better think of a better, more convincing way to say “no.”

‘Déjame ver/checar’

This one is similar to “a lo mejor sí” in that it’s very likely to be an actual “no.” It means “Let me see” and “Let me check.” Spoiler alert: they will likely conclude, and may or may not tell you, that the result of the seeing/checking was negative.

‘Ahorita’

This is one that my kid uses on me all the time, and it drives me crazy. We speak in English together, so her version is “in a minute.” “Ahorita” could be when someone will definitely do something right then. Or it could mean anywhere from right that moment to when hell freezes over.

In my experience, it’s typically the latter, or after the person’s finally been worn down from enough nagging about it. So beware, people. If you’re hearing “ahorita” from your partner frequently and it’s not turning out to be “right now for real” kind, there will probably be some frustration in your future.

‘Estamos en contacto’

This one is kind of fun because it sounds so official and business-like. “We’ll be in touch.” Oh, will we? Most people don’t intend for this to be a lie; it’s just nicer to say than, “We may never see each other again, I don’t know, but you’re pleasant enough.”

Alas, this is a short list. I’ve got a word limit! But I’d love to hear more examples of “This is what they actually meant” in the comments. Consider this your official call for stories!

Sarah DeVries is a writer and translator based in Xalapa, Veracruz. She can be reached through her website, sarahedevries.substack.com.

World.title: Mexico’s week in review: Independence Day fireworks give way to trade deal hopes
World.content:
Listen to this article

Mexico’s Independence Day on Sept. 16 was the focal point this past week, even as less celebratory news circulated. Over the weekend, 21-year-old Spanish exchange student Claudia Tacoronte Aguilera, attending the Autonomous University of Morelos (UAEM) in Cuernavaca, Morelos, was stabbed and killed in Cuautla — the fourth femicide of a UAEM student just this year. On Thursday, Morelos authorities announced the arrest of a suspect, Francisco Javier “N,” but the attack on Tacoronte and the emergency medical response were met with indignation both locally and in Spain.

Also on Sept. 12, Pemex admitted it had contained another oil spill off the coast of Campeche, which the Navy and the state oil company moved quickly to seal and clean up — a contrast to the government’s slower handling of a major spill in February. Meanwhile, the peso spent most of the week trading above 17 to the dollar, weakening toward its worst week since March as markets digested the U.S. Federal Reserve’s decision to raise interest rates for the first time since 2023, narrowing the Mexico-U.S. rate differential.

Didn’t have time to catch this week’s top stories? Here’s what you missed.

Industrial activity posts best growth in years

Mexico’s industrial sector delivered its strongest annual performance in nearly three years in July, with industrial activity up 2.4% in seasonally adjusted terms, according to INEGI — triple June’s 0.8% reading and the best showing since November 2023.

Construction led the gains, climbing 6.7% annually, while mining rose 1.6% and manufacturing grew 1.3%. Month-over-month growth was 0.5%, a second straight month of sequential gains. Still, industrial activity is up just 0.4% for the first seven months of 2026, a modest rebound after a 1.3% contraction in 2025, with manufacturing down 0.7% year-to-date. Economists at Grupo Financiero Monex expect only “moderate” growth ahead, citing USMCA-related uncertainty and U.S. tariffs on vehicles, steel and aluminum.

Coahuila is Mexico’s safest state

For the first time, Coahuila topped INEGI’s national safety perception survey, the 2026 ENVIPE, with just 27.8% of residents calling the state unsafe due to crime — a 9.9-point improvement that pushed Baja California Sur out of the top spot.

Coahuila registered only 100 homicides in 2025, a turnaround from more than 1,100 killings in 2012, when cartels such as Los Zetas and the Gulf Cartel dominated large swaths of the state. Analysts credited beefed-up federal forces and prevention programs. Governor Manolo Jiménez Salinas, in office since December 2023, credited “great teamwork.” Nationally, the picture is less rosy: 74% of adults still consider their state unsafe, and México state overtook Morelos this year as Mexico’s least safe state, with 90% of respondents reporting security concerns.

Mexico’s independence is celebrated at home and abroad

On Tuesday night, President Sheinbaum delivered her second Grito de Independencia from the National Palace balcony before a crowd the Mexico City government estimated at more than 300,000 in the Zócalo, marking 216 years since Miguel Hidalgo’s original Cry of Dolores.

Sheinbaum issued 21 arengas honoring independence heroes including Hidalgo, Josefa Ortiz, Leona Vicario and Vicente Guerrero, alongside Mexico’s Indigenous and Afro-Mexican peoples and migrants abroad, several of whom were included in a national Grito for the first time.

Abroad, Iran marked the holiday by lighting Tehran’s Azadi Tower in green, white and red, the first time the landmark has been illuminated in tribute to Mexico — an occasion the Mexican ambassador to Iran called “a great gesture of friendship.” In New York City, Mayor Zohran Mamdani served as grand marshal of Brooklyn’s Mexican Independence Day parade, days after U.S. Vice President JD Vance mocked a Mexican flag-carrying protester at a Dallas rally.

Antitrust regulators probe Liga MX

Mexico’s National Antitrust Commission (CNA) has opened an investigation into whether Liga MX operates as a monopoly, examining whether a small group is unfairly controlling “affiliation, organization and access” to professional soccer competitions in violation of federal competition law. The probe follows Liga MX’s 2020 decision — upheld through the 2026-27 season by the Court of Arbitration for Sport — to scrap promotion and relegation with the second-tier Liga Expansión and end payouts to lower-tier clubs, a move Liga Expansión officials fiercely disputed. No defendants have been named; the probe can run up to 120 business days and be extended. If wrongdoing is found, Liga MX and its clubs could face fines of up to 10% of annual income.

CFE advances Project Oasis in Baja California Sur

The Federal Electricity Commission unveiled Project Oasis BCS, a solar, battery and green hydrogen initiative meant to bring reliable power to the isolated Mulegé region, which has no direct connection to the national grid and has historically relied on fossil fuels.

The project pairs a 72-megawatt photovoltaic plant with a battery system, electrolyzers to produce hydrogen and fuel cells to convert it back into electricity for use when sunlight is scarce. CFE projects the initiative will serve 40,000 households and cut emissions equivalent to taking more than 31,000 vehicles off the road annually. If completed, it would be CFE’s first-ever green hydrogen power generation project.

Democracy index shows modest gains

According to International IDEA’s annual Global State of Democracy report, released on Tuesday, Mexico’s democracy score edged up slightly in 2025 — Sheinbaum’s first full year in office — rising to 1.778 out of 4 from 1.770 the year before. The country improved in rule of law and participation, held steady in rights and declined in representation, its best-ranked category at 83rd out of 173 nations. Mexico ranked in the top 100 in only one of the four measured categories. The report’s authors flagged rising political polarization and “us versus them” identity politics as threats across Latin America, while separately noting democratic backsliding tied to the Trump administration’s consolidation of executive power in the U.S.

Sheinbaum responds to Trump cartel pressure

Responding to a Trump “presidential determination” pressuring Mexico to take “additional action” against cartels and arrest complicit officials, Sheinbaum turned the spotlight on U.S. drug consumption, asking what Washington is doing to curb domestic drug demand, money laundering and the flow of American-made weapons into Mexico.

“We don’t need to be judged from the outside,” Sheinbaum said, insisting “we know what Mexico’s problems are and we act against them every day.” Trump’s determination, submitted to Congress on Tuesday, named Mexico among 23 countries as major drug producers or transit points and singled out Sinaloa Governor Rubén Rocha Moya — on leave amid U.S. accusations of cartel collusion but still free — as an official Washington wants arrested. The exchange came a week after Secretary of State Marco Rubio said Mexico isn’t doing enough against cartels, even as he acknowledged Mexican efforts had increased.

Record fuel bust in Guanajuato

Authorities announced on Thursday that they had seized 59 million liters of stolen fuel at a property in San José Iturbide, Guanajuato — the largest single-site fuel bust in Mexican history and roughly five times last year’s record seizure in Tamaulipas. The operation traces to a July 3 arrest involving a tanker truck loaded with stolen fuel, which led investigators to the storage facility, capable of holding up to 80 million liters. No arrests had been made as of Friday, and officials say specialized personnel will be needed to safely handle the seized hydrocarbons. Guanajuato’s security minister said the bust would help choke off a funding source for organized crime in a state that has seen four smaller fuel-theft busts this year.

Trade talks hover ahead of US midterms

The fourth round of formal USMCA-related trade talks between Mexico and the United States is tentatively set for next week, with officials on both sides eager to hammer out a deal before U.S. midterm elections on Nov. 3, according to sources interviewed by Reuters.

A framework deal would benefit both governments: Trump wants an economic win as he risks losing control of Congress, while Mexico is contending with investor unease and a cooling economy. The push follows the collapse last month of parallel U.S.-Canada trade talks, making the Mexico-U.S. track an effort at an interim bilateral deal.

According to José Medina Mora, president of Mexico’s Business Coordinating Council (CCE), the elimination of Section 232 tariffs, which place duties on aluminum, steel and automobiles, is expected to be a primary focus.

Pups in the news

Rollo, an adopted mixed-breed puppy, is the National Palace’s newest resident, officially tasked with supporting “the emotional well-being of everyone,” per government videos; his brother Theo still awaits adoption, and the palace’s resident cats, including Coco and Zeus, remain in place.

In Morelia, a dog named Maple dressed as a taco stand won the city’s inaugural Patriotic Pup Contest, beating roughly 40 costumed competitors, with runners-up dressed as an elote-and-pork-loin vendor and a pozole bowl nearly twice their size.

Looking ahead

Next week brings a busy convergence of bilateral trade and security missions as well as the potential for currency swings.

The fourth round of USMCA-focused trade talks in Washington, D.C., could yield either a resolution or more setbacks. According to reporting by Politico, a preparatory call between Trump and Sheinbaum on Wednesday may have placed more topics on the discussion table than just Section 232 tariffs. However, Sheinbaum said after the call that “we’re making progress on trade issues.”

Any signs of progress or friction on tariffs are poised to move the peso. Meanwhile, 139 U.S. Army soldiers from the 101st Airborne Division are scheduled to land in Chihuahua on Sept. 20 for 11 days of joint training exercises with Mexican forces at the Centro Nacional de Adiestramiento, the military’s largest training facility.

Mexico News Daily

World.title: Junípero Serra: A complex character with a controversial legacy
World.content:
Standing in the plaza of Jalpan de Serra, a town in Querétaro’s remote, mountainous Sierra Gorda, I gazed up in awe at an enormous, intricately designed mission. Having lived in California for 30 years, I was familiar with the missions, designed by the Franciscan priest Junípero Serra, and for whom one of the busiest freeways in the Bay Area is named. But none of the California missions I’d visited were anywhere near as elaborate and baroque as this structure. In fact, I later learned that the style of the five Sierra Gorda missions is known as “mestizo baroque.”

Junípero Serra, a priest from the island of Mallorca, achieved his dream of becoming a missionary in the Americas at the age of 36, in 1749. After disembarking in Veracruz, he refused to ride horseback to Mexico City, instead journeying on foot the entire 270 miles, despite a severe leg injury. Five months later, he walked another 175 miles from Mexico City to the Sierra Gorda. He used the motto siempre adelante (always forward) to drive his missionary zeal.

In the Sierra Gorda, he evangelized the local population and used the sweat of the Pame, local Indigenous people, to build the five missions that, 250 years later, would become a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

There are several reasons for the dramatic difference in style between the two sets of missions, those in the interior of Mexico and the later ones on the Pacific coast, from Baja California to present-day San Francisco.

Location

The Sierra Gorda missions were close to rich colonial centers, like Mexico City, Querétaro and Guadalajara, which served as supply hubs, as well as to well-established trade routes and ample financial backing from New Spain.

On the other hand, the missions in Alta California (now the U.S. state of California) were built in remote, isolated outposts, thousands of miles from supply ports. Few overland routes existed, which forced Serra to rely on infrequent supply ships.

Skilled labor

In Mexico, the local Pame and other Indigenous artisans had been carving stone for centuries. After being converted, they blended Catholic iconography with Indigenous symbols, creating a hybrid of rich, intricate facades that look as if carved from stone filigree rather than masonry.

In contrast, unskilled workers in Alta California used local sun-dried adobe bricks, timber and river stones, resulting in a much simpler style.

The goal of the missions

In Mexico, the imposing mission architecture was designed to convey permanent control over wealthy interior mining and agricultural zones, whereas in Alta California the missions were built as a military strategy. International law at the time required actual physical settlement to hold a region. Placing missions next to military forts along the coast created a visible barrier against Russian fur traders moving south from Alaska and British explorers from the Pacific Northwest.

Leadership style differences

In addition to architecture, Serra’s way of governing also differed. While he used the same forced Catholic conversion and paternalism in both areas, his treatment of the locals differed. In the Sierra Gorda, he spent nine years learning the Pame language, translating catechisms, teaching European farming techniques and helping the Pames defend their agricultural plots from predatory Spanish soldiers and landowners. And he allowed the well-integrated Pames a high degree of freedom.

In California, however, Serra’s treatment of the Indigenous people was very mixed. On one hand, he wrote letters and reports condemning the violence, rape and mistreatment of native women by Spanish military officers, even walking hundreds of miles to Mexico City to meet directly with the viceroy to secure a “bill of rights” for Indigenous people.

But he was a harsh disciplinarian. Indigenous people were subjected to confinement in crowded, unsanitary conditions; forced labor; and corporal punishment if they tried to leave. Tragically, the isolated missions in Baja and Alta California also became vectors for European epidemic diseases, to which the local population had no immunity, leading to huge population decline, whereas the Pame had already developed relative immunity.

Reactions to Serra’s canonization

Pope Francis canonized Serra in 2015, during a visit to the United States. After such a complicated life, it’s no wonder that his canonization was greeted with very mixed reactions, especially in the U.S. Many traditional Hispanics cheered the decision, seeing it as a long-overdue acknowledgment by the Church of the role the Spanish-speaking missionaries played in bringing the faith to the Americas.

Others condemned the canonization, protesting at the archdioceses in Los Angeles and Washington, D.C., and dubbing Serra the “saint of genocide.” They were also disappointed that Pope Francis canonized Serra when only a few months earlier he had apologized for the “grave sins” committed against Indigenous peoples during the conquest of the Americas.

Mexicans were ambivalent. Because most Mexicans are mestizo — a mix of Spanish Catholic and Indigenous — people wrestled with practicing a deep faith that they loved, yet with the painful awareness that it was introduced through brutal colonial subjugation.

Clearly, Junípero Serra was a complex character. On one hand, he went out of his way to defend Indigenous and women’s rights, yet at the same time betrayed a lack of respect for their human dignity and agency. I suspect he will always be viewed as a complicated historical figure with a controversial legacy.

Louisa Rogers and her husband Barry Evans divide their lives between Guanajuato and Eureka, on California’s North Coast. Louisa writes articles and essays about expat life, Mexico, travel, physical and psychological health, retirement and spirituality. Her recent articles are available on her website, authory.com/LouisaRogers.

World.title: The story of Hotel Mocambo, Mexico’s original luxury beach resort
World.content:
When it comes to tourism in Mexico, one of the most popular options for international visitors is to spend a few nights at a majestic beach resort. From Cancún to Los Cabos, Mexico has established itself as a premier destination for world-class beach getaways, with Mexico’s Ministry of Tourism reporting that nearly half of Mexico’s visitors opt for ritzy coastal areas — where sprawling luxurious properties abound.

The shift toward Mexico’s coastline

The numbers show just how vital Mexico’s top-tier beaches are to its national tourism economy: Despite an overall lower number of visitors this year and a massive blow from U.S. airlines this summer, Cancún still leads the nation in international flight arrivals, accounting for 45% of Mexico’s airport activity as of June, with 4,844,588 reported flight arrivals.

Besides Mexico City, Guadalajara and Monterrey, which are among the 10 most active airports in Mexico, every other visit is largely due to Mexico’s beaches. This year, Los Cabos, Puerto Vallarta, Tulum, Cozumel and Mazatlán have generated the most airport traffic, respectively, with roughly 66% of Mexico’s inbound flights touching down near those beaches.

And yet, Mexico’s identity as a destination for opulent beach resorts originated in a region that is nowadays overlooked, particularly by international visitors. But if you know where to look, a time-travel beach experience awaits along the Gulf Coast, with its own kind of grandeur and charm.

Hotel Mocambo: Mexico’s first grand luxury resort

It’s impossible to overstate the historical significance of Veracruz and its port city, where the Spanish colonization of continental Latin America began in 1519. Over centuries, many of the country’s earliest contributions can be traced back to its Gulf Coast origins, including coffee, jalapeños, vanilla and more.

Add to that list: Mexico’s first grand luxury beach resort.

In 1938, Hotel Mocambo — named after Playa Mocambo, the beach where the hotel was built, and which originally derived from an Afro-Portuguese word denoting the region’s legacy as a refuge for escaped African slaves — began construction, making it among the earliest (if not the first) major beachfront resort in all of Mexico.

A midcentury haven for Mexican stars and cinema

During its heyday, Hotel Mocambo became a national treasure, with famous Mexican actors, musicians and celebrities — including Agustín Lara, Chavela Vargas and Pedro Infante — becoming regulars throughout the midcentury.

In 1943, “María Eugenia,” starring the iconic Mexican actress María Félix (and featuring a cameo from popular Veracruz singer Toña la Negra, who also personally frequented the hotel in those days), was filmed at Mocambo, demarcating the Golden Age of Mexican cinema.

Mocambo began as a 15-room property with a palm tree-studded view of the coastline to be enjoyed from extensive outdoor terrazas, grand staircases, arched hallways and open-air patios. A large outdoor pool and nearby barroom with high ceilings and jacuzzis can be found on separate levels, with a staircase that connects everything and inevitably descends to the beach.

Spanish influence and architectural expansion

The hotel’s walkways are breezy and bedecked with a combination of maritime decorations and Moorish structural features designed by Jesús Martí Martín, an avant-garde architect who was exiled from Madrid, Spain, after the Spanish Civil War. Martín was commissioned by Gov. Miguel Alemán Valdés to lead the hotel’s design atop the highest coastal hill in Boca del Río — the city just south of the port of Veracruz, which sits on the Jamapa River along the Gulf of Mexico — around the time that other beach hotels were starting to sprout up in the Pacific states of Guerrero and Sonora.

Under the governorship of Alemán Valdés, who would go on to become Mexico’s president, Hotel Mocambo aimed to become the first grand-scale beach resort attraction in all of Mexico.

And for a time, it was.

Just two years after opening, the hotel’s first expansion was overseen by another Spanish architect, Enrique Segarra. At one point, the hotel grew to include 110 rooms, though today that number has dwindled to 70 (for context, Mexico’s grandest beach resorts can now exceed more than 2,000 rooms).

Though it is no longer the nexus of Mexican aristocracy that it once was, Mocambo remains an important historical fixture in Mexico’s development as an attractive beach resort destination.

Preserving the legacy of Mexico’s Golden Age

Before Mocambo and the subsequent rise of beach resorts all over Mexico, the country’s most opulent buildings and high-end tourist attractions were centered in Mexico’s cosmopolitan inland cities. Not until Mocambo in Veracruz — and the rise of Acapulco shortly after — did Mexico gain extreme popularity for its prime coastal real estate and beach resort culture.

Ironically, or perhaps symbolically, the once-tranquil escape of Mocambo is now surrounded by modern buildings, major avenues, parking lots and the nonstop bustle of Mexico’s largest port city on the Gulf Coast. One of the neighboring buildings is a recently built high-rise apartment that juxtaposes interestingly with the dilapidated glory of Hotel Mocambo. And the state’s largest and most glamorous mall is within a short walking distance, as modernity has crept up to overtake Mocambo’s place.

Although the paint is faded and signs of decay are apparent in its grand facades, the resort is still worthy of a visit — simply for the pleasure of reliving Mexico’s Golden Age origins of beachside luxury.

Alan Chazaro is the author of “These Spaceships Weren’t Built For Us” (Tia Chucha Press, 2026), “Notes from the Eastern Span of the Bay Bridge” (Ghost City Press, 2021), “Piñata Theory” (Black Lawrence Press, 2020), and “This Is Not a Frank Ocean Cover Album” (Black Lawrence Press, 2019). He is a graduate of June Jordan’s Poetry for the People program at UC Berkeley and was selected as a Lawrence Ferlinghetti Poetry Fellow at the University of San Francisco. His work can be found in NPR, The Guardian, SLAM, GQ, L.A. Times, and more. He is currently based in Veracruz.

World.title: Latin America Defense Monitor — September 12–19, 2026
World.content:
The Latin America Defense Monitor: military moves, arms deals and security policy across Latin America and the Caribbean, in plain language

Weekly Edition · Sunday, 20 September 2026 · Issue #22

Executive Summary The Big Picture: This week’s Latin America Defense Monitor opens in Caracas. On 16 September, Washington removed Venezuela from its list of countries that “failed demonstrably” to fight drug trafficking. A day later, the interim government and the opposition opened a second round of US-backed transition talks. On 18 September, the White House confirmed that President Trump will meet acting president Delcy Rodríguez at the UN General Assembly next week — the first such meeting since US forces captured Nicolás Maduro in January. Eight months after the operation, Venezuela has moved from target to partner. In Colombia, the war met a harder test. The ELN confirmed it holds four people kidnapped on 17 August — an army major, two police patrol officers and a civilian — and proposed an exchange. President de la Espriella refused. He demanded unconditional release and ordered operations reinforced. A strike killed a senior ELN commander. On 18–19 September, chairing a security council in Cartagena, he moved the DIMAR maritime authority from Bogotá to the coast and named the commanders his forces will hunt in Bolívar. Ecuador produced the week’s quiet landmark: the first institutional pushback against the US presence. President Noboa removed the air force chief by decree after the general asked for legal rules covering US flights at Taura air base. Days earlier, Ecuadorian courts had freed 56 crew members of vessels seized in US operations. The Bottom Line Up Front: The region’s two tracks are now visible at once. The diplomatic track delivered Venezuela’s rehabilitation — removed from the failed-states list, talking transition, signing with TotalEnergies, and heading for a Trump–Rodríguez meeting. The military track ground on: three more US boat strikes, a hostage crisis in Colombia, and the first open friction inside a partner’s armed forces over what US operations may legally do. The Latin America Defense Monitor tracks both tracks every week.

Latin America Defense Monitor: Where Things Stand

Country Status What’s Happening Venezuela High Removed from the US “failed demonstrably” drug list (16 September); second round of transition talks opened (17 September); Trump–Rodríguez meeting set for UNGA week; TotalEnergies deal signed; some censored news sites unblocked. Colombia High ELN holds four hostages since 17 August and proposed an exchange; government refuses and reinforces operations; senior ELN commander killed in a strike; Cartagena security council names targets in Bolívar; DIMAR moves to the coast. Ecuador Elevated Air force chief removed after requesting legal rules for US flights at Taura; courts freed 56 crew members of seized vessels; US$45 million security package still pending in Washington. US (SOUTHCOM) Elevated Boat-strike campaign continued with lethal strikes on 16 and 19 September; cumulative toll uncertain — public tallies differ and no official count exists. Peru Active UNITAS LXVII in its second week at Callao — amphibious and live-fire phases with US Marines; exercise closes 24 September. Argentina Watch Falklands dispute quiet this week; four US-approved Black Hawks in the pipeline; Tierra del Fuego naval-base funding stands. Brazil Watch Election season dominates; Tamandaré batch-2 frigates and Gripen assembly proceed without announcements. Mexico Watch On the US major-transit list but not designated as failing; no new border incidents reported.

01 The Week’s Key Stories 12–19 September 2026

VENEZUELA 1. From failed state to partner in one signature On 15 September, the White House sent Congress its annual determination on major drug-transit countries. Venezuela stays on that list, alongside Colombia, Mexico, Peru, Ecuador and Bolivia. But the decisive line came a day later: Venezuela is no longer designated as having “failed demonstrably” to meet counternarcotics obligations. The document cites “positive steps taken under interim President Delcy Rodríguez,” including the June operation that killed Niño Guerrero, the Tren de Aragua leader. Only Afghanistan, Bolivia, Burma and Colombia keep the failed designation. The diplomatic sequence moved fast after that. On 17 September, government and opposition opened a second round of US-backed transition talks in Caracas, with Jorge Rodríguez leading the government side. On 18 September, the telecoms regulator unblocked 17 news sites that had been censored for years, and the White House confirmed that Trump will meet Rodríguez in New York during the UN General Assembly, which runs 22–26 September. On 19 September, Rodríguez signed an agreement with the French oil company TotalEnergies. Money frames all of it. Washington says it secured majority control of more than 65 billion barrels of Venezuelan reserves in August. Trump said on 13 September that Venezuelan revenue has “paid for the war many times,” referring to Iran. A US$4 billion gold reserve is leaving the Bank of England for a US Treasury account. Reuters reports that Washington now wants access to gold, bauxite and nickel. What is not known: the legal basis of Rodríguez’s presidency (the constitution’s 180-day caretaker limit passed in July, unpublished), and whether any election date exists at all. What it means: For defense planners, Venezuela is no longer a contingency; it is a platform. The security relationship is being built on oil revenue and counternarcotics cooperation, not on a published legal framework. That makes it fast and fragile at the same time. The UNGA meeting will show the price: Rodríguez needs recognition, Washington needs the cooperation to keep working. The spectrum runs from normalized partnership to protectorate, and this week moved the marker clearly toward partnership. The question the region’s governments are asking is which direction their own relationship with Washington is moving.

COLOMBIA 2. The hostage test: four captives and a refused exchange The ELN confirmed it holds four people kidnapped on 17 August: army major Fredy Alexis Russi González, police patrol officers Erika Tatiana Monroy Hurtado and Edinson Yesid Medina Traslaviña, and civilian Angi Jácome. The guerrilla group proposed what it called a hostage exchange. On 17 September, President de la Espriella rejected the idea publicly. The four must be released unconditionally, he said, and operations to find them will be intensified. The same week brought the offensive’s continued rhythm. A strike killed a senior ELN commander, after which the president warned remaining fighters they would be pursued. On 18–19 September, in Cartagena, he chaired a security council and announced two things: the DIMAR maritime authority will move from Bogotá to Cartagena, and operations in Bolívar will target named commanders of the ELN, the Segunda Marquetalia, the Estado Mayor de Bloques and the Clan del Golfo — their financial networks included. His words to them: surrender or face an expiration date. Around the hard line, the accountability debate continues. A judge ordered the presidency’s corpse videos hidden temporarily pending a final ruling. Congress is weighing a submission-law framework for criminal groups without political status: reduced sentences for full confessions and asset forfeiture. And the 2027 budget — roughly 635 trillion pesos, about US$204 billion — has opened a public fight with former president Petro over who owns the deficit. What it means: Hostage situations test offensive doctrines in a way body counts do not. Negotiating an exchange would undercut the government’s stated position that these groups are terrorists, not belligerents. Refusing one risks four lives. The Cartagena council shows the strategy widening from killing commanders to attacking finances — a slower method whose results take longer to see. The direction of movement is clear: no talks, more pressure. What is stabilizing: the courts are working, the budget debate is public, and the submission law offers a legal exit ramp for groups that take it.

ECUADOR 3. The first pushback: a fired general and 56 freed crew On 10 September, President Noboa removed the air force chief, General Salazar, by decree. The dismissal became public knowledge this week, along with its cause: the general had asked for legal rules governing US military flights at Taura air base. Two days before the decree, an Ecuadorian court in the Galápagos had freed 28 crew members of vessels seized in US counter-drug operations. Another 28 had been freed in Manta the previous weekend. The sequence matters. US special forces operate inside Ecuador with 180-day visa-free entry. Two US warships are expected. A US$45 million security package is pending in Washington, along with a Coast Guard cutter and five interceptor boats for Ecuador’s navy. Inside that expanding presence, Ecuador’s own institutions have now asked, twice in one week, what the legal limits are — one through a general’s letter, one through judges’ rulings. What it means: This is the sovereignty question arriving on schedule. It is not anti-Americanism; the general asked for rules, not withdrawal, and the courts applied Ecuadorian law to Ecuadorian detainees. But every deep security partnership reaches the point where the host country’s institutions test its edges. Noboa’s answer — removing the officer — signals he will not let the military slow the US track. That resolves the question politically, not legally. Watch whether the courts keep releasing crews: each release is a quiet ruling on the evidence behind the interdictions.

CARIBBEAN 4. The boat campaign continues; the count does not add up US forces struck suspected drug boats on 16 September, killing three people, and again on 19 September, killing two, according to US Southern Command. A further strike was reported on 20 September, killing four. The campaign has now run for over a year across the Caribbean and the eastern Pacific. The cumulative toll is genuinely uncertain. This publication reported more than 230 dead across at least 75 strikes earlier this month, based on open-source tracking. Some wire reports this week cited a figure near 180. The difference reflects method, not necessarily error: trackers disagree on which incidents to include, and no official public count exists. What is also not public: the identities of most of the dead, the evidence against each vessel, and the legal review behind individual strikes. What it means: A year in, the campaign is routine enough to merit a paragraph in regional coverage and lethal enough to fill that paragraph weekly. The accountability gap is now the story: a sustained lethal operation whose public record does not allow an exact death toll. For the region’s governments, the practical question is unchanged — the interdictions happen in shared waters, and the intelligence behind them is not shared. Ecuador’s courts (story 3) are the first institution to test that record formally.

PERU 5. UNITAS, week two: from the harbor to the beach UNITAS LXVII continued at Callao through its second week. The 67th edition of the Americas’ longest-running multinational naval exercise involves 24 countries, more than 5,700 personnel, 26 ships and three submarines. This week moved from harbor and classroom phases to live fire: Peruvian marines on pistol ranges, US Marines training alongside Peruvian and Bolivian personnel, amphibious work at the naval infantry base. The littoral combat ship USS Minneapolis–Saint Paul is among the US participants. The exercise closes on 24 September. What it means: Peru is spending its “golden era” capital visibly. Hosting the region’s largest exercise in the same month it joined the Shield of the Americas and became a major non-NATO ally is a deliberate stacking of signals: Lima wants to be the Pacific anchor of the US security architecture. The amphibious and riverine phases matter more than the fleet review — they rehearse the terrain where the region’s actual operations happen. What could reverse it: the unresolved F-16 procurement scandal from April still sits with Congress, and big-ticket deals remain politically radioactive.

02 What’s Being Bought

Country The Deal Where It Stands Why It Matters Venezuela US control of 65bn+ barrels; TotalEnergies agreement; US$4bn gold transfer Signed/moving; terms partly unpublished The security relationship is financed through resources, not appropriations Ecuador US$45m security package, one Coast Guard cutter, five interceptors Pending in Washington Funds the US presence; first delivery will test the Taura legal question Argentina Four UH-60 Black Hawks (US approval) Approved; delivery pending First US rotorcraft in years; arrives mid-Falklands tension Brazil Tamandaré batch-2 frigates; Gripen assembly Proceeding quietly The region’s only serious naval-industrial program keeps building Venezuela (legacy) Russian air-defense systems (S-300VM, Buk, Pantsir) Neutralized in January; no replacement announced The gap in Venezuelan air defense is now a US planning assumption

03 The Big Powers

United States The dominant week. Venezuela removed from the failed list, a UNGA meeting scheduled, oil revenue publicly credited with paying for the Iran war, three more boat strikes. The model is now explicit: security cooperation paid for with resource access. A Reuters/Ipsos poll says only a quarter of Americans consider the Iran war worthwhile — the domestic constraint on the model’s next theater. France Back in the hemisphere through the side door: TotalEnergies signed with Rodríguez on 19 September, the first major European energy return to Venezuela since January. Paris gains position in the oil sector Washington now controls. China The stated target of Washington’s push into Venezuelan gold, bauxite and nickel. Beijing’s regional position this week is defined by what the US is trying to pre-empt. Russia No regional moves. Its two-decade military position in Venezuela remains a memory and a procurement lesson. Brazil Quiet by choice: election season, no new programs announced, frigate and Gripen work continuing. The hemisphere’s largest democracy is sitting out the alignment season.

04 What to Watch Next 7–30 Days

What the coming editions of the Latin America Defense Monitor will be tracking:

VENEZUELA The Trump–Rodríguez meeting at UNGA (22–26 September); outcome of the second transition-talks round; any published legal basis for the interim presidency; terms of the TotalEnergies agreement. COLOMBIA The fate of the four ELN hostages; results of the reinforced Bolívar operations; the submission law’s path through Congress; the budget fight with Petro. ECUADOR Whether courts keep freeing seized crews; arrival of the pledged US vessels; any legal framework for Taura replacing the removed general’s request. CARIBBEAN The strike tempo and any official accounting of the campaign’s toll. PERU UNITAS closing on 24 September; any F-16 movement after the exercise spotlight fades.

05 The Bottom Line

Eight months ago, US forces captured a sitting president in Caracas. This week, his successor prepared to meet the US president in New York — removed from the failed-states list, signing with a French oil major, unblocking news sites. Whatever one thinks of the method, the speed of that arc has no recent precedent in the hemisphere. The same week showed the costs of the harder track. In Colombia, four kidnapped people wait while their government refuses the exchange their captors proposed. In Ecuador, a general lost his job for asking what rules govern US flights, and judges keep quietly releasing the crews that US interdictions deliver. In the Caribbean, boats keep sinking, and the public record cannot say exactly how many people have died. Alignment, last week’s theme, now has its invoice. The Latin America Defense Monitor will keep counting both sides of it.

World.title: Latin America Security: Colombia Frees Hostages, Bolivia Expels PCC Suspect
World.content:
Latin America · Defence

Key Facts — The rescue. Colombia’s army rescued four hostages, one a minor, held by FARC dissidents in Antioquia on Saturday. — The operation. Two alleged guerrillas were killed and one captured during the rescue in rural Gómez Plata. — The expulsion. Bolivia expelled an alleged PCC member and handed him to Brazil’s Federal Police at Puerto Suárez. — The frigate. Argentina’s ARA Libertad returned to Buenos Aires after a 161-day training voyage of about 15,900 nautical miles. — The exercise. Southern Vanguard 2026 ran from 8 to 18 September in Peru’s jungle with US, Argentine and Chilean troops. — The missile. Brazil’s Army and Avibras test-launched the AV-MTC cruise missile on 26 August in Rio de Janeiro.

Colombia’s army rescued four people, including a minor, from FARC dissidents in rural Antioquia on Saturday 19 September. Two alleged guerrillas were killed and one captured in the operation, according to Noticias RCN and Infobae.

The same weekend, Bolivia expelled an alleged member of Brazil’s largest criminal group and handed him to Brazilian police. Argentina’s navy training ship returned home, and a jungle exercise with US troops wrapped up in Peru.

The Argentine navy’s training frigate ARA Libertad, which returned to Buenos Aires on 19 September after 161 days at sea (Photo: Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 3.0 via Wikimedia Commons)

Colombia Rescues Four Hostages in Antioquia

The rescue took place in the countryside of Gómez Plata, a municipality in Antioquia department, on Saturday 19 September. The four had been held since the previous Thursday, Noticias RCN reported.

They were guarded by five men said to belong to the security detail of a commander known as La Mona. That unit is part of Estructura 36, a FARC dissident group under a commander known as Calarcá.

President Abelardo de la Espriella hailed the operation on X as a blow against the E36 terrorist group, Infobae reported. The names of those rescued have not been released.

FARC dissidents are factions that rejected the 2016 peace agreement with the former guerrilla army. They finance themselves through drug trafficking, extortion and illegal mining.

Bolivia Expels Alleged PCC Member to Brazil

Bolivia expelled a Brazilian citizen described as highly dangerous and allegedly linked to the Primeiro Comando da Capital on Saturday 19 September. The PCC, born in São Paulo’s prisons, is Brazil’s largest criminal organisation and is active across South America.

He was driven under police escort to the border town of Puerto Suárez, in Santa Cruz department, La Patria and ERBOL reported. After an expulsion order was served at the migration office at 09:45, he was handed to Brazil’s Federal Police.

His name has not been released, and no court has ruled on his alleged links to the gang. On 18 September The Rio Times reported that Bolivia’s interior minister warned lawmakers that Brazilian gangs are recruiting Bolivians.

Argentina’s ARA Libertad Returns After 54th Voyage

The Argentine navy’s training frigate ARA Libertad returned to Buenos Aires on Saturday 19 September. It docked at the navy’s berth in the capital after its 54th training voyage, which began on 11 April.

The ship spent 161 days at sea and covered about 15,900 nautical miles, Zona Militar reported. That is roughly 29,400 kilometres, about three-quarters of the way around the Earth.

The Libertad is a three-masted sailing ship that trains Argentine naval cadets on long ocean voyages. It is one of the country’s best-known ambassadors, visiting ports around the world.

Southern Vanguard 2026 Trains Troops in Peru’s Jungle

Southern Vanguard 2026, known in Spanish as Vanguardia Sur, took place in Peru’s Amazon jungle from 8 to 18 September. The exercise was hosted at the Peruvian Army’s Jungle School in Sauce, near Tarapoto.

Troops from the United States, Argentina, Chile and Peru took part. US Army South, the US Army component for Latin America and the Caribbean, backed the initiative, according to Defensa.com.

The instruction phase moved into field training on 15 September, according to DVIDSHub. The exercise tested interoperability in a demanding environment: heat, rain, rivers and dense forest.

The location matters because the Amazon is a zone of drug trafficking, illegal mining and armed groups. Training there prepares forces for real missions in the region.

Brazil Tests Cruise Missile With Avibras

Brazil’s Army and the defence company Avibras test-launched the AV-MTC tactical cruise missile on 26 August. The firing took place at the Marambaia Test Field in Rio de Janeiro, run by the Army Evaluation Center.

The test was reported by Airspace Review on 11 September. It resumed certification flights after a pause of about four years caused by Avibras’s financial troubles.

The missile has a range of up to 300 kilometres. In June the company said three more flights were needed to complete certification, with the next expected in November 2026.

Avibras, based in São José dos Campos, is also known for the ASTROS rocket artillery system. The programme is part of Brazil’s effort to build up its domestic defence industry.

Colombia Reports Guerrilla Cells in Public Universities

Colombian authorities have identified clandestine cells of the ELN and FARC dissidents in 10 public universities, according to an intelligence document seen by Semana. Infobae reported the finding on 19 September.

The universities named include the National University of Colombia and the District University in Bogotá. In Medellín, the list includes the University of Antioquia and the Jaime Isaza Cadavid Polytechnic.

The report says the groups recruit and instrumentalise young people through student collectives and social organisations. No court has verified the intelligence findings, and the universities have not confirmed them.

Medellín’s mayor said on 14 September that 22 radical groups were pressuring the city’s public universities. That statement, reported by Caracol Radio, referred broadly to public universities in the city.

Why the Weekend Matters for Regional Security

The weekend’s events show how security problems cross borders in South America. A Brazilian gang suspect was caught in Bolivia, while Colombian armed groups hold hostages and recruit on campuses.

Colombia’s government under President de la Espriella has promised a harder line against armed groups, and the rescue is an early test. Joint training with the United States, as in Peru, remains central to how the region’s armies prepare.

Frequently Asked Questions

Who were the hostages rescued in Colombia? Four people, including one minor, were rescued in Gómez Plata, Antioquia, on 19 September. They had been held since the previous Thursday by alleged FARC dissidents. What is the PCC? The Primeiro Comando da Capital is Brazil’s largest criminal organisation, founded in São Paulo prisons. It operates across South America and is involved in drug trafficking and other crimes. Why did the ARA Libertad’s return matter? The frigate completed its 54th training voyage, covering about 15,900 nautical miles over 161 days. The voyages train Argentine naval cadets and show the flag abroad. What was Southern Vanguard 2026? It was a jungle training exercise in Peru from 8 to 18 September with troops from the US, Argentina, Chile and Peru. It focused on interoperability in the Amazon. What is the AV-MTC missile? It is a Brazilian tactical cruise missile with a range of up to 300 kilometres, developed by Avibras and the Army. A test launch took place on 26 August in Rio de Janeiro.

World.title: Latin America Business: Petrobras Subsidy, Chile Lithium and Remittances
World.content:
Latin America · Business

Key Facts — Petrobras decision. Petrobras’ board approved joining a new federal diesel subsidy of R$1 (about US$0.19) per litre on Friday 18 September. — How it works. The subsidy cancels out a matching Petrobras price rise for 30 days, extendable by another 30. — Ethanol contract. Vibra Energia signed a R$1.28 billion (about US$249 million) ethanol supply contract with Inpasa. — Lithium exports. Chile’s lithium exports reached US$4.332 billion in 2026 so far, roughly tripling returns. — Remittances. El Salvador, Guatemala and Honduras received US$29.064 billion in remittances from January to July, up 7.1%. — El Niño risk. WTW says El Niño could raise Latin American logistics costs by up to 15%.

Brazil’s state oil company Petrobras will join a new federal diesel subsidy worth R$1 (about US$0.19) per litre. Its board approved the move on Friday 18 September, and the company disclosed the decision the next day.

Elsewhere in Latin America, Chile’s lithium export revenue reached US$4.332 billion in 2026 so far, roughly tripling last year’s returns. Central American remittances kept rising, and insurers warned that El Niño could lift regional logistics costs by up to 15%.

Petrobras headquarters in Rio de Janeiro; the company’s board approved joining the new federal diesel subsidy on 18 September (Photo: Pavel Špindler, CC BY 3.0 via Wikimedia Commons)

Petrobras Joins New Diesel Subsidy

Petrobras, Brazil’s state-controlled oil company, said on Saturday 19 September that its board approved joining a new government diesel subsidy. The board met on Friday 18 September and approved the company’s participation, according to Reuters and Valor Econômico.

The subsidy is set at R$1 (about US$0.19) per litre of road diesel and is valid for 30 days. It can be extended for another 30 under a provisional measure of 11 September and a finance ministry order of 16 September.

The mechanism neutralises a R$1 (about US$0.19) increase in Petrobras’ diesel price to distributors. Petrobras raised its wholesale price by R$1 (about US$0.19), but the federal government finances a matching discount, so the company’s net price stays unchanged.

The new subsidy is cumulative with an existing R$1.12 (about US$0.22) per litre subsidy. That brings total support to R$2.12 (about US$0.41) per litre while both are in force, Reuters reported.

Reuters also reported that Brazil released R$13 billion (about US$2.5 billion) in fuel subsidies alongside tax cuts. No source breaks out the cost of this specific diesel programme.

Vibra Signs Ethanol Supply Deal With Inpasa

Vibra Energia, a Brazilian fuel distributor, signed a contract with Inpasa Agroindustrial for ethanol supply valued at R$1.28 billion (about US$249 million). The deal was reported by Valor Econômico on 18 September and by CNN Brasil the following day.

The ethanol will supply Vibra’s network of fuel stations and help meet regulatory obligations under ANP Resolution 946/2023. Inpasa is considered a related party because its chief executive, Éder Odvar Lopes, sits on Vibra’s board.

Reports differ on the contract’s term, with end dates ranging from August 2027 to 2029. Valor gave 1 September 2026 to 31 August 2027, citing the company’s filing.

Vibra said the contract was negotiated on market-compatible terms used for other suppliers. Those terms considered price, availability, logistics and delivery, and no specific volumes were disclosed.

Chile Lithium Exports Triple

Chile’s lithium exports reached US$4.332 billion in 2026 so far, roughly tripling returns compared with 2025, according to SoyChile. The figure covers the calendar year to date and was reported on 19 September.

In the first half of 2026, lithium export revenue was US$3.2 billion, according to Chile’s central bank. That was about three times the same period in 2025 and 34.4% higher than total lithium exports for all of 2025.

Chile is the world’s second-largest lithium producer, and the metal is a key input for electric vehicle batteries. Rising prices and strong demand have lifted export values sharply this year.

Central America Remittances Rise 7.1%

El Salvador, Guatemala and Honduras received US$29.064 billion in family remittances between January and July 2026, up 7.1% from the same period in 2025. The figures were compiled by the International Organization for Migration and reported by Infobae and ABC Color.

Guatemala received US$15.447 billion, or 53.1% of the total. Honduras received US$7.692 billion (26.5%) and El Salvador US$5.925 billion (20.4%).

Remittances are a major source of foreign income for these economies, supporting household consumption. Most of the money comes from workers in the United States.

El Niño Could Raise Logistics Costs

El Niño could raise logistics costs for Latin American companies by up to 15%, according to the insurance broker WTW. Infobae reported the warning on 19 September, citing transport bottlenecks and higher insurance premiums.

Fitch Ratings issued a similar warning in June 2026, saying El Niño would add to credit pressures for Latin American agribusiness. The ratings agency also pointed to freight bottlenecks and rising insurance costs.

El Niño can bring droughts, floods and storms that disrupt roads, ports and shipping schedules. For exporters of agricultural and mining goods, even small delays can raise costs and delay deliveries.

Costa Rica Widens Data Leak Probe

Costa Rica’s data protection agency, Prodhab, opened an administrative case on 16 September over the possible exposure of personal data on the dark web. It acted on its own initiative, La Nación and The Tico Times reported.

The science and technology ministry, Micitt, began checking the claims on 14 September. The cybercrime prosecutors opened their own criminal inquiry on 16 September.

A hacker claimed on a forum to hold millions of records with personal, financial, employment and judicial data. Authorities say they cannot yet confirm that the data is authentic or recent.

Frequently Asked Questions

What did Petrobras’ board approve? Petrobras’ board approved the company’s participation in a new federal diesel subsidy of R$1 (about US$0.19) per litre. The decision was made at a meeting on Friday 18 September and disclosed the next day. How long will the diesel subsidy last? The subsidy is valid for 30 days and can be extended for another 30 days. It is cumulative with an existing R$1.12 (about US$0.22) per litre subsidy while both are in force. How much are Chile’s lithium exports worth in 2026? Chile’s lithium exports reached US$4.332 billion in 2026 so far, roughly tripling returns compared with 2025. In the first half of 2026, exports were US$3.2 billion, according to the central bank. How much did Central American remittances rise? El Salvador, Guatemala and Honduras received US$29.064 billion in remittances from January to July 2026, up 7.1% from the same period in 2025. Guatemala accounted for just over half of the total. What is the Costa Rica data leak investigation about? Costa Rican authorities are investigating the alleged exposure of millions of personal records on the dark web. Prodhab, Micitt and the cybercrime prosecutor’s office have all opened cases.

World.title: Cuba Sanctions: US Targets Nickel Firms and Military Officers
World.content:
Cuba · Sanctions

Key Facts — The action. The United States sanctioned 11 Cuban targets linked to nickel and the military on Thursday 17 September. — The targets. Secretary of State Marco Rubio listed four state nickel companies, four military research firms and three officers. — The effect. Their assets under US jurisdiction are frozen, and Americans may not do business with them. — The stated reason. Washington says the firms belong to a system that enriches Cuba’s elite while ordinary Cubans suffer. — A neighbour’s verdict. Costa Rica’s foreign minister called Cuba’s government a vile tyranny on Saturday 19 September. — The backdrop. Cuba is living through blackouts and shortages, and nickel is one of its few hard-currency exports.

The United States has tightened the screws on the two pillars of Cuba’s state economy, its nickel mines and its military. On Thursday 17 September Washington sanctioned 11 Cuban targets, from state mining companies to senior officers.

Two days later Costa Rica, which broke off relations with Havana in March, called the island’s government a vile tyranny. Together the moves show Cuba’s isolation deepening in its own region as well as in Washington.

Nickel mining land near Moa in eastern Cuba; the island’s nickel sector is the main target of the new US sanctions (Photo: Ceever, CC BY-SA 4.0 via Wikimedia Commons)

What Washington Did

Rubio said the package covered four state companies tied to nickel reserves and four military research firms, including developers of weapons systems. Three military officers complete the list, Reuters reported.

The targets were added to the Specially Designated Nationals list kept by the Treasury’s Office of Foreign Assets Control. Any assets they hold under US jurisdiction are blocked, and US persons may not deal with them.

The exile news site CiberCuba named four nickel-sector entities: the supplier SERCONI, engineers CEPRONIQUEL, the research centre CEDINIQ and the geologists PINARES. The trade outlet ChemNet gave a partly different list, and no official list has been found.

The designations rest on an executive order President Donald Trump signed in May 2026. It widened the grounds for sanctioning people and companies that do business in Cuba.

Why Nickel Matters

Nickel is one of Cuba’s few large sources of foreign currency, alongside tourism and remittances. Its mines around Moa, in the eastern province of Holguín, have long been the island’s main industrial export.

In May Washington had already sanctioned GAESA, the military conglomerate that controls much of the economy, and its head, General Ania Guillermina Lastres Morera. It also listed Moa Nickel, a joint venture of Canada’s Sherritt International and Cuba’s state nickel company.

Sherritt, long the largest Western investor in Cuba, suspended its direct participation in Cuban joint ventures on 7 May. It halted metals refining at its plant in Fort Saskatchewan, Canada, on 22 June, the company said in a September update.

The new round reaches the service, engineering and research companies around the mines. It makes it harder for Cuba to find foreign partners willing to keep the industry running.

The Official Reasoning

The State Department said the targets are part of a system that enriches the elite while hurting ordinary Cubans, Reuters reported. Rubio also said the government threatens US national security.

Rubio, the son of Cuban immigrants, has made pressure on Havana a hallmark of his time as secretary of state. The September package is the latest of several rounds of Cuba sanctions this year.

Havana has long argued that American sanctions are the main cause of its economic crisis. A reaction to this specific package had not been found by Sunday.

Costa Rica’s Vile Tyranny

Costa Rica is not indifferent to a vile tyranny that has denied Cubans freedom and prosperity for six decades, wrote Foreign Minister Manuel Tovar. He added on X that his country stood firm in its break with the Castro regime, EFE reported.

The post answered a Cuban foreign ministry statement about the rupture, which Costa Rica had announced in March 2026. San José has made any return conditional on freedom and transparent elections in Cuba, Infobae reported.

A Country Running on Empty

The sanctions land on an island already in deep trouble. On Friday 18 September the national grid failed again, cutting power to millions of Cubans, as The Rio Times reported.

Fuel shortages, food scarcity and emigration have emptied towns and strained public services. Each new sanction narrows the room of a government that has few hard-currency earners left.

Cuba’s power plants are old and short of fuel, and failures of the whole grid have become a recurring event. The energy and mines ministry blamed Friday’s shutdown of the whole system on two high-voltage lines that tripped.

What It Means for Foreign Business

A listing on the sanctions list is not a criminal charge, but its reach extends beyond the United States. Banks, shippers and insurers that use the US financial system tend to avoid anyone on it.

For Canadian, European and Latin American firms still active in Cuba, the compliance risk has grown again. Any partner of the named nickel and military companies now needs to check its exposure.

Further designations remain possible under the May executive order. It covers Cuba’s energy, defence, metals and mining, financial services and security sectors.

Frequently Asked Questions

What did the US sanction in Cuba? It sanctioned 11 targets on 17 September: four state companies tied to nickel reserves, four military research firms and three military officers. What does the sanction do? It freezes any assets the targets hold under US jurisdiction and bars US persons from dealing with them. Foreign banks and shippers linked to the US financial system usually avoid them too. Why is nickel important to Cuba? It is one of the island’s few large sources of foreign currency, mined mainly around Moa in eastern Cuba. What did Costa Rica say about Cuba? Foreign Minister Manuel Tovar called Cuba’s government a vile tyranny on 19 September and reaffirmed the break in relations announced in March. Were these the first nickel sanctions this year? No. In May Washington sanctioned the military conglomerate GAESA and Moa Nickel, Sherritt International’s joint venture with Cuba.

Sources: Reuters, on the 17 September sanctions, U.S. News & World Report, Rubio’s breakdown, CiberCuba, on the entities named, ChemNet, on the nickel entities, Miami Herald, on the May sanctions, EFE, on Tovar’s statement

World.title: Honduras Declares Three Gangs Terrorist Groups but Keeps Their Names Secret
World.content:
Honduras · Security

Key Facts — The decision. Honduras declared three criminal groups terrorist on Saturday 19 September 2026. — Who announced it. Congress president Tomás Zambrano announced the decision and said the names stay secret. — The legal base. Decree 84-2026, published on 22 May 2026, made maras and pandillas terrorist associations. — Who signed it. President Nasry Asfura signed the penal code reform that made gangs terrorist associations in May. — The penalties. Leaders face 15 to 20 years; members face 10 to 15 years in prison. — What is unclear. No report names MS-13 or Barrio 18 among the three declared groups.

Honduras has declared three criminal groups terrorist organisations but will not say which ones. Tomás Zambrano, president of the National Congress, announced the decision of the National Defence and Security Council on Saturday 19 September.

The declaration rests on Decree 84-2026, a penal code reform published in the official gazette on 22 May 2026. That reform, signed by President Nasry Asfura, made maras and pandillas terrorist associations under Honduran law.

Tegucigalpa, the Honduran capital, where the National Defence and Security Council met on 18 September (Photo: Eduarg23, CC0 via Wikimedia Commons)

Three Groups Declared Without Public Names

The council, known by its Spanish initials CNDS, brings together the president, security ministers and prosecutors. It approved the declaration at the presidential palace on the night of Friday 18 September, El Heraldo reported.

Zambrano, who also sits on the council, confirmed the decision to reporters the following day in El Progreso, Yoro department. He said the names would not be released because publication could affect operations against the groups.

“We will not give their names because after that decision they will take different actions,” he said, according to La Prensa, a Honduran daily. The three groups were described only as criminal organizations with reach beyond Honduras into other Central American countries.

No official list has been published as of Sunday 20 September. The government has not said when, or whether, it will publish the names of the three declared groups.

The May Reform That Made This Possible

Decree 84-2026 amended article 587 of the Honduran penal code, which defines terrorist association. The reform was approved by Congress and signed by Asfura.

It extended the definition to cover groups that use systematic violence, collective intimidation, territorial control or coercion against the population. The text also covers organizations linked to drug trafficking, kidnapping and other criminal networks that seek to spread fear or pressure the state.

Maras and pandillas fall inside that definition, according to the government news service TNH. The reform raised penalties for extortion, organized crime and the financing of criminal structures.

Leaders, promoters and financiers face 15 to 20 years in prison and fines of thousands of days’ wages. Active members face 10 to 15 years.

Life Sentences When Victims Die

Under the reform, courts can impose life imprisonment when victims die as a result of these crimes, TNH reported. It is one of the toughest sentencing changes in Honduras in years.

Military Patrols and Maximum-Security Prisons

The declaration is part of a broader security strategy announced by Asfura’s government. It includes more soldiers and police in high-risk areas and new specialized mechanisms to prosecute members of the declared groups.

The plan also calls for maximum-security prisons, according to Infobae Honduras. Zambrano ruled out a state of exception, saying the government would act against criminal structures within ordinary legal rules.

Honduran outlets also reported that a new director of the National Anti-Crime Agency would be named. No arrests or operations tied to the declaration had been announced by Sunday.

Are MS-13 and Barrio 18 Among Them?

MS-13, also called Mara Salvatrucha, and Barrio 18 are the two best-known gangs in Honduras. The United States designated both as foreign terrorist organisations in 2025.

International coverage, including DW’s, cited both gangs as background to the Honduran announcement. No report has confirmed that either is among the three groups the council declared.

Zambrano described the three only as criminal organisations with branches elsewhere in Central America, DW reported. That description would fit several of the region’s larger networks.

How Honduras Compares With El Salvador

El Salvador took a different route. In August 2015 its Supreme Court’s constitutional chamber declared MS-13 and Barrio 18 terrorist groups under the country’s anti-terrorism law.

Honduras weighed a similar step as early as 2017, InSight Crime reported at the time. It has now done so by statute, with the executive choosing which groups the label covers.

President Nayib Bukele’s El Salvador later went much further, with a state of exception in force since 2022 and mass detentions. Zambrano explicitly ruled out that model for now.

Concerns About How Far the Law Reaches

Jurists and human rights defenders warned in May that the broadened terrorism definition could be applied too widely. Criterio.hn reported their concern that it could be used against protest movements and social organizations.

The reform’s language includes concepts such as social dominance, territorial presence and collective submission. Critics say those terms are vague and could cover conduct far from organized crime.

No court has yet ruled on how the new definition applies in practice. Keeping the names of the declared groups secret will make that scrutiny harder.

Frequently Asked Questions

Did Honduras name MS-13 and Barrio 18 as terrorist groups? No. The government declared three criminal groups terrorist but kept their names confidential, and no report confirms which gangs they are. The United States designated MS-13 and Barrio 18 as terrorist groups in 2025. What law did Honduras use for this declaration? The declaration rests on Decree 84-2026, a penal code reform published in the official gazette on 22 May 2026. It amended article 587 to classify maras and pandillas as terrorist associations. Who announced the decision? Tomás Zambrano, president of Honduras’ National Congress, announced it on Saturday 19 September 2026. The National Defence and Security Council, which includes President Nasry Asfura, approved it the night before. What penalties do the declared groups face? Leaders, promoters and financiers face 15 to 20 years in prison and heavy fines. Active members face 10 to 15 years, and life imprisonment is possible when victims die. Why are the group names secret? Zambrano said publishing the names could affect operations against the groups. He ruled out a state of exception, saying the government would act within ordinary legal rules.

Sources: Infobae Honduras, 19 September 2026, DW en español, 19 September 2026, TNH, government news service, 24 May 2026, Criterio.hn, 21 May 2026, La Prensa Honduras, 19 September 2026, O Povo, 19 September 2026, Insight Crime, 28 March 2017

World.title: Argentina’s Luis Caputo Faces Criminal Complaint Over Central Puerto Deal
World.content:
Argentina · Politics

Key Facts — The complaint. Lawyer Virginia Marta Cassola filed a criminal complaint against Economy Minister Luis Caputo on Friday 18 September. — The deal. Central Puerto paid US$25 million for a stake in AbraSilver in 2024 and sold it for US$163 million. — The allegation. Cassola asks whether Caputo improperly steered tax benefits to the silver project to enrich Central Puerto. — The court. The case went to federal court 11, currently run by Judge Ariel Lijo as a substitute. — The caveat. A complaint starts a review, not a prosecution, and no court has found any wrongdoing. — The politics. It lands as the ruling coalition argues over election rules and Patricia Bullrich’s growing weight.

Argentina’s economy minister, Luis Caputo, faces a criminal complaint over a mining deal that made a power company six times its money. A lawyer filed it in a Buenos Aires federal court on Friday 18 September.

A complaint is only a request to investigate, and no court has found any wrongdoing. It still gives the opposition a legal hook for a political attack on President Javier Milei’s flagship investment regime.

The Palacio de Hacienda in Buenos Aires, seat of the Economy Ministry led by Luis Caputo (Photo: Horacio Cambeiro, CC BY-SA 4.0 via Wikimedia Commons)

What the Complaint Says

The lawyer Virginia Marta Cassola named Caputo and the directors and shareholders of Central Puerto, a major power generator, La Política Online reported. The case fell to federal court number 11, now run on an interim basis by Judge Ariel Lijo.

She asks investigators to examine possible negotiations incompatible with public office, breach of official duties, fraud and misuse of privileged information. At the centre is whether Caputo intervened irregularly to approve tax benefits for AbraSilver’s Diablillos project.

Diablillos is a gold and silver project straddling the provinces of Salta and Catamarca in the north-west. The complaint argues the approval was meant to produce an extraordinary gain for Central Puerto.

No prosecutor had been named by Sunday, and no response from Caputo or Central Puerto to the complaint was found. Judge Lijo must first decide whether to pass it to a prosecutor for investigation.
