World.title: Four from four! Hungary’s chess team on a winning streak after perfect Olympiad start
World.content:
Hungary’s open chess team continued its unbeaten run at the Chess Olympiad in Uzbekistan on Saturday, defeating Israel to secure a fourth consecutive match victory. With three of the four games ending in draws, Benjamin Gledura’s game proved decisive. Hungary’s women’s team, meanwhile, suffered their first defeat of the tournament against China after opening with three victories.

The 46th Chess Olympiad is taking place in Samarkand, Uzbekistan, bringing together national teams from across the world. The open competition features 206 teams, while 188 are competing in the women’s section. The tournament runs until 27 September.

For readers less familiar with team chess, each match consists of four individual games. A win earns one game point, a draw half a point and a loss none. The combined scores determine which team wins the match, with a victory worth two match points.

Hungary defeated Israel 2.5–1.5 in the fourth round, following earlier victories over Malta, Colombia and Slovenia. The team, captained by Csaba Balogh, therefore have the maximum eight match points from their opening four encounters.

Benjamin Gledura delivers another crucial victory

Hungary rested experienced grandmaster Peter Leko for the match against Israel. Richard Rapport played on the top board, followed by Benjamin Gledura, Tamas Banusz and Gleb Dudin. Rapport, Banusz and Dudin all drew their games, leaving Gledura’s encounter with Avital Boruchovsky to decide the match.

Gledura won in 44 moves, securing the point Hungary needed for another 2.5–1.5 victory. The result was particularly welcome for the Hungarian grandmaster, who had lost his opening-round game against Malta but has since contributed two wins to the team’s campaign.

All four of Hungary’s matches have ended by the same narrow margin. Under the Olympiad’s scoring system, however, the size of a victory does not affect the match points awarded: each win is worth two points.

What are Hungary’s prospects at the Olympiad?

Hungary entered the open competition as the eighth-seeded team. Balogh said before the tournament that he hoped his players would finish in the top ten. The competition also has a recent connection to Hungary: Budapest hosted the previous Chess Olympiad in 2024, when the Hungarian open team finished 11th.

With seven rounds still to play, the team’s four-match winning streak has given them a strong start, although their final position remains to be decided.

China end Hungarian women’s winning streak

Hungary’s women’s team also began the Olympiad with three victories, beating Venezuela, Japan and the Philippines. Their unbeaten run ended in the fourth round, when China secured a 3.5–0.5 victory.

Zsoka Gaal, Szidonia Lazarne Vajda and Petra Papp lost their respective games. Nomin-Erdene Davaademberel earned Hungary’s only half-point with a draw against Zhai Mo.

Hungary’s women entered the tournament as the 18th-seeded team. Both Hungarian squads have seven more rounds ahead of them before the Olympiad concludes on 27 September.

World.title: EU President to Skip Serbia and Bosnia on Balkan Tour
World.content:
The European Commission announced on Friday that President Ursula von der Leyen will miss Serbia and Bosnia and Herzegovina during her trip to the Western Balkans between September 30 and October 2, citing upcoming elections in the two countries.

“In light of the upcoming parliamentary and general elections in Bosnia-Herzegovina and in Serbia, the president intends to visit these countries at a later date,” a Commission spokesperson, Arianna Podesta, said on Friday.

During the trip, von der Leyen will visit Albania, Kosovo, Montenegro and North Macedonia where she will meet leaders and look at EU-funded projects.

After the EU announcement, Serbia’s President hinted that looming elections were not the only reason for the no-show – hinting at her recent criticism of his administration.

“Ursula von der Leyen is far too wise and intelligent a woman to have any illusions about, or to be unaware of, public opinion in Serbia. So I’m sure she knows very well… [but] let’s not get into that,” Vucic said.

Von der Leyen and other EU officials have condemned Serbia’s government over the glorification of the convicted Bosnian Serb war criminal Ratko Mladic, whose funeral in Belgrade on September 7 was attended by ministers and high officials both from Serbia and Bosnia’s Serb-led entity, Republika Srpska.

“I was horrified by the pictures from Ratko Mladic’s funeral in Belgrade last week. He committed the most atrocious crimes against humanity. Glorifying war criminals simply has no place in the European Union,” von der Leyen said on September 16. Serbia is an EU candidate state.

A day after Mladic’s funeral, von der Leyen also wrote on X that “the elements of official support and the presence of some senior Serbian officials at the funeral are deeply regrettable”.

Earlier in September, EU Enlargement Commissioner Marta Kos cancelled her planned visit to Serbia, the day after Mladic’s body was transported on a government plane to Belgrade, where it was met by officials and an army honour guard.

Early parliamentary elections will be held in Serbia on October 25. President Vucic called the elections after a year-and-a-half of anti-government protesters demanding snap elections.

The elections will be Vucic’s most challenging test since he came to power in 2012. The main rival to his ruling Serbian Progressive Party, SNS, is the Student List, a political list formed by Serbian students who have been protesting since November 2024, following the deadly collapse of a railway station canopy in Novi Sad.

Bosnia and Herzegovina will hold presidential ​and parliamentary elections ‌on October 4.

World.title: Week in Review: Campaigns, Crackdowns and Clan Wars
World.content:
Wildfires have blazed across the Balkans over the last couple of months amid another scorching summer. Around the Albanian coastal city of Himara, they forced evacuations, destroyed homes and olive groves.

The Albanian government has identified the growing threat from wildfires as an expected consequence of climate change. But there’s a lack of readiness and coordination to confront the challenge, experts are warning.

World.title: Discontent Simmers in Kosovo as Protesters Denounce Hague War Crimes Verdict
World.content:
The KLA War Veterans’ Organisation, which staged Friday’s protest, called for the dismissal of Justice Minister Donika Gervalla, the repeal or amendment of the Law on the Kosovo Specialist Chambers, unlimited funding for the defence of the four former KLA leaders in their upcoming appeal against the verdict, and the engagement of top international experts for their defence.

Hysni Gucati, head of the organisation, accused minister Gervalla of submitting evidence for the case to the Kosovo Specialist Chambers in The Hague.

“We are telling [Prime Minister] Albin Kurti to remove these people from the government starting today; he should not keep them in the government. People who collaborate with the enemy are enemies of my nation, and we do not want them among us,” Gucati said.

“Donika Gervalla has still not come forward to apologise,” he added. Gervalla has not commented publicly about the allegation so far.

World.title: Fining Bosnia’s Parties for Campaign Violations Won’t Deter Them, Expert Warns
World.content:
The unprecedented fines imposed this week by Bosnia’s Central Election Commission won’t stop ruling parties from exploiting state resources to secure votes, Dario Jovanovic, project manager of the fair-elections campaign group Pod Lupom, told BIRN on Friday.

“Parties in Bosnia view these fines as a minor, predictable cost of doing business,” Jovanovic said. “When a ruling party controls millions in public budgets, a few thousand euros will not stop them from exploiting state resources to secure votes.”

The state Election Commission imposed unprecedented penalties exceeding 100,000 euros during a single session in Sarajevo on Thursday, heavily targeting major political entities for premature campaigning and abusing public resources ahead of the polls on October 4.

The primary target of Election Commission’s sanctions was the Alliance of Independent Social Democrats, SNSD, the Bosnian Serb ruling party led by Milorad Dodik.

The SNSD, which holds power in Bosnia’s Serb-led entity, Republika Srpska, was directly fined about 41,900 euros, while individual sanctions against its candidates brought the party’s total penalty to 52,700 euros, effectively accounting for over half of the entire session’s fines.

The regulatory body cited multiple severe violations of Bosnia’s Election Law, focusing on the unlawful exploitation of public infrastructure projects for partisan gain and the illegal use of children for political marketing.

Dodik himself was personally fined around 4,600 euros over an Instagram post in which he took direct credit on behalf of his party for taxpayer-funded public works. A member of the state parliament, Sanja Vulic, was fined 4,100 euros for inaccurate media statements and premature campaigning during a television broadcast.

The financial sweep extended beyond the SNSD. The Drasko Stanivukovic – Safe Srpska Movement coalition received the second-highest cumulative penalty, of some 13,000 euros. Following the ruling, Stanivukovic, mayor of Banja Luka, the main city in Republika Srpska, criticised the decision.

“They are fining us simply for doing our jobs and presenting infrastructure projects to the citizens,” Stanivukovic stated to media. “These decisions are rigid and politically targeted to diminish our campaign visibility.”

Other penalised entities included the Social Democratic Party, SDP, which was fined 8,700 euros, and Nedeljko Stevandic’s United Srpska, at 7,200 euros.

Major political entities from Bosnia’s other entity, the Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina, including the Party of Democratic Action, SDA and a five-party Croat coalition, were also hit with financial sanctions.

With voters set to elect the state’s tripartite Presidency and entity parliaments in less than three weeks, the watchdog’s latest financial targeting represents an aggressive institutional effort to enforce compliance in a highly polarized race.

World.title: Greece Mourns Margarita Papandreou, Pioneering Feminist
World.content:
Margarita Papandreou with her three sons Photo: Nikos Papandreou/Facebook.

Greek feminist and author Margarita Papandreou, who was the wife of prime minister and centre-left PASOK party founder Andreas Papandreou, died in Athens on Friday. On September 20, she would have turned 103 years old.

Margarita (Margaret) Chant-Papandreou, originally from the US, studied journalism and pursued postgraduate studies in Public Health. Her name became linked to one of the most prominent political dynasties in Greek history, as well as to a series of significant reforms regarding gender equality.

She was the second wife from 1951 to 1989 of Andreas Papandreou; together they had four children, including former PM George Papandreou and PASOK MEP Nikos Papandreou.

“Margarita Papandreou linked her name to the struggle for women’s rights and social progress,” stated PASOK’s current leader, Nikos Androulakis.

Margarita met Andreas in the US in 1948 and the couple moved to Greece in 1961. Following the military takeover and Andreas’s arrest in 1967, she campaigned for his release. They left Greece for Sweden, and then Canada, returning to Greece after the fall of the military junta in 1974, when Andreas announced the founding of PASOK.

Margarita did not remain in her husband’s shadow; in 1976, alongside other women, she founded the Women’s Union of Greece, a women’s non-profit.

She played a pivotal role in promoting, drafting and passing legislation that improved the social status of Greek women. Key measures included the introduction of civil marriage in 1982, the abolition of the dowry system, the legalisation of divorce by mutual consent, the right of women to retain their maiden names after marriage in 1983, and the legalisation of abortion in 1986.

In her book, Love and Power, she recounted her turbulent relationship with her husband – marked by infidelity, their acrimonious divorce and his subsequent marriage to a younger woman.

Her son, Nikos Papandreou, wrote in the preface: “She may have stood by the side of the Greek politician who transformed Greece – Andreas – but she also created and led the country’s most significant feminist movement, the one that exerted the greatest influence regarding women’s rights in Greece.”

World.title: Turkey Arrests Fund Managers Over Stock Market Manipulation Scandal
World.content:
Turkish authorities arrested four suspects on Friday, including investment fund board members, and imposed travel bans on 51 others, as part of an investigation into alleged manipulation of the stock market, Justice Minister Akin Gurlek announced.

Courts have also imposed precautionary measures on accounts and other assets linked to those under investigation, to prevent their transfer, Gurlek said.

“Those who exploit the sweat, labour and savings of our citizens will be held accountable before the law,” he added.

Turkey’s Capital Markets Board, SPK, has filed criminal complaints about alleged manipulative transactions in several funds and listed shares.

In a separate investigation, a court ordered access blocked to 246 social media accounts accused of publishing speculative material capable of causing fear or panic among investors.

Another investigation by prosecutors in Istanbul’s Bakirkoy District has resulted in 16 arrests over social media posts allegedly intended to manipulate capital markets, Gurlek said.

Turkish Interior Minister Mustafa Ciftci on Thursday said operations related to the stock market investigation would continue, suggesting further action is likely.

On Thursday the SPK ordered the liquidation of 130 funds managed by seven portfolio management companies after liquidity problems contributed to sharp market losses.

Trading on Istanbul Stock Exchange was temporarily suspended on Wednesday after the benchmark BIST 100 index fell by more than 6 per cent, triggering a market-wide circuit breaker.

Estimates of the combined size of the 130 funds differ.

According to Reuters, their assets are worth around 21.4 billion US dollars, involving about 353,000 investors. CNBC-e puts the total at about 19.8 billion US dollars and the number of investors at more than 514,000.

Liquidation does not mean that the investors’ money has been confiscated. Instead, banks are being tasked to deliver citizens’ money in these funds. Is Bank has been appointed to handle the liquidation of funds managed by Tera Portfoy, while state-owned Ziraat Bank will oversee funds belonging to the six other managers.

The proceeds will be distributed to investors according to their holdings. However, investors may not recover the last reported value of their holdings, as the final amount will depend on prices achieved when the assets are sold.

The crisis intensified after regulatory changes targeted risks associated with funds concentrated in thinly traded shares.

“It has been observed that some funds have caused price movements that cannot be explained by the financial realities of companies,” the SPK said on Thursday, adding that the new measures were aimed at preventing market manipulation and increasing transparency.

World.title: Expelled by Greece’s Ruling Party, Ex-PM Samaras Plots His Revenge
World.content:
At the beginning of September, former Greek prime minister Antonis Samaras seized on a newspaper report that users of the online platform of the Greek health service were allowed to specify gender options beyond ‘Male’ and ‘Female’, to include ‘Other’ and ‘Undetermined’.

Samaras was expelled from Greece’s ruling New Democracy party last year, and still bears a grudge.

He promptly took to Facebook to accuse the conservative government of promoting a “woke agenda” and echoed erroneous claims that school textbooks were depicting families with same-sex parents.

“The only thing ‘undetermined’ here is the extent of the ideological shift within the ruling party,” Samaras wrote. Greek families “need support, not redefinition”, he claimed.

World.title: EU Should Not Turn a Blind Eye to Montenegro’s Bloody Clan War
World.content:
When Montenegro declared independence in 2006, it identified EU and NATO integration as its strategic priorities. The country applied for EU membership in 2008, accession negotiations began in 2012, and NATO membership followed in 2017.

Yet, beneath the language of democratisation and Europeanisation lies a far less reassuring reality: a country where rival organised crime clans have waged a conflict for more than a decade, with dozens of people murdered, including innocent bystanders – and where allegations of links between criminal groups, police officers, and senior judicial figures have repeatedly surfaced

The question is not merely why Montenegro has struggled to defeat organised crime. It is why this conflict appears to have become increasingly peripheral to the European Union’s public assessment of the country.

The origins of Montenegro’s interclan war are generally traced to a dispute involving the disappearance of almost 200 kilograms of cocaine in Valencia, Spain, in 2014. What followed was a violent confrontation between two criminal groups based in the coastal town of Kotor – the Kavac and Skaljari clans. Most of the country’s organised crime groups eventually aligned themselves with one of the two rival groups.

Kotor itself became a symbol of the problem. The UNESCO World Heritage Site and historic home of both clans was described by then Interior Minister Goran Danilovic as a “hostage town.” Investigations subsequently alleged the existence of surveillance networks used by criminal gangs and the disclosure of confidential police information to members of the Kavac clan.

World.title: Croatian Prices Rise Once Again in August
World.content:
September the 20th, 2026 – Croatian prices rose once again this August, with restaurants, housing and fuel in particular all climbing up.

The prices of goods and services for personal consumption, measured by the consumer price index, in August 2026 compared to August 2025 (on an annual basis) were on average higher by 4.2%, while compared to July 2026 (on a monthly basis) they were on average higher by 0.4%.

Morski reports that when observed according to the main groups of the ECOICOP classification, ver. 2, on an annual basis, the largest increase in consumer prices on average was recorded in the groups Transport, by 13.5% (contribution to the increase of +1.88 percentage points), Housing, water, electricity, gas and other fuels, by 10.8% (+1.62 percentage points), Restaurants and accommodation services, by 6.1% (+0.34 percentage points), Health, by 5.1% (+0.14 percentage points), Alcoholic beverages and tobacco, by 3.9% (+0.19 percentage points), Insurance services and financial services, by 3.6% (+0.07 percentage points), Personal care, social protection and miscellaneous goods and services, by 2.8% (+0.14 percentage points), Information and communication, by 2.7% (+0.16 percentage points), and Recreation, sport and culture, by 2.4% (+0.09 percentage points). The increase in prices on an annual basis was mitigated by a fall in prices in the groups Clothing and footwear, by 5.1% (contribution to the fall of -0.36 percentage points), Education services, by 2.0% (-0.01 percentage points), Food and non-alcoholic beverages, by 0.6% (-0.16 percentage points), and Furnishings, household equipment and routine household maintenance, by 0.3% (-0.02 percentage points).

According to the main components of the index (special aggregates), an increase in prices on an annual basis was recorded in the components Energy, by 17.6%, Services, by 7.2%, and Food, beverages and tobacco, by 0.1%, while a fall in prices is observed in the component Industrial non-food products excluding energy, by 1.3%. An increase in prices on a monthly basis was recorded in the components Energy, by 3.9%, and Services, by 0.1%, while a fall in prices appeared in the components Industrial non-food products excluding energy, by 0.9%, and Food, beverages and tobacco, by 0.2%.

The prices of goods and services for personal consumption, measured by the harmonised index of consumer prices, in August 2026 compared to August 2025 (on an annual basis) were on average higher by 3.7%. Compared to July 2026 (on a monthly basis) they were on average higher by 0.3%.

World.title: FlixBus Expands Network to 258 Destinations in Croatia
World.content:
September the 20th, 2026 – The popular coach service FlixBus has expanded its already enviable network to 258 destinations in Croatia.

Croatia is an important part of the Flix Europe East region, and Central, Eastern and Southeastern Europe are among the areas with great potential for further development, says Michal Leman from Flix. Sinisa Malus reports for Poslovni that a decade of FlixBus operations in Croatia has now officially been marked. The company began providing services back in 2016 in four Croatian cities and in cooperation with four bus partners, and today in the wider Flix network it has more than 258 connected destinations in Croatia and 390 cities across Europe.

Michal Leman, Vice President Europe East of Flix, emphasises that the anniversary is not only a look back. “Croatia is now entering a new chapter in which we want to further develop domestic and international connectivity, in cooperation with our local partners. Croatia is an important part of the Flix Europe East region, and Central, Eastern and Southeastern Europe are among the areas with great potential for further development.

We therefore see the future not only in new lines, but in even stronger partnerships, better connected markets and a greater number of opportunities for passengers,” Leman says. In the first ten years of operations, FlixBus in Croatia has transported 16.3 million passengers, and the growth of the network is best shown by the connectivity data: the number of direct connections to and from Croatia increased from 375 in 2016 to 4,471 in 2026.

The number of bus partners simultaneously rose from four to 15, while during 2026 FlixBus records an average of around 9,100 departures per month. Today a total of 128 lines operate from and to Croatia. Ten years of development has not meant only an increase in the number of lines and destinations, but above all growth in opportunities for passengers – from a greater choice of destinations and travel times to stronger linking of Croatian cities with neighbouring countries and the rest of Europe.

From the very beginning Croatia, was part of a wider story of regional connectivity. Only a year after entering the Croatian market, in 2017, FlixBus expanded to Bosnia and Herzegovina, Serbia and Slovenia, thereby laying the foundations for stronger connectivity of Central and Southeastern Europe. Flix sees particular potential in Southeastern Europe, where stronger domestic and international connectivity can further bring individual markets closer together, but also better connect them with the rest of the European network.

World.title: The Croatian Bell Tower That Offers Views into Three Countries
World.content:
September the 20th, 2026 – There’s a Croatian bell tower hidden away in an old Istrian town which, on clear days, offers spectacular views into three different countries.

A trip to the gorgeous old settlement of Buje is a perfect combination of history, untouched nature and excellent gastronomy, and nearby are the Momjan castle and the unusual Istrian desert of Piski. Putni kofer/Ivana Vasarevic writes that for all their abundant beauty, very few parts of Croatia look as fairy-tale-like as the interior of Istria. Astonishingly beautiful towns surrounded by untouched nature never cease to delight us, and one of them is certainly Buje. Situated on a fertile hill, in the firm embrace of centuries-old vineyards and olive groves, this Istrian gem was already inhabited in the Bronze Age and today has around 3,000 inhabitants. It is only 13 kilometres from the crystal-clear Adriatic Sea (Umag), and the Slovenian border is also very close.

the guardian of buje

Picchio4ever, Daniele Kovacic – Opera propria

Its ancient population once lived in a fortified hillfort, of which there are as many as about 20 remains in Buje and the surrounding area! A labyrinth of paved streets full of charm will take you to the core of the old town and Freedom Square, where the magnificent Church of St. Servulus and the 15th-century bell tower will greet you. From it, in fine weather, there is a fantastic view of as many as three neighbouring countries: Slovenia, Italy and Austria. This beautiful bell tower is one of the tallest in Istria, and given that it stands at 222 metres above sea level, it was once a lookout and watchtower, so it received the nicknames guardian of the town and watch of Istria. In addition, its image also adorned the town seal from the 13th century.

IT wAS FIRST MENTIONED IN DOCUMENTS AS EARLY AS 981 AS CASTRUM BUGLE

And there is also the bell tower that proudly stands next to the Church of Our Lady of Mercy (St. Mary of Mercy). It dates from the 17th century, is 22 metres high, is adorned with a clock, and at its base there is a characteristic passageway, opposite which is the ethnographic museum. At the same time, in the aforementioned church you can see the sculpture of Our Lady of Mercy, one of the most beautiful wooden statues in Istria. In the Iron Age, the wider area around Buje was inhabited by the Histri, the first documented people to settle on the Istrian peninsula, and the Romans also had their colonies in Terra Magica. In the Middle Ages a fortified medieval town developed, and it is first mentioned in documents, i.e. in a charter of the German-Roman Emperor Otto II, as early as 981 as Castrum Bugle.

THE MAGNIFICENT TOWER wAS ONCE PART OF THE VENETIAN WALLS

At the beginning of the 15th century the entire Buje area came under the rule of the Venetian Republic, and over the next four centuries the magnificent bell tower, the impressive Church of St. Servulus (the town’s patron saint) and the town loggia, which was located on Freedom Square, were built there. To this day, the Tower of St. Martin, which was part of the Venetian walls, has been preserved from that period. And after the fall of the once mighty Venetian empire in 1797, the French, the Austro-Hungarian Monarchy and the Kingdom of Italy successively ruled in Buje. After the end of the Second World War, the town and its surroundings ended up in the Free Territory of Trieste. Its status was settled only in 1954, when it was agreed that the northern part of the Territory, Trieste and the surroundings, would belong to Italy, and the southern part, including Buje, to the then Yugoslavia.

THE ETHNOGRAPHIC MUSEUM iS HOME TO AN OLIVE PROCESSING PLANT AND AN OLD BLACKSMITH’S WORKSHOP

If you find yourself in Buje, also take a look at the aforementioned ethnographic collection in the local museum, which preserves handicrafts of folk material culture from the entire Buje area. It is located in a magnificent four-storey building, and tools, furniture and everything that made up a typical old household, once oriented towards agriculture and ancient crafts, are exhibited in it. Down in the basement, you will find a blacksmith’s workshop and an old olive processing plant, i.e. a press, millstone and stone vessels with wooden lids in which olive oil was stored. Traditional Istrian cuisine and valuable pottery items are exhibited on the first floor, and the greatest attraction of this part of the museum is the hearth, the lifeblood of every Istrian household.

NEARBY LIE THE MEDIEVAL MOMJAN CASTLE AND THE ISTRIAN DESERT OF PISKI

The second and third floors are reserved for a loom and antique carved chests in which clothes and other personal items were kept. In addition to all of the above, the third floor is often used for occasional exhibitions of an ethnographic and historical character. Near Buje are also the picturesque settlement of Momjan with its imposing medieval castle above the Dragonja River and the Istrian desert of Piski, a unique natural phenomenon, i.e. marl dunes, one of the greatest attractions of northwestern Istria that really looks impressive.

tHE HOME OF BEER MISU!

Momjan – Fraxinus Croat

And after sightseeing this magical little town, it is time to explore the wine and olive oil roads of the Buje area. Enjoy the delicious Istrian cuisine and excellent wines, but also the excellent local beer that has been produced since 2013 at the San Servolo brewery in Buje. Only four ingredients are responsible for its perfect taste: barley malt, hops, yeast and natural water from the St. John spring, which is located in the valley of the Mirna River. In the pub you can also taste dishes such as beer soup or beer misu.

World.title: Croatian Military Special Forces Take 1st Place at FPV Drone Pilots Competition
World.content:
September the 20th, 2026 – Croatian military special forces have won 1st place at an international FPV drone pilots competition.

Members of the Croatian Special Forces Command of the Armed Forces recently won first place at the international military competition for FPV drone pilots in the TACTICAL category. Morski reports that this win means they have achieved an outstanding result in competition with international military teams.

The competition was held from the 13th to the 18th of September at the Royal Military Academy Sandhurst in the UK. Called the international military competition for FPV drone pilots “British Army Tactical Drone Competition – BADCT and Military International Drone Racing Tournament – MIDRT”, the Croatian team certainly wowed. Croatia was represented at the competition by members of the Special Forces Command of the Croatian Armed Forces who, thanks to an exceptional level of training, professionalism and teamwork, won first place in the TACTICAL category. Second place was taken by Ukraine, while Germany came third.

an extremely demanding competition

The competition brought together more than 80 competitors, members of the armed forces from several countries, and during the multi-day programme the participants demonstrated a high level of knowledge and skills in controlling FPV drones. In the first part of the competition, a contest in the tactical use of drones was held, which included an obstacle course, dropping a bomb with a drone and intercepting another aircraft in the air, in which the members of the Special Forces Command achieved an enviable result in an international military environment. The continuation of the competition included FPV drone races.

In addition to Croatia, Ukraine and Germany, representatives of Australia, Australian cadets, the United States of America, the United Kingdom, American veterans, New Zealand, Sweden and France also took part in the competition. This result represents significant recognition for the members of the Special Forces Command of the Croatian Armed Forces and confirms their knowledge, skills and ability to apply modern technology in a demanding international environment.

World.title: If Government Fails to Intervene, Croatia’s Most Expensive Diesel is Coming
World.content:
September the 19th, 2026 – If the government fails to intervene, then Croatia’s most expensive diesel so far is on its way next week.

From next Tuesday, drivers at petrol stations could be met with higher fuel prices. Index reports that according to what currently remains unofficial information, all types of fuel are becoming more expensive, and diesel could reach a historic high in Croatia. These are the prices that will apply if the government fails to properly intervene, reports RTL.

expected price increases

If there is no government intervention, the price of a litre of eurosuper should rise by one cent and amount to €1.74. Eurodiesel would become more expensive by ten cents, so its new price would be €1.95 per litre. The largest price increase is expected for blue diesel, which should rise by 11 cents to €1.51.

historic highs for diesel…

If the government does not make a different decision, the diesel price of €1.95 per litre would be the highest recorded in Croatia’s history. Until now Croatia has had some of the lower fuel prices in Europe, but that could change from next week.

why are diesel and oil prices rising like this?

The background to the new blow to drivers’ pockets lies in the global disruptions caused by the US war against Iran, which has been shaking the world energy market for months. The situation escalated further after drone attacks on the Saudi East-West oil pipeline, a key alternative route for transporting crude oil after navigation through the Strait of Hormuz became unsafe. As a result, Brent crude prices jumped above $100 a barrel, and some deliveries in Europe exceeded $120.

As energy expert Davor Štern warned, the price increases are not only a consequence of a physical shortage of fuel, but primarily of stock-market speculation. “We follow the markets, and the markets do what they do. The exchanges have again returned to their traditional bookmaking methods – it is not so much a real shortage of diesel as expectations that there will not be enough of it that have driven the price up,” Štern explained.

the croatian government’s hands are tied…

On whether the state even has mechanisms with which it could stop this rise, Professor Marijana Ivanov from the Department of Finance at the Faculty of Economics in Zagreb spoke for Index. She warns that the geopolitical circumstances are extremely unfavourable and that the Government is running out of instruments with which it could cushion new blows.

“I think the room for preventing a further rise in fuel prices is quite limited. With excise duties there is almost none, especially with diesel, while with petrol it is also very narrow,” Ivanov points out. Although cutting the VAT rate is often mentioned in public, the economist considers that this would not be a good move: “In principle it is possible to reduce VAT on fuel, but I would not suggest it because public finances are already under pressure from the risk of a larger deficit. A third option would be further cutting of distributors’ margins, but we know that even at these levels they have become unsustainable for small traders.”

World.title: Will Croatia Have Enough Energy Capacities to Match Consumption Growth?
World.content:
September the 19th, 2026 – Will Croatia have enough energy capacities for both the general public and for the economy as consumption increases?

Experts keep on emphasising that without a stronger electricity grid and larger energy storage capacities it will not be possible to keep up with the growth in consumption. The question in many minds now is whether or not Croatia will have enough energy capacities for the economy, the public and new industry, and at competitive prices? Poslovni reports that this was one of the key questions at the ENERGREEN – Energy Security of Croatia 2027 conference.

The focus was primarily placed on the security of gas supply, the LNG terminal on Krk and the Okoli storage facility, as well as the accelerated development of solar and wind power plants, as reported by HRT. Experts emphasise that without a stronger electricity grid and larger energy storage capacities it will not be possible to keep up with the growth in consumption. When it comes to heating, people have no reason to worry. “Croatia has a relatively good energy situation due to its geostrategic position, and the country is home to an LNG terminal, storage, and good transport infrastructure, which means that we will always have enough gas, because now we’re no longer last in line but first,” explained Dalibor Pudić, president of the Croatian Professional Gas Association.

“As you’ve already seen, the 11th package of measures has also been adopted. The government is very much continuing to protect the general public and the concrete economy; in addition, there is also supply stability through certain measures, limiting retail fuel prices, and supply stability is also ensured through the filling of gas storage facilities,” concluded Željko Krevzelj, director of the Energy Directorate at the Ministry of the Economy.

World.title: Renovated University Campus Worth Over €50 Million Opens in Zagreb
World.content:
September the 19th, 2026 – A newly renovated university campus worth over €50 million has opened as part of FER in Zagreb.

After two years of extensive works, Buildings B and C of the campus of the Faculty of Electrical Engineering and Computing of the University of Zagreb (FER) were solemnly opened. The complete renovation amounting to €50 million excluding VAT was co-financed with European Union funds from the Solidarity Fund and the Recovery and Resilience Facility. Poslovni reports that this concerns an area spanning 18,000 square metres in Unska Street that includes five modern amphitheatre lecture halls with a capacity of 900 seats, 153 office rooms and 26 classrooms and laboratories for teaching. The newly opened FER premises were visited by representatives of the state leadership, the City of Zagreb, the University of Zagreb and prominent entrepreneurs, members of the Faculty’s Alumni Board.

FER Dean Prof. Vedran Bilas, PhD, said that the investment in the renovation is the initial phase of the campus development, which was last expanded at the end of the 1980s, when the faculty had almost half as many employees, fewer study programmes and many times fewer research projects than today.

“Generations of professors and students before us built this institution, its competences, significance and values. FER is a synonym of excellence in the Croatian public, academic and business community. This renovation and this ceremony are stations on a path that continues. The Faculty has an experienced and proven team and capacity for the implementation of complex infrastructure projects, ready to continue cooperation with the Ministry of Science, Education and Youth on campus development projects,” Bilas said and announced a new spatial expansion: “The Government of the Republic of Croatia, through a Loan Agreement with the World Bank, is financing the preparation of the main project for the reconstruction of Building A, which will be completed by the end of this year. The reconstructed building will have three underground and nine above-ground floors, five more than now.”

Prime Minister Andrej Plenković praised the Faculty’s results and emphasised its contribution to society.

“By renovating these buildings we aren’t investing merely in space, but in Croatia’s ability to understand, shape and lead the technological changes that in the decades ahead will determine the economic strength, security and technological independence of states. FER is one of the central places where Croatia creates knowledge for the digital age, and we count on its professors, researchers and students also in responding to the challenges of artificial intelligence, cyber security and quantum computing. Our vision is clear: Croatia must not be only a user of other people’s technology, but must develop and export its own high value-added solutions,” said Prime Minister Plenković.

“Through patient work, persistence and joint action we have arrived at a result that benefits our teachers and those most important for our future, and that is our students. I believe that the Faculty in the renovated premises will develop new visions and continue to lead in the IT sector and digital transformation, recognising what society and the state need,” said Rector of the University of Zagreb, Prof. Stjepan Lakušić, PhD.

The FER team responsible for the implementation of the renovation guided representatives of the Government, Prime Minister Plenković, Minister of Construction and State Property Branko Bačić, Minister of the Economy Ante Šušnjar and other high-ranking guests through the newly renovated premises, and the tour ended on the 13th floor with a spectacular panoramic view of the whole of Zagreb. The contractor for the extensive works was the construction company TROMONT d.o.o., and a complete energy, fire-protection and multimedia renovation was carried out.

The programme and celebration of the opening will continue in the afternoon. From 18:00 a parking party for friends, fellow citizens and neighbours is planned on the FER car park in Unska Street, with musicians Duška Brčić, Vjeko Ključarić, Filip Rudan, young up-and-coming bands and the Disco section of KSET.

World.title: “Forever Chemicals” Found in Lika Water Following Waste Scandal
World.content:
September the 19th, 2026 – So-called “forever chemicals” have unfortunately been found in Lika water following the shameful hazardous waste scandal.

The Croatian Institute of Public Health (HZJZ) and the Public Health Institute of Lika-Senj County have published the results of extraordinary water sampling in the Lika area. Index reports that the results have revealed that dangerous PFAS compounds, so-called “forever chemicals,” were found in two private wells downstream from an illegal waste dump near Gospić, but they assure the public that the pollution is exclusively of a local character and that water from the public water supply is not endangered.

the chemicals were found in two wells near the illegal waste dump

According to the HZJZ statement, from the 20th of August to the 9th of September water was sampled from 43 private facilities – 38 wells, three cisterns and two springs. The Institute states that in one well in the immediate vicinity of the dump a concentration of PFAS compounds of 0.3018 µg/L was recorded, which is three times higher than the maximum permitted limit of 0.1 µg/L. In the second well 0.0265 µg/L was measured, which is within the permitted limits. HZJZ claims that the owners of the disputed wells are connected to the public water supply and do not use that water for drinking. As for the other findings, the Institute claims that in 33 facilities only “usual microbiological pollution characteristic of untreated water” was recorded, while elevated physical-chemical values in a further 10 samples are attributed to the natural properties of the karst, and not to the dumped waste.

the people of lika feel betrayed by the government

The statement comes at a moment when the scandal surrounding the illegal burial of as many as 37,000 tonnes of hazardous waste in Divoselo and Benkovačko Selo near Gospić has grown into a first-class political scandal. HZJZ Director Krunoslav Capak personally sits on the newly established Scientific Council of Prime Minister Andrej Plenković, a body that the government formed precisely with the aim of “correctly interpreting” in public the dramatic findings of the USKOK investigation into the pollution of soil and waters in Lika. The documents that Plenković’s Scientific Council is supposed to put into the “correct context” were signed by authorised institutions and are quite exact.

The expert examination by the “Josip Juraj Strossmayer” Water Institute for the Divoselo location established that the water passing immediately under the dump carries 89 percent of the total detected plastic, while upstream it is clean. 737 micrograms of Styrofoam per litre were measured, and the presence of Teflon from the group of “forever chemicals” (PFAS) was also recorded, with the expert’s note that the Lika River is a directly connected water body.

the prime minister is at the council’s helm

Although formally composed of professors from technical and natural science faculties, the Council has been placed under the direct authority of the Prime Minister. According to the government decision, the sessions are convened and chaired by Plenković himself, operational tasks are carried out by his office, and there are no prescribed obligations for the publication of minutes, expert conclusions or any dissenting opinions of members. The entire manoeuvre of forming the Council is taking place at a time when the remediation is only being prepared, and political pressure on the ruling party is growing after a mass protest in Zagreb and a drop in HDZ’s rating.

is there any real reason to panic?

Despite this, HZJZ persists in the claim that there is no reason for panic. They state that the fact that such compounds were not found in other wells across the county proves that it is “pollution of a local character in a narrower circle.” They also repeat that private wells in any case do not fall under regular state supervision and that the responsibility lies with the owners themselves. The Institute finally states that all regular tests confirm that water from the public water supply in the entire Lika-Senj County area, as well as on the islands of Pag and Rab, is completely health-safe and that they will continue monitoring the situation on the ground.

World.title: Estonia's defense agency takes Datasel dispute to Swiss arbitration
World.content:
The disputes are being heard under the rules of the International Chamber of Commerce (ICC), according to ERR's information. The RKIK has taken disputes over several contracts to international arbitration, with one joint contract dispute before Harju County Court — together worth a reported €59.8 million.

"Arbitration fees alone — the fees ultimately paid to the arbitrators and the arbitration institution for administering the proceedings — amount to hundreds of thousands," said lawyer Paul Keres, who is among the arbitrators representing Estonia at the ICC. Experts and lawyers' fees will add significantly more, he added, though the payoff is a faster and more specialized decision.

Keres said Swiss arbitration was a good choice. "Swiss arbitration is by no means a bad option: they are efficient and very good. I have been there myself, and everything is very well organized," he said.

Keres said taking disputes to arbitration is as yet not particularly common in Estonia.

Paul Keres. Source: Ken Mürk/ERR

"It is not as common as in some countries that have enjoyed democracy for longer. But there are more and more of these disputes, and they are becoming bigger and more interesting. Estonia is also gaining more representatives who know arbitration proceedings and are competent in the field. So I think we are moving in the right direction," Keres said.

Contracts often name the court in advance; without such a clause, cases go where the defendant is based. Datasel is incorporated in Italy, though its owners are Indian.

"What may cause confusion is who the owners are. If it is an SRL, I believe it is still an Italian company registered in Italy — by that logic, the case would have to be brought in Italy. But if it is an Indian company, you would have to go to India. I am glad for my colleagues that they do not have to deal with it. It is so confusing and fragmented, really very complicated," Keres said.

According to Keres, a case can end up in arbitration in two ways: "Firstly, it may have been agreed in advance — the contract contains a separate arbitration clause stipulating that the parties will resolve their dispute through arbitration. A proper arbitration agreement also specifies where the arbitration will take place, which institution will administer it, how many arbitrators there will be, and so on. Secondly, it is also possible to reach such agreements after a dispute has arisen. The contract may not provide for arbitration but, for example, for the jurisdiction of an ordinary court, yet the parties may decide that, for whatever reason, it would be more practical to resolve the dispute outside the courts, usually through arbitration," Keres explained, adding that an arbitrary award has the same legal force and is just as binding and enforceable as an ordinary court judgment.

RKIK signage. Source: Ken Mürk/ERR

"There are simply elements of speed and perhaps specialization that may persuade the parties that arbitration makes more sense," Keres said.

"Usually, the parties have greater control over the proceedings, starting with who adjudicates the case — they can choose the arbitrators themselves. The course of the proceedings is more under the parties' control, generally confidential and usually faster than national courts. In addition, some institutions that administer arbitration, such as the ICC, offer particularly strong supervision and intensive review of drafted awards," Keres said.

This review ensures the award is well reasoned, logical and free of errors, and cannot later be challenged even on the narrow grounds on which arbitrary awards may be contested.

Keres declined to speculate on the outcome: "It could turn out that the Estonian state has to pay additional money, or it could turn out that the advance payment is recovered. Both sides have filed claims: there is a claim and a counterclaim."

Background

Datasel, an Italian firm acquired in 2024 by Indian-owned Neco Defense Munitions, signed four contracts with RKIK to supply artillery shells for Ukraine with roughly €70 million paid up front, but delayed and substandard deliveries led the RKIK to terminate the agreements and pursue legal action; none of the ammunition reached Ukraine.

The RKIK has now rejected Datasel's proposal for a joint working group, saying the European Peace Facility funding period has expired and it has no budgetary resources to accept further ammunition, while Datasel's lawyer insists the company has the resources and supply chain to fulfill its obligations — the two sides also remain at odds over whether the terminations were valid.

The fallout contributed to Defense Minister Hanno Pevkur's resignation on September 2, alongside wider accounting and oversight problems at the Defense Forces.

Auditor General Janar Holm said the defense scandals pose no security threat and that open discussion makes Estonia stronger, but warned several problems are systemic and money flowing into the sector is increasing confusion.

World.title: Giant pumpkin, 14kg cabbage draw 20,000 to Paunvere fair
World.content:
A 53-kilogram pumpkin and a cabbage weighing 14 kilograms were among the attractions as the Paunvere exhibition, in Jõgeva County over the weekend.

The fair, held for the 27th time, showcased giant and unusual vegetables, while growers reported a mixed year shaped by weather and cheap imports. and fair drew 20,000 people to Palamuse, population around 550.

The most interesting exhibits were the unusual, strange or giant vegetables. The 53-kilogram giant pumpkin was on display at the Palamuse cuteness contest. According to its owner, growing a winter squash of these proportions requires not only rich soil but also a lot of love.

"You still have to go and pet it, water it. It won't grow weeds, because the pumpkin is so big. But especially cabbage, because cabbage worms are so industrious," said Toomas Puusepp, cultivator of the giant pumpkin.

His giant fruits — a 53-kilogram and a 42-kilogram pumpkin and a 14-kilogram cabbage — arrived at the exhibition on a lawn tractor. The oversized produce found new homes at the fair's auction.

While some real giants could be seen in the "cute tent" (Nunnutelk), this year's vegetable harvest offered mixed feelings for gardeners.

"You can't complain. Compared to last year, we had quite a harvest this year. Everything grew. I could complain about today's sale, there aren't as many people as there have been in previous years," said vegetable grower Tatjana.

However, cool and rainy spring weather almost completely ruined the open-field cucumber and tomato harvest, while the marketing of domestic vegetables is being made more difficult by cheaper imported goods.

"The year was not very productive. There are half as many cucumbers as last year. While we used to pick 300 kilos of cucumbers in the spring, now we only take a total of 300 kilos to Tartu stores. Previously, we took 300 kilos to one store and 300 kilos to another," said vegetable grower Igor.

Meanwhile, a more exotic fruit managed to defy the local cold. Southern Estonian watermelon grower Raimo harvested a whopping four tons of watermelon.

"We grow them in the open field, so that we have them under plastic and in the spring you bury them beautifully with a covering and keep them warm and under a blanket like you would yourself, and that's how they grow," he said.

The Paunvere exhibition was held for the 27th time.

World.title: Attempted kidnapping in Tallinn of Australian tech billionaire was hatched in Moscow
World.content:
A 2024 plan to kidnap Australian-born IT billionaire in Tallinn's Old Town was hatched in Moscow, Eesti Ekspress reported .

In july 2024 men were sent to Estonia to abduct Yolo Group founder Tim Heath as he entered his home on Rataskaevu, posing as painters to attack him in the stairwell.

The gang intended to force him into a van and drive him to a rented sauna house near Kakerdaja bog, around 60 kilometers from Tallinn, where they would have demanded the keys to his cryptocurrency wallet.

Heath resisted forcefully, something which caught the assailants by surprise, and they fled without him; first to Riga and then further afield.

On Thursday, Harju County Court convicted Oleg Marco, one of the attackers, after he agreed to a seven-year prison sentence under a plea bargain.

Marco, from Moldova, was brought from prison to the hearing wearing a T-shirt reading the slogan "Never give up."

His accomplices had already been convicted: Azerbaijani Allahverdi Allahverdiyev received seven and a half years, and Georgian citizen Ilgar Mamedov eight years and nine months.

The fourth member of the gang, Azerbaijani Najaf Najafli, led the kidnapping attempt but will not stand trial in Estonia as Azerbaijan does not extradite its citizens.

Questioned by Azerbaijani authorities, Najafli said he became involved because of debts, was deployed to Tallinn by a Chechen figure in Moscow's criminal underworld, and while he realized something was not right, he was in too deep to refuse.

The gang had reportedly used well-known platforms to rent accommodation and transport, making tracking them down easier.

Heath, 48, arrived in Estonia in the early 2000s, built the IT company Yolo Group from scratch, and has been estimated by Australian business media to be worth €1.4 billion

World.title: International interest mounts in Estonian scientists' drug-detection meter
World.content:
Researchers in Estonia have developed a portable drug analyzer that can identify both the substance taken and the amount, returning results in as little as 15 minutes.

Developers at Tallinn University of Technology (TalTech) and startup SafePAS say the "Narcometer" device has drawn international interest, and they now aim to make it smaller and drug detection as easy as a breathalyzer test.

When police or ambulance crews need to determine possible drug intoxication at the scene, they currently rely primarily on rapid tests, but whose accuracy often leaves much to be desired. To determine the exact substance present in a sample and its quantity, positive samples need to be sent to the lab for further testing. However, it can sometimes take days to receive those lab results.

If police can find time for additional testing as part of investigative procedures, every minute counts when assessing a person's medical condition. This is particularly important with substances that break down rapidly in the body, for example GHB, commonly known as a date-rape drug.

TalTech researchers and the startup SafePAS have for more than a decade now been developing an analytical device with the English name Drug Hunter, whose aim is to take accurate and rapid drug testing beyond the laboratory. The researchers' analyzer can identify both a narcotic substance and its quantity in just about 15 minutes.

Up to now now, the tech has been tested in close cooperation with the Police and Border Guard Board (PPA), but this summer the team also worked with organizers of major events, such as festivals. According to Jekaterina Mazina-Šinkar, an assistant professor at TalTech and the SafePAS founder, the aim was to understand how the device could be used by private individuals themselves. "A saliva test can be carried out on people who, for example, suspect that a narcotic substance has been put into their cocktail. Or someone may have taken something and feel very unwell but not know what it was," the researcher explained.

SafePAS co-founder Jelena Gorbatšova and older and newer versions of Drug Hunter. Source: Jekaterina Mazina-Šinkar

An ever-changing black market

The device uses capillary electrophoresis technology, which is also used to analyze DNA. "This is a very sensitive method in which we first separate all the substances present in the sample, excite them and detect them with a detector. We then not only identify the substance but also quantify it," Mazina-Šinkar, said, describing how the device works. Positive samples will always undergo additional testing under laboratory conditions too, she noted.

Drug Hunter can at present detect common narcotic substances such as cocaine, amphetamine, methamphetamine and MDMA (ecstasy). The device can also identify tramadol, codeine and morphine, as well as THC.

However, the prevalence of narcotic substances varies considerably by time and place, meaning researchers must constantly keep up with developments on the illicit drugs market. "Research is underway into new narcotic substances, their metabolism and how they can subsequently be detected in the human body. At the same time, so-called classic drugs account for 97 percent of all cases of use, while only three percent involve new narcotic substances," Mazina-Šinkar noted.

The Drug Hunter device tested at festivals and in the course of traffic enforcement is about the size of a computer printer. A year ago, however, the development team received €2.5 million in funding from the Estonian Business and Innovation Agency (EIS) to make the device more compact. The next-generation model, which was tested for the first time in August this year, is already down to about the size of a shoebox.

"The biggest challenge is not simply making the device smaller, but ensuring the reliability of the final result. We tested not only the technology, which we already know works, but also the analyzer's ease of use. We looked for aspects that could be further improved or simplified," Mazina-Šinkar went on.

The next generation Drug Hunter device is considerably smaller than its predecessor. Source: Jekaterina Mazina-Šinkar

From lab to international market

The TalTech researchers say their next goal is to render drug detection as simple and reliable as using a conventional alcohol breathalyzer is today. "Technologically, we are already quite close to that, but a distinction has to be made between the technology itself and its official adoption," the researcher said, stressing the role of legislation.

She also noted that greater complexity lies behind even the humble breathalyzer.

"When we think of a breathalyzer, it seems a very simple thing to us today: a person blows into it, the device displays a number and a decision can be made based on that. In reality, this is backed by decades of scientific knowledge and established threshold values. With narcotic substances, it is even more complex because there are different substances with different effects, metabolism and concentrations," she added

All this means that when entering foreign markets, the device's parameters must be adapted precisely to local laws and threshold values in force in the target country. There is, in any case, undoubtedly international demand for fast and reliable analysis. Over the past year, SafePAS has shared its experience with police in England, forensic experts in Germany, and experts in Spain and the Czech Republic. According to Mazina-Šinkar, bringing a research-intensive device out of the lab and into practical use has provided important lessons. "A good scientific result is not yet a finished product," she said, summing up more than a decade of development work. While researchers always seek maximum sensitivity and accuracy, end users are primarily concerned with maintenance, speed of analysis and reliability, she noted.

"Our goal is not simply to bring out yet another rapid test," Mazina-Šinkar stressed. "Our goal is to bring reliable instrumental measurement out of the laboratory and directly to where decisions need to be made."

World.title: Foreign Minister: Russia's State Duma elections a 'political performance'
World.content:
Tsahkna said the ongoing elections have been neither free nor fair and had the sole purpose of consolidating Vladimir Putin's grip on power.

"The Kremlin imposed particularly severe restrictions on the opposition and its supporters ahead of these elections," Tsahkna noted. He said candidates deemed unacceptable by the regime, and critics of Russia's war against Ukraine, were excluded from political competition, with distorted registration requirements, administrative measures and criminal prosecutions used to that end.

Tsahkna cited the banning from running of Yabloko, the only registered party running on a peace platform, as "a telling example of the Kremlin's determination to cling to its monopoly on power."

The minister said the absence of independent international observers, alongside growing repression and systematic suppression of the opposition, meant "this political performance orchestrated by Putin bears no resemblance to free elections." He described it as "yet another ritual intended to reaffirm and prolong Putin's rule."

Minister of Foreign Affairs Margus Tsahkna (Eesti 200). Source: Priit Mürk/ERR

Tsahkna also condemned the holding of elections in Ukrainian territories illegally occupied by Russia: Crimea and the Donetsk, Luhansk, Zaporizhzhia and Kherson oblasts. The minister noted this constitutes a clear violation of international law and of Ukraine's sovereignty and territorial integrity.

"Through these so-called elections, Russia seeks to legitimize its illegal occupation policy and create a legal basis for extending its jurisdiction in Ukraine," Tsahkna said. He said Estonia unequivocally condemns this and is working to ensure the organization of elections in occupied Ukrainian territory is met with clear international consequences.

Tsahkna reiterated Estonia's support for Ukraine's independence, sovereignty and territorial integrity.

Ukraine launched what Moscow's mayor called the biggest ever drone attack on the Russian capital on Sunday, but the Kremlin said the attempt to disrupt the final day of a parliamentary election had failed. The State Duma vote, the first since the full-scale invasion of Ukraine started in 2022, is expected to see Putin's party, United Russia ,retain its dominance in a system critics say does not tolerate dissent, with most anti-war candidates barred from the ballot. Putin has cast the election as a test of public support for the war, and is likely to present the outcome as evidence of national unity.

World.title: Estonia's Niina Petrõkina wins Bergamo figure skating round
World.content:
Two-time European figure skating champion Niina Petrõkina took first place at the ISU Challenger event in Bergamo, Italy.

Petrõkina improved her personal best by nearly seven points in the short program to take the lead, then finished second in Saturday's free skate with 133.21 points. She attempted the quadruple jump she has added to her program this season but could not land it, and also made a small mistake on a triple lutz. Her personal best remains 145.53, set at the European Championships earlier this year.

South Korea's Shin Ji-a won the free skate, scoring 1.12 points more than Petrõkina, while Lara Naki Gutmann finished third on 132.14 in front of her home crowd.

Petrõkina won the competition with a combined 210.41 points, just under six short of her personal best. Ji-a took second with 209.26 and Gutmann third with 202.74.

Of other Estonian competitors, Maria Eliise Kaljuvere was fourth after the short program and scored 94.32 in the free skate, placing tenth in that segment and ninth overall with 157.84 points.

In the men's singles, Mihhail Selevko leads after the short program with 91.09 points, with the free skate to follow on Sunday afternoon.

World.title: Estonian experts say social media should be improved for children instead of banned
World.content:
The European Union is discussing a safe‑internet regulation that includes several restrictions planned for minors' use of social media. While EU plans propose setting a minimum age of 13, Estonian social scientists argue that blunt bans will not solve all problems and may even create new ones.

Tallinn University media professor Indrek Ibrus is critical of the EU initiative, saying the planned restrictions conflict with children's fundamental rights.

"In my opinion, it's generally a pretty bad idea," Ibrus said, explaining that it ignores the UN Convention on the Rights of the Child. "Children must have opportunities for self‑expression and free access to information to support their development and identity. Any age‑based restriction on access to information essentially disregards children's rights," Ibrus said.

According to Ibrus, the European Commission is effectively giving up by proposing restrictions.

Indrek Ibrus. Source: Siim Lõvi /ERR

"Instead of working on these environments, these platforms, these spaces in a way that would make them safe and suitable for children, the European Commission throws up its hands and gives up. They don't have the strength to deal with regulation, even though the regulatory framework — the Digital Services Act — already exists and simply needs to be enforced. In a sense, children are being sacrificed because of the Commission's own inability," he said.

University of Tartu media studies professor Andra Siibak agreed that relying solely on bans and restrictions is not the best solution, highlighting the need to change platform business models. Siibak said it is positive that the EU demands concrete measures from service providers to make platforms more protective of children's rights, well‑being and privacy.

Like Ibrus, Siibak pointed out that all these recommended changes are already written into earlier EU regulations — whether the Digital Services Act or the AI Act. "The European Union itself must start thinking carefully about how to demand these changes from platforms and monitor that they actually implement them," Siibak said.

Andra Siibak Autor/allikas: ERR/Lauri Varik

Tallinn University participation‑culture professor Katrin Tiidenberg warned against overly rigid bans, citing Australia's experience.

"Based on what we know from Australia and how their ban doesn't actually work, children under 16 are still online, which mainly means we don't know what they're doing on social media or where they're logged in," Tiidenberg said.

One of the biggest questions surrounding the EU Kids Act is how to verify users' ages without massively violating people's privacy.

Ibrus sees major risks in age verification. "It may be a direct privacy intrusion, and it may also be harmful in the sense that platforms could use identification for more precise profiling of users, which can be dangerous in several ways," he explained.

Ibrus added that although the EU is developing a digital wallet solution that could provide secure infrastructure in the future, any restrictions must be approached with extreme caution.

Siibak also noted that finding a reliable and transparent age‑verification method is currently difficult. Attempts with facial‑recognition software have not worked, and young people easily bypass restrictions using, for example, their parents' documents.

"We know from Australia's experience how skillfully young people bypass such age‑assessment apps and solutions. To access a platform, they show their parents' documents or take a photo with a famous footballer's poster in the background instead of showing their own face. Young people certainly have many ways to get around such systems. Finding a method acceptable to all member states will be a very difficult discussion," Siibak said.

Katrin Tiidenberg Autor/allikas: Priit Mürk/ERR

Tiidenberg also stressed that mechanical age‑verification methods bring risks. "It's a very important issue, because if it means a child must log in with an ID card, then it means everyone must log in with an ID card. We want to avoid mass surveillance and monitoring of which sites we visit and who does what. In my view, maintaining freedom is important," Tiidenberg said.

"That doesn't mean age verification cannot be done in a reasonably safe way, but the method must be developed very carefully and not by quickly trusting the first private company that says: 'Look, I built you a solution,'" Tiidenberg said.

Experts say protecting children and young people on social media should focus on improving the platforms themselves.

Tiidenberg highlighted the need to pressure platforms to create well‑being‑oriented and responsible design. This means placing strong emphasis on curbing addictive algorithms — for example, giving users the option to choose between a chronological feed and recommendation algorithms. She also supports separate child‑ and youth‑friendly accounts (for example, ages 13–15) where harmful content is automatically limited.

Ibrus reminded that in addition to tightening rules, it is important to support young people's digital skills and critical thinking instead of creating artificial barriers that do not actually protect them online.

"Instead of bluntly banning communication environments because they may involve certain risks, those risks must be addressed. Platforms must be adapted, regulated, existing regulations enforced, and at the same time media literacy must be developed for different age and social groups," Ibrus said.

Tiidenberg added that digital skills are important, but a person can be both competent and helpless at the same time — including children.

"Critical awareness is very important, but obviously children have different self‑regulation abilities at different ages. Even many adults do not have very good self‑regulation. You may know something is harmful to you, but you still may not be able to avoid certain social media content," she said.

"Skills are important — they are part of the toolkit — but they are not enough if we allow user interfaces to be designed manipulatively, because they still measure the user's slowing finger while scrolling. If we do not regulate how quickly systems must respond when I say that I or my child does not want to see certain content, then digital skills alone are of little use," Tiidenberg added.

On Thursday, the European Commission adopted the safe‑internet regulation (EU Kids Act), which increases children's online safety in the EU. The package includes proposals to ban social media use for children under 13 and to require companies providing online services to create safe accounts for children.

Under the proposal — which EU member states and the European Parliament will negotiate — accounts for children aged 13–15 would be under parental control.

Social media and video services, online games and AI‑based companions and chatbots intended for users under 18 would be subject to a list of permitted and prohibited activities.

World.title: Reintroduced dormice face a fox that moved to predator‑free island
World.content:
The garden dormice released on Suur‑Pakri Island this summer to rewild the species have encountered an unexpected co‑inhabitant who may consider the newcomers gourmet food.

The garden dormouse (Eliomys quercinus), a native Estonian species, went extinct in Estonia due to human activity. The exact cause is unknown. The last wild garden dormouse was seen in 1986. Around the same time, the species disappeared from neighboring countries as well. This summer, the first small colony was released on Suur‑Pakri Island.

"When we last left the island a couple of weeks ago, more than half of the 20 animals released were definitely alive. For a small zoo animal, that's a surprisingly good result. We're optimistic that maybe they'll even survive until spring," said ecologist Marko Mägi.

"Since it's a small animal with a very short lifespan and could end up in a predator's jaws during winter — even though it sleeps through winter — we don't know whether any of them will still see daylight in spring," Mägi noted.

Suur‑Pakri was chosen for reintroduction because it lacked predators.

"Last autumn we carried out control surveys and studied small mammals to determine whether the island was safe for garden dormice. At that time we could say there were no predators that would threaten them. We had a very harsh winter that covered the sea with ice, and a fox easily crossed over to the island," Mägi explained.

"This summer we discovered that a fox is indeed on the island. We saw it on trail cameras, and it was also spotted running through the forest. Now we're curious to see what happens by spring: will the fox win, or the garden dormice?"

"Although the garden dormouse is active at night and gladly climbs trees, where a fox cannot reach, their paths may still cross. But fortunately for the dormice, the island has plenty of other small rodents that interest the fox more. For the fox, the garden dormouse would be a true gourmet meal," Mägi said.
